Abstract:
Material Extrusion-Based Additive Manufacturing Process (ME-AMP) via Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) offers a higher geometric flexibility than conventional technologies to fabricate thermoplastic lightweight sandwich structures. This study used polylactic acid/polyhydroxyalkanoate (PLA/PHA) biodegradable material and a 3D printer to manufacture lightweight sandwich structures with honeycomb, diamond-celled and corrugated core shapes as a single part. In this paper, compression, three-point bending and tensile tests were performed to evaluate the performance of lightweight sandwich structures with different core topologies. In addition, the main failure modes of the sandwich structures subjected to mechanical tests were evaluated. The main failure modes that were observed from mechanical tests of the sandwich structure were the following: face yielding, face wrinkling, core/skin debonding. Elasto-plastic finite element analysis allowed predicting the global behavior of the structure and stressing distribution in the elements of lightweight sandwich structures. The comparison between the results of bending experiments and finite element analyses indicated acceptable similarity in terms of failure behavior and force reactions. Finally, the three honeycomb, diamond-celled and corrugated core typologies were used in the leading edge of the wing and were impact tested and the results created favorable premises for using such structures on aircraft models and helicopter blade structures.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing has emerged as a promising technology to fabricate customized polymer parts, but the mechanical performance of printed components often falls short of bulk material properties. Among the different techniques, fused filament fabrication is the most accessible and widely adopted. However, previous studies addressing its processing parameters have produced fragmented or contradictory conclusions, limiting the ability to establish guidelines for mechanical optimization. This work addresses this gap by systematically investigating the influence of key parameters—extrusion temperature, printing speed, infill type and density, layer height, and number of walls—on the tensile properties of three commonly used thermoplastics: PLA, ABS, and PETG. A total of 495 standardized specimens were produced and tested under controlled conditions. The results demonstrate that increasing infill density and wall number consistently enhances tensile strength, with PLA showing an improvement of 1173 N when infill was raised from 20 to 80%, and PETG doubling its strength from 559 N with one wall to 1207 N with five walls. Layer height also had a positive effect, with PLA rising from 995 N at 0.10 mm to 1355 N at 0.30 mm. In contrast, higher printing speeds reduced mechanical performance (PLA decreased by 13% between 20 and 50 mm·s−1). Temperature exhibited material-dependent trends: PLA benefited up to 230 °C (+17%), while ABS strength decreased beyond 220 °C. Overall, the study provides a quantitative assessment of how processing parameters control mechanical reliability in polymer parts, offering practical guidelines for improved design and manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
3D printing is a rapidly advancing method in digital manufacturing techniques and produces objects in layers. Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) is a 3D printing technology where the material is melted in a hot nozzle and then placed on a build platform to create a prototype layer by layer. In this study, the effects of different raster angles (0°, 45°, 90°, 45°/-45°, 0°/90°) on dimensional accuracy for PLA, PETG and ABS materials produced using FDM were investigated. The results show that PETG generally shows higher dimensional deviations compared to PLA and ABS, and samples with a scan angle of 90° generally have lower deviation percentages than other angles. Width deviations (approximately 1.5% on average) were lower than thickness deviations (approximately 9.5% on average). Analysis of the cross-sectional areas shows that all samples are above the theoretical area (41.6 mm2). PETG samples with a scan angle of 45°/-45° exhibit the largest cross-sectional area (46.78 mm2), while ABS samples with a scan angle of 90° exhibit the smallest (45.46 mm2). This study is important to understand the impact of material selection and raster angle on dimensional accuracy, and it is recommended to account for cross-sectional deviations and calculate the stress based on the actual cross-sectional area to achieve more accurate results in applications requiring precise measurements. These data offer valuable information for those interested in 3D printing and its professionals and can lead to further research in this field, so that printing techniques can be further developed and product quality can be improved.

Abstract:
Fused deposition modeling (FDM) is one of the most accessible additive manufacturing (AM) technologies for processing polymeric materials. It allows processing most of thermoplastic polymers, with polyethylene terephthalate glycol-modified (PET-G) and polylactic acid (PLA). AM parts tend to display anisotropic behavior because of layer-by-layer fabrication and various technological parameters that can be set for 3D print, so it is hard to predict and analyze how the manufactured parts would behave under load. This research presents results of classic tensile strength tests performed on 57 PET-G specimens and 57 PLA specimens manufactured with varying technological parameters such as: printing temperature, print orientation, layer height, and infill percentage. Afterward, a comparative analysis is performed, proposing specific tensile strength (STS) as a benchmark to determine how 3D printed parts strength is varying due to beforementioned parameters, eliminating bias induced by varying weight of specimens. The biggest relative increase of UTS and the biggest relative decrease of STS was noted for variable infill percentage (increasing infill—PLA: 37.27% UTS increase and 30.41% STS decrease; PET-G: 24.42% UTS increase and 37.69% STS decrease). The biggest relative increase of STS between examined parameters was observed for both materials as the printing temperature was increased (27.53% for PLA and 12.69% for PET-G). Similar trends in STS changes were observed for both materials. Obtained data shows which FDM AM parameters are the most important to obtain the biggest UTS of manufactured parts, and those do not overlap with parameters needed to obtain optimal strength-to-weight ratio.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Significant advances in fused deposition modeling (FDM), as well as its myriad applications, have led to its growing prominence among additive manufacturing (AM) technologies. When the technology was first developed, it was used for rapid prototyping to examine and analyze a product in the design stage. FDM facilitates rapid production, requires inexpensive tools, and can fabricate complex-shaped parts; it, therefore, became popular and its use widespread. However, various FDM processing parameters have proven to affect the printed part’s mechanical properties to different extents. The values for the printing process parameters are carefully selected based on the part’s application. This study investigates the effects of four process parameters (raster angle, layer thickness, infill percentage, and printing speed) on the mechanical behavior of printed parts that are based on available literature data. These process parameter’s influence on part’s mechanical properties varies depending on the FDM material. The study focuses on four FDM materials: polylactic acid (PLA), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polyether ether ketone (PEEK), and polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG). This paper summarizes the state-of-the-art literature to show how sensitive the material’s mechanical properties are to each process parameter. The effect of each parameter on each material was quantified and ranked using analysis of variance (ANOVA). The results show that infill percentage then layer thickness are the most influential process parameter on most of the material’s mechanical properties. In addition, this work identifies gaps in existing studies and highlights opportunities for future research.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this study, the strain rate sensitivity of five different thermoplastic polymers processed via Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) Additive Manufacturing (AM) is reported. Namely, Polylactic Acid (PLA), Acrylonitrile-Butadiene-Styrene (ABS), Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol (PETG), Polyamide 6 (PA6), and Polypropylene (PP) were thoroughly investigated under static tensile loading conditions at different strain rates. Strain rates have been selected representing the most common applications of polymeric materials manufactured by Three-Dimensional (3D) Printing. Each polymer was exposed to five different strain rates in order to elucidate the dependency and sensitivity of the tensile properties, i.e., stiffness, strength, and toughness on the applied strain rate. Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) was employed to investigate the 3D printed samples’ fractured surfaces, as a means to derive important information regarding the fracture process, the type of fracture (brittle or ductile), as well as correlate the fractured surface characteristics with the mechanical response under certain strain rate conditions. An Expectation–Maximization (EM) analysis was carried out. Finally, a comparison is presented calculating the strain rate sensitivity index “m” and toughness of all materials at the different applied strain rates.

Abstract:
Advances in the development of additive manufacturing materials (AM) and the low availability of studies on the impact response of AM specimens are the main reasons for this paper. Therefore, the influence of building orientation (vertical and horizontal) and the angle of the raster (15°/−75°, 30°/−60°, 45°/−45°, and 0°/90°) on the tensile and impact strength of AM specimens was investigated. The polylactic acid (PLA)-PolyMax, Mediflex and acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene (ABS) filaments were chosen to provide a comprehensive characterization of AM materials with versatile mechanical properties. The experimental results of this study show that the tensile strength and toughness of PolyMax PLA specimens are comparable to ABS specimens, while Mediflex samples are characterized by their higher toughness, but lower impact force needed to break the samples. The Mediflex Charpy fracture surfaces exhibit a ductile character compared to those of brittle ABS and PLA. Furthermore, fracture surface morphology shows the allocation of voids, which helps us to understand differences in mechanical properties, and allows one to properly interpret the results of the geometrical accuracy of AM specimens with various printing settings.

Abstract:
Fused filament fabrication (FFF) is the most popular additive manufacturing method, which allows the production of highly complex three-dimensional parts with minimal material waste. On the other hand, polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG) has been used to replace traditional polymers for 3D printing due to its chemical resistance and mechanical performance, among other benefits. However, when fibres are added, these PETG-based composites can be suitable for many different applications. Nevertheless, to guarantee their good performance in-service in these applications, and even extend to new ones, it is necessary for their mechanical properties to be maximized. Therefore, this study intends to optimize the printing parameters (nozzle temperature, printing speed, layer height and filling) in order to maximize the mechanical properties of printed PETG, PETG+CF (carbon fibre-reinforced PETG composites) and PETG+KF (aramid fibre-reinforced PETG composites). The Taguchi method was used for the experimental procedure design, and the specimens were produced according to the L16 orthogonal array. Finally, an analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed, with a 95% confidence interval, to analyse the effect of the printing parameters on the bending properties. It was possible to conclude that the best bending properties for PETG, PETG+CF and PETG+KF were obtained for extrusion temperatures of 265 °C, 195 °C and 265 °C, printing speeds of 20, 60 and 20 mm/s, layer heights of 0.4, 0.53 and 0.35 mm and an infill density of 100% for the three materials, respectively.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'scetta2021straininducedstrengthening pages 6-12'.

Giorgia Scetta, Jianzhu Ju, Nathan Selles, Patrick Heuillet, Matteo Ciccotti, and Costantino Creton. Strain induced strengthening of soft thermoplastic polyurethanes under cyclic deformation. ArXiv, 59:685-696, Apr 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2104.02504, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2104.02504. This article has 49 citations.

The excerpt discusses Mullins-like behavior and strong residual deformation in thermoplastic polyurethanes (TPU) caused by lack of chemical crosslinks and plastic deformation of hard domains. All TPUs showed a similar fraction of residual stretch for a given maximum applied stretch, whereas crosslinked SBR has much lower residual stretch. The authors emphasize that engineering stress–strain curves can misleadingly suggest cyclic softening in TPU because they ignore accumulated residual strain; true stress vs. Hencky strain representation should be used instead. Their cyclic protocol evaluates linear modulus Ek from unloading slopes and compares Ek to the pristine modulus E0 to quantify damage. They shift each unloading curve to the origin to compensate residual strain and build a master curve by superposition (least-squares fit to the first unloading curve) to obtain a rescaling factor α and define large- and small-strain damage metrics. Experimentally, TPU materials typically show initial softening (damage increases) with increasing max Hencky strain followed, beyond ~1.5 Hencky strain, by stiffening (damage decreases and can become negative, especially at 60°C and for TPU_XTAL). SBR, by contrast, shows monotonic softening and lower residual plasticity.

The paper studies cyclic uniaxial tension on three commercial Elastollan™ TPU and quantifies structural changes under cyclic loading. Contrary to the classical Mullins behavior in chemically crosslinked filled rubbers, the authors observe a "stiffening effect after conditioning in step cyclic loading" for these soft TPUs. However, their step-strain cyclic tests at 23°C also show "Large hysteresis between the first load-unload cycle," "Very pronounced softening after the first loading, and recovery of the monotonic test behavior envelope only when the material is stretched to higher values than those previously applied (Mullins effect)," and "Marked residual deformation." The residual stretch is linked to the lack of chemical crosslinks and "plastic deformation of the hard domains following the application of large strains." The authors propose a mechanism where "fragmentation of hard domains, naturally present in TPU, in smaller but more numerous sub-units" creates additional physical crosslinking, producing persistent self-reinforcement analogous to strain-induced crystallization (notably observed in TPU_XTAL). They reference a methodology that uses "two damage parameters: one to account for the reduction in linear modulus and the other to account for the change in the onset of strain hardening in large strain" to separate small-strain modulus changes from large-strain behavior.

These effects stem from strain-dependent changes to the hard-domain morphology and the lack of chemical crosslinks, which also leads to creep and viscoplastic deformation under repeated stretch. ## pqac-00000013

From text 'scetta2021cyclicfatiguefailure pages 2-3'.

Giorgia Scetta, Nathan Selles, Patrick Heuillet, Matteo Ciccotti, and Costantino Creton. Cyclic fatigue failure of tpu using a crack propagation approach. May 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymertesting.2021.107140, doi:10.1016/j.polymertesting.2021.107140. This article has 62 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt contrasts standard preconditioning protocols used for filled rubbers with the challenges encountered when applying them to thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). For filled rubbers, pre-straining (thousands of cycles at larger stretches) is commonly used to remove transient Mullins damage so that a stable energy release rate G(λ) can be evaluated. However, TPUs "typically show significant residual deformation when unloaded," and this residual (plastic) stretch accumulates with cycling, altering the stress–stretch response and making the effective energy release rate depend on both maximum stretch and cycle number, i.e. G(λ,n). Allowing full unloading to the original reference (λmin = 1) can cause buckling during unloading and additional damage. Standard pre-conditioning would require very large stretches for TPU (risking damage) and even modest preconditioning to λp slightly above the test stretch makes the calculated G dependent on λp: G(λ,λp). Therefore, conventional preconditioning to remove Mullins-like transients is not directly transferable to TPU; specific cyclic loading protocols and definitions of reference state are needed to obtain reproducible crack propagation/fatigue data.

The excerpt emphasizes porosity (and thus relative density) as the primary control on stiffness and strength for additively manufactured cellular materials. Experiment, CAD and µCT-derived FE models show a clear trend: stiffness increases as porosity decreases. Small porosity differences (~5% lower porosity in experimental samples versus µCT models) materially increase stiffness and yield strength, explaining why experimental 0.2% yield strengths (60–100 MPa) exceed CAD-as-designed predictions (20–30 MPa). The authors find tensile testing gives the most consistent Young’s modulus (smallest monotonic vs. cyclic differences) and therefore use tensile data and µCT-based FE models for comparisons. They note modeling choices (multi-linear isotropic material model and bulk material data) can slightly affect FE results but that porosity differences dominate. Failure locations depend on topology (cubic-regular: mid-strut; cubic-irregular: junctions and struts; trabecular: junctions), which can influence effective mechanical scaling. The manuscript states the next step is to apply the Gibson–Ashby model using Young’s modulus values from experimental, CAD and µCT sources to relate stiffness to relative density.

The excerpt defines nondimensional (relative) variables used in Gibson–Ashby scaling: relative density ρ* = ρlatt./ρsol., relative modulus E* = Elatt./Esol., and relative ultimate strength σU* = σUlatt./σUsol. Gibson and Ashby propose the semi-empirical scaling E* = C1 ρ*^m, where for open, bending-dominated cells (e.g. BCC) m = 2. The prefactor C1 “includes all of the geometric constants of proportionality” and therefore must subsume nearly all geometric information except relative density; the authors stress C1 depends on unit cell type, global shape, stress type and cell size. For strength and fracture properties, Gibson–Ashby relations also include cell-size dependence via a Weibull-like parameter mw: mw governs size sensitivity (e.g. mw = 6 implies cell-size independence for fracture toughness, mw > 6 gives toughness increasing with cell size). The excerpt cites an experimental example (Young’s modulus dropping from ≈306 to 241 MPa when cell size increased from 2 to 8 mm) and shows Table 1 listing unit cell widths and number of cells in gauge volumes—highlighting that reporting cell size and number of cells (or gauge dimensions) is important when comparing nondimensional stiffness across specimens.

The paper uses the standard Gibson–Ashby style scaling E/Es = C p^n (with p = ρ/ρs the reduced density) as a non-dimensional representation of stiffness. Es and ρs are the Young’s modulus and density of the solid skeleton, so stiffness and density are non-dimensionalized by the base solid properties. The constants C and n depend on microstructure; n typically lies between 1 and 4, with closed-cell foams often showing 1 < n < 2. Mechanisms map to exponents: edge-bending gives n = 2, cell-wall bending n = 3 (Gibson–Ashby), and cell-wall stretching n = 1; experimental and model disorder can shift effective n above the ideal periodic-model value (e.g., tetrakaidecahedral models give n ≈ 1, but disorder increases density dependence). The authors compute E and Poisson’s ratio for isotropic random models (Voronoi tessellations and level-cut Gaussian random fields) using FEM over scales ≈100 cells, and report FEM numerical errors ≲10%. For comparing specimens of different sizes or materials, use E/Es versus p = ρ/ρs and fit a power law E/Es = C p^n (typically in the low-density limit) to obtain size- and microstructure-independent non-dimensional stiffness.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'pahari2024analysisofthe pages 60-65'.

S Pahari. Analysis of the interface properties of multi-material 3d printed structures. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt highlights that multi-material FFF printing is under-explored and that interfacial adhesion critically controls the mechanical performance of multi-material parts. Studies (notably PLA/TPU examples) report that multi-material specimens exhibit lower tensile modulus than homogeneous counterparts, with weak zones and ruptures localized at the material boundary. FFF-specific issues—porosity and anisotropy from layer-by-layer deposition—contribute to weak layer adhesion and reduced strength. Emerging multi-extruder/IDEX printers enable multi-material FFF, but interface bonding between heterogeneous polymers remains a primary challenge. The text also cites a range of experimental full-field deformation measurement methods (optical microscope+DIC, fluorescent image correlation, confocal microscopy with digital volume correlation, nanoscale DIC) used for resolving deformation and local stresses at micro/nano scales. These measurement techniques are directly relevant for characterizing interfacial behavior, detecting localized strain concentrations, and could be applied to identify interface failure modes (delamination, slippage) that would manifest in mechanical tests (e.g., anomalies or sudden events in load–displacement curves). The excerpt emphasizes the need for more macroscopic and microscopic data to improve multi-material interface performance.

In printed parts, performance under bending and load is strongly influenced by internal architecture: "build orientation, infill pattern and density" and by interlayer phenomena such as "micro-delaminations and void deformation," meaning interfacial adhesion and deposition strategy critically affect joint strength. Processing windows that favor strong interlayer bonding are given: nozzle 215–235 °C, bed 70–90 °C, and moderate speeds (commonly 30–50 mm/s), plus careful retraction tuning to avoid stringing/oozing. PETG is hygroscopic; "absorbed water chemically attacks the polyester chains via hydrolysis," so filament drying is important to avoid covert loss of strength. Thermal limits are indicated by a Tg of ~67.5–77.3 °C, implying softening/creep risk near these temperatures. Asymmetric tension–compression connectivity governs deformation delocalization in truss-based metamaterials Valid Text Names: 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 1-2', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 2-4', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 4-5', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 5-8', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 8-9', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 9-10', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 10-10' BibTex: @article{ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity, author = "Ruffini, Franco N. and Rimoli, Julian J.", title = "Asymmetric tension–compression connectivity governs deformation delocalization in truss-based metamaterials", year = "2026", journal = "npj Metamaterials", volume = "2", month = "Mar", doi = "10.1038/s44455-026-00020-1", url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/s44455-026-00020-1" } Abstract: Abstract

Failure in most material systems is characterized by strain localization, where deformation concentrates within a narrow region. Recently, a class of truss-based metamaterials has been shown to undergo severe deformation without exhibiting localization [1]. The mechanisms underlying this unusual delocalized response remain unknown. Here, we employ graph theory to elucidate the origins of this behavior. Each lattice is represented as a pair of graphs—the tension and compression networks—and their topological properties are quantified using graph-theoretic metrics. We find that the onset of localization correlates strongly with connectivity measures of these graphs. Specifically, deformation delocalization arises from an asymmetry in connectivity between these networks: when the tension graph remains more connected than the compression graph, deformation spreads throughout the structure instead of localizing. Connectivity measures such as average global efficiency[2] capture this transition quantitatively. This framework provides design principles for creating materials and metamaterials that intrinsically resist failure localization.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study introduces a minimalist design strategy to engineer wave propagation in cellularmetamaterials by applying a single-parameter twist to the classical Kelvin unit cell. By breaking the cell’s symmetry while preserving its lattice topology, this geometric modification activates and tunes band-gap frequencies with only a 3% mass increase, thereby obviating increased geometric complexity and significant mass augmentation often required to achieve wave-filtering performance at low frequencies. The proposed strategy relies on complex-valued Bloch–Floquet analysis of quasi-one-dimensional periodic chains (but is not restricted to) that reveals symmetry-breaking triggers activating two distinct wave attenuation mechanisms: wide Bragg-type and narrow polarization-dependent band gaps arising from longitudinal–torsional mode coupling.These findings are substantiated by a physics-driven analytical model that captures the mode coupling-induced avoided crossings and provides key insight into the wave characteristics of twisted architectures. The predictive fidelity of this approach is validated by transmissionmeasurements on SLA three-cell specimens, which reveal up to 20 dB of wave attenuation. Wealso demonstrate that accounting for material viscoelasticity is essential for accurate prediction, as idealized linear-elastic models are insufficient to capture band-gap frequencies in polymer-based chains. Overall, we proved that modest, well-defined modifications to a classical parentgeometry yield advanced wave-filtering performance at low frequencies. This offers a tractableand methodologically complete design strategy for vibration control in lightweight lattices.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000038

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 7-8'.

Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes tensegrity metamaterials designed to produce delocalized deformation, which yields distributed elastic stable buckling (reversible) rather than localized member failure, giving exceptional failure resistance and high energy absorption. Specimens were 3D-printed by two-photon polymerization (TPP-DLW) in IP-Dip (Nanoscribe) on fused silica. Quasi-static compression testing used full stress–strain characterization: E taken as maximum slope of the linear regime, σy from 0.2% offset, plateau strength σp averaged between 20–40% strain, and absorbed energy U as the integral of the stress–strain curve to densification or failure. Internal deformation maps were measured by DIC to quantify delocalization (ηd). Finite-element simulations (ABAQUS, modified RIKS) modeled 6×6×6 elementary-cell tensegrity, octet and iso trusses with small randomized imperfections and matched experimental dimensions; results were reported scale-independent and indicate translatability to metals. Numerically optimized tensegrity showed 3–18× (σ vs U) and 2–7× (E vs U) improvements versus first-order beam lattices, and experiments showed up to 5× higher σ–U combinations, demonstrating that tensegrity architectures outperform many beam-, shell- and hierarchical lightweight designs for reversible, high-energy-absorbing, failure-resistant compression behavior.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 2-3'.

Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The authors fabricated space-tileable 3D tensegrity metamaterials by recursively reflecting truncated-octahedron elementary cells and 3D-printed them using two-photon polymerization direct laser writing (TPP-DLW). Cells contain tensile members along edges and isolated compressive members inside, satisfying tensegrity topology. Specimens (6×6×6 cells) covered relative densities of 4–12%; truss members were square bars with ≈950 nm edge length and cell sizes 10–20 µm. Mechanical testing used displacement-controlled uniaxial compression with in situ imaging and digital image correlation (DIC) to map local deformation (map element areas a relative to a0). Compared with octet and Kelvin lattices, the tensegrity showed highly uniform, strain-independent deformation and no detectable localized damage up to at least 30% strain. The tensegrity exhibited a fully stable, monotonic stress–strain response with a smooth, elongated post-yield plateau and densification above ε ≈ 62.5%. By contrast, the octet underwent localized damage and system instability at ε ≈ 2.6% and its delocalization efficiency ηd fell to 35%; the Kelvin foam localized above ε ≈ 17% with ηd dropping to 67%. The tensegrity maintained ηd > 90% throughout, linking delocalized deformation to improved energy absorption and failure resistance.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 6-7'.

Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports monotonic compressive testing and finite-element simulations comparing 3D-printed tensegrity lattices to octet and Kelvin continuous-compression architectures at matched density/strength (notably 4% relative density). Experiments and simulations show tensegrity lattices exhibit delocalized deformation, stable stress–strain responses, and greatly enhanced damage resistance: the tensegrity retained load-bearing capacity up to densification (ε = 62.5%), and at εc = 70% the octet had only 7% of its initial stiffness versus 70% for the tensegrity. Although the octet’s initial stiffness/strength were higher (≈14× and 9×), tensegrity absorbed far more energy before failure (≈13× vs octet and ≈2× vs Kelvin in experiments). Strain energy U was computed as the area under stress–strain curves up to failure/densification. Simulations reproduced experiments, showed localization and unstable stress drops in octet/Kelvin, and enabled numerical optimization of tensile/compressive member cross-sections to double tensegrity performance and further increase absorbed energy (up to 26× and 4× vs octet/Kelvin; down to very low densities predicted energy-absorption gains up to 225×). Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000046

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 29-34'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt cites ASTM E111-04 (Standard test method for Young’s modulus, tangent modulus, and chord modulus) and ASTM E83-06 (verification and classification of extensometer systems), indicating the study references the formal standards for modulus determination and extensometer verification. Relevant methodological research is cited: Graham & Adler (2011) on determining slope and quality of fit for the linear part of a test record, and Scibetta & Schuurmans (2004) on an algorithm to determine the initial linear portion of a force–displacement record—both directly related to toe correction and selection of tangent/secant regions. Figures report measured modulus and 0.2% offset yield strength as a function of number/usage of extensometers, highlighting the influence of extensometer configuration on modulus determination. Another figure notes lubricant effects on stress–strain behavior, which can affect initial contact/toe behavior. While the excerpt references standards and studies relevant to tangent/secant modulus, toe correction, and extensometer practices, it does not present a detailed machine load-frame compliance correction protocol in these pages.


---

## pqac-00000047

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 24-26'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt describes a reanalysis of compression stress-strain curves (per ASTM E111) to obtain consistent elastic modulus values (EGA) using a Scibetta–Schuurmans based nine-step procedure. Laboratories often used ASTM E83 Class B-2 extensometers, and E9 Section 9.2 permits B-2 when yield strength is primary; ASTM E111 would require a Class B-1 for modulus as the primary parameter. The nine steps include: locating the knee of the curve (points e1 at s1 = 0.05 max(s), eo=e1 with so=0.2 max(s), and finding (et,st) tangent through (eo,so)); truncating and normalizing data at (et,st); checking digital resolution (with a rule that no more than 25% of points should have zero change); applying the Scibetta–Schuurmans algorithm to find the optimal fit window (considering all subsets with at least 20% of data and selecting lowest residual std. dev.); checking noise (standard error in strain or stress ≤ 0.01); extending the fit to include points within one standard error; refitting to get EGA; checking residual curvature (slope in outer quartiles ≤ 0.05) and ensuring the optimal fit stress range > 0.4st. Quality metrics are defined for digital resolution, noise, curvature, and fit range. The accepted aluminum modulus used for error assessment was EaccAl = 75.2 GPa and the absolute error is defined as ∆EGA = |EaccAl − EGA|.


---

## pqac-00000048

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 6-11'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

This interlaboratory compression study followed ASTM E9 and required fixture qualification per E9 Section 6.6. Participants used at least one extensometer (gauge lengths reported in Table 3, e.g. G = 25.4 mm or 12.7 mm), ran tests at a nominal strain rate of 0.005 min−1, and intentionally did not report strain from actuator displacement. Laboratories used a variety of fixturing/alignment approaches (sub-presses, precision-ground sub-presses, adjustable platens, two-opposed extensometers) to control alignment and reduce fixturing effects. Electronic stress-strain traces were collected and returned. For ‘toe’ correction the organizers (or analysts) shifted each stress-strain curve along the strain axis so that a linear fit to the stress-strain data in the range 50–175 MPa intercepted the origin — effectively removing initial offset before determining modulus. These details imply recommended practice for tangent/secant modulus determination: use extensometer-measured strain (not actuator displacement), collect high-resolution stress-strain traces, qualify fixtures per E9, control alignment (sub-press/precision platens), and apply a linear-fit-based toe correction over an appropriate stress range prior to modulus extraction. The excerpt does not provide a step-by-step machine compliance correction protocol, but fixture qualification and avoidance of actuator-displacement strain measurement are emphasized.

## pqac-00000049

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 21-24'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt references ASTM E111 as the standard for validating compression test fixtures for elastic modulus: laboratories should measure aluminum 2024-T4 per E111 and obtain measurements on five consecutive specimens within 5% of E = 73.8 GPa. ASTM E111 expects the more accurate Class B-1 extensometer, but most participating labs used ASTM E83 Class B-2 devices (roughly half the accuracy). In this interlaboratory study all labs used specimen-mounted extensometers (typically G = 25.4 mm, with contact points about one diameter from the specimen ends), which complies with E9 and minimizes end-effect influence. The paper notes that calculating true stress from actuator/platen displacement—when corrected for machine compliance—is common but produced values ~6 MPa (1.4%) higher than extensometer-based measures; however no laboratory measured strain that way here. Finite-element analysis showed that extensometer gauge length and friction extremes did not account for the observed interlaboratory differences in yield. The excerpt does not provide ASTM E111’s explicit formulas or step-by-step procedures for tangent vs. secant modulus determination, toe-region correction, or detailed machine-compliance correction protocols, so the authoritative ASTM E111 text or other procedural guidance is needed for those specifics.

## pqac-00000050

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 1-6'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

This interlaboratory study of ASTM E9 compression testing reports key points relevant to measuring elastic modulus and yield strength in compression. Participants commonly used extensometers attached to the specimen; using diametrically opposed extensometers (vs a single extensometer) substantially improved precision. The authors reanalyzed modulus from stress–strain data with a technique that selects an optimal fit range and applies quality checks, and they found modulus error increases markedly when the fit range drops below about 40% of the stress range. ASTM E9 includes requirements for calibrating and qualifying the testing machine and extensometers and for aligning fixtures/specimens, but the standard does not require an extensometer in contact with the specimen—many implementations instead infer strain from actuator displacement. The study also found that whether specimen ends were lubricated affected measured yield and modulus values, and a finite-element analysis could not fully explain that discrepancy. The report’s results were incorporated into E9’s precision/bias statement (2009).

## pqac-00000051

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 18-21'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt does not describe ASTM E111 toe-correction algorithms or a machine/frame compliance correction protocol directly, but it provides relevant observations about factors that affect measured modulus and yield on compression stress–strain data. Labs that used two-opposed extensometers reported modulus values closest to the accepted value; two extensometers "will tend to average the effect of non-axial loading" and reduce bias from bending. By contrast, single-extensometer setups often produced lab means systematically above or below the grand average, implicating compression-fixture alignment rather than specimen machining as the source of non-axiality. The fixed geometric relation between extensometer and loading fixturing can cause consistent over- or under-estimation of strain when bending is present. Lubrication of specimen ends also affected results: unlubricated labs reported average YS ~10.6 MPa (3.1%) lower and E ~4.1 GPa (5.7%) smaller. The paper also supplies standard definitions and formulas for repeatability (within-lab) and reproducibility (between-lab) standard deviations (sr, sR) and coefficients of variation, useful for quantifying variability before/after any toe or compliance corrections. Overall, the text supports using dual extensometers, careful alignment and lubrication control and statistical characterization, but does not give toe-correction or load-frame compliance procedures.

## pqac-00000052

From text 'biesiekierski2020mechanicaltestingof pages 13-16'.

Arne Biesiekierski, Khurram Munir, Yuncang Li, and Cuie Wen. Mechanical testing of metallic biomaterials. Metallic Biomaterials Processing and Medical Device Manufacturing, pages 427-467, Jan 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-08-102965-7.00013-8, doi:10.1016/b978-0-08-102965-7.00013-8. This article has 5 citations.

The excerpt emphasizes that accurate strain measurement is essential to determine modulus (E), elongation and other mechanical properties. It warns that using crosshead displacement (displacement sensor divided by gauge length) is the least accurate because the integrated displacement sensor cannot distinguish sample deformation from load-frame distortion; that distortion depends on the geometry and stiffness of both the test frame and the sample. This underscores the need to account for machine compliance when determining elastic moduli. Alternative measurement options discussed include bonded strain gauges (limited to small strains and single use), clip-on extensometers ("substantially more accurate and precise than bonded foil gauges" and reusable, but may distort small samples or be damaged), and non-contact digital image methods (DIC) which allow the camera to be separated from the specimen and map strain fields but are sensitive to optical issues. The excerpt also cites ASTM E8M strain-rate recommendations for tensile testing and provides true-compression conversions (σ0 = -σ(1-ε) and ε0 = -ln(1-ε)). The text does not give ASTM E111-specific tangent/secant modulus procedures, a toe-correction algorithm for compression curves, or a step-by-step machine compliance correction protocol, but it provides the measurement-method and correction context relevant to implementing those procedures (i.e., use of local extensometry or DIC to avoid frame compliance errors and conversion to true stress/strain for compression).

## pqac-00000053

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 26-29'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

This excerpt (ASTM E9 compression interlaboratory study) discusses procedures and quality metrics for estimating elastic modulus from compression stress–strain curves. It recommends checking curvature by examining residual slope in the outer quartiles: if that slope exceeds 5% of the optimal-region slope the fit is excessive. More importantly, the size of the final fit range (Rf) is the strongest predictor of modulus quality; a minimum Rf ≥ 0.4 (40% of the elastic-region stress range) is used, and tests with Rf < 0.4 show ≈2.5× larger mean modulus error (4.88 vs. 1.95 GPa). Linear regression showed no relation between residual-slope magnitude and modulus error. For strain measurement, using two diametrically opposed extensometers can improve precision by over two times. The study also reports repeatability and reproducibility for yield strength measured per ASTM E9 (~1.1% and ~2.0% of the mean, respectively). These points inform fit selection, fit-range limits, and extensometer practice for reliable modulus estimation in compression testing, though the excerpt does not describe ASTM E111-specific tangent/secant definitions, toe-correction, or machine compliance correction protocols.

| ISO 604 | Plastics — Determination of Compressive Properties | Compressive stress-strain response and modulus of plastics | Prismatic/cylindrical bulk-plastic specimens with prescribed dimensions and end parallelism; homogeneous material assumption | Constant compression rate specified by standard by specimen type/material | Same gap as D695: appropriate for printed PETG/PLA coupons, not for sparse multi-material cells with large void fraction and mechanism-driven deformation | **Normative** for bulk plastic coupons; **informative only** for unit cells |
| ASTM D1621 | Compressive Properties of Rigid Cellular Plastics | Compressive stress-strain, strength, and apparent modulus of rigid foams/cellular plastics | Minimum specimen commonly interpreted as ~25.4 mm cube in practice for cellular materials; full specimen should be representative through thickness | Constant rate of crosshead motion selected to achieve specified nominal strain-rate regime for foams | Closest analog for single-cell or tiled rigid-dominant lattice/cellular specimens, but your specimens are open, architected, anisotropic, and multi-material rather than stochastic rigid foam. Must report architecture, loading direction, contact area definition, relative density, and any departures from cube geometry | **Normative-adjacent / preferred primary citation** for quasi-static compression of rigid-dominant cellular specimens if adapted and deviations disclosed |

### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Phase | Step | Checklist item | Target / setting | Record in metadata / file | Why / note | Citation |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-Test | 1 | Verify specimen has been conditioned before test | 48 h at 23 °C, 50 % RH | `conditioning_time_h`, `conditioning_temp_C`, `conditioning_RH_pct` | Reduces moisture/history variability in PETG/TPU; aligns with AM polymer coupon practice | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000031) |
| Pre-Test | 2 | Inspect specimen visually before handling | No obvious warp, cracked struts, delaminated tendons, detached joints | `pretest_visual_status`, `notes` | Reject obviously defective prints before loading | (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000033) |
| Pre-Test | 3 | Assign and confirm unique specimen ID | Use permanent ID on bag + worksheet + CSV | `specimen_id` | Prevents data/design mismatch in later BO loop | (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000037) |
| Pre-Test | 4 | Measure mass | 0.01 g scale; 2 repeated readings if difference >0.02 g, take third and average | `mass_g` | Needed for relative density checks and SEA later | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022) |
| Pre-Test | 5 | Measure overall geometry | Calipers, 0.01 mm resolution; measure height and two orthogonal widths at 3 locations each | `height_mm`, `width_x_mm`, `width_y_mm`, `bounding_cube_mm` | Use measured dimensions, not CAD only | (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022) |
| Pre-Test | 6 | Measure key feature sizes if accessible | Strut diameter and tendon diameter at 3 representative locations | `strut_diameter_mm`, `tendon_diameter_mm` | As-built dimensions can differ from nominal and affect stiffness | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000022) |
| Pre-Test | 7 | Photograph specimen before test | All faces + top/bottom + isometric, with ruler/scale bar and specimen ID visible | image filenames in `photo_pre_paths` | Supports later failure/joint-slip interpretation | (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032) |
| Pre-Test | 8 | Verify required print metadata is complete | Confirm print log is attached | `design_family`, `n_bars`, `cell_type`, `strut_material`, `tendon_material`, `joint_type`, `relative_density`, `print_date`, `printer_id`, `nozzle_temp_C`, `bed_temp_C`, `layer_height_mm`, `infill_pct`, `raster_angle_deg`, `build_orientation` | Essential for AM reproducibility/reporting | (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000031) |
| Mounting | 9 | Select load cell and confirm zero/load range | Prefer smallest verified cell that keeps peak load in useful range; if only available, use 5 kN and verify low-load resolution | `load_cell_kN`, `load_cell_serial`, `E4_class_if_known` | Low-load tendon-dominated response is sensitive to poor load resolution | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004) |
| Mounting | 10 | Confirm platen condition | Clean flat platens; remove debris; inspect for nicks | `platen_type`, `platen_surface_condition` | Surface condition affects initial contact stiffness | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000050) |
| Mounting | 11 | Decide whether to use PTFE / low-friction film | Use PTFE film only if barreling/friction suspected; keep choice fixed within a batch | `interface_film_used`, `film_type` | Friction/lubrication changes apparent modulus and yield | (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000048) |
| Mounting | 12 | Center specimen on lower platen | Align projected center of specimen with platen centerline | `mounting_centered_yes_no` | Reduces bending/eccentric loading | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000051) |
| Mounting | 13 | Check parallelism / alignment | Bring upper platen close without contact; verify specimen top is visually parallel; adjust if needed | `alignment_checked_yes_no` | Non-axial loading biases stiffness | (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000051) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 14 | Start data acquisition before contact | Record from before first contact | raw file name in `raw_data_path` | Preserves toe/contact region for later correction | (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000046) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 15 | Approach slowly to contact | Crosshead speed 0.5 mm/min until preload threshold reached | `contact_find_speed_mm_min` | Gentle seating limits impact/contact artifact | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 16 | Set preload / contact criterion | Detect 0.5–1.0 N sustained preload | `preload_N` | Defines test zero consistently for soft specimens | (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000052) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 17 | Hold briefly after preload | 3–5 s hold after preload before zeroing displacement | `preload_hold_s` | Lets load settle before zeroing | (pqac-00000052) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 18 | Zero displacement at preload | Zero crosshead position at preload; if DIC/video extensometry is used, also define local zero | `zero_method` | Needed for repeatable structural stiffness extraction | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000052) |
| Preconditioning | 19 | Run preconditioning cycles | 5 cycles to 5 % nominal strain at 1 mm/min | `preconditioning_cycles`, `preconditioning_strain_pct`, `preconditioning_speed_mm_min` | TPU and elastomeric systems show first-cycle softening/hysteresis/history effects | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| Preconditioning | 20 | Pause between cycles | 30 s between cycles | `preconditioning_pause_s` | Improves comparability of cyclic response | (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012) |
| Preconditioning | 21 | Watch live force–displacement trace during cycling | Look for settling after first cycle and any sudden drops/clicks | `preconditioning_observation`, `notes` | Helps identify joint slip versus normal Mullins-like behavior | (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036) |
| Preconditioning | 22 | Stop and flag if damage occurs during preconditioning | Abort if visible joint tearing, tendon detachment, or force drop >20 % at same displacement | `abort_reason` if applicable | First stiffness run should not consume specimen in preconditioning | (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000045) |
| Monotonic Stiffness Test | 23 | Set main loading rate | 1 mm/min constant crosshead speed | `crosshead_speed_mm_min` | Matches common quasi-static lattice practice | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) |
| Monotonic Stiffness Test | 24 | Load specimen in compression | Load to 15–20 % nominal strain, unless early instability/slip occurs | `max_nominal_strain_pct`, `termination_reason` | First run should characterize small-strain stiffness without going to densification | (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000038) |
| Monotonic Stiffness Test | 25 | Unload at same rate | 1 mm/min back to preload or near-zero force | `unload_speed_mm_min` | Enables hysteresis and unloading stiffness estimation | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000038) |
| Monotonic Stiffness Test | 26 | Record full force–displacement cycle | Minimum 10 Hz; prefer higher if available | `sample_rate_Hz` | Required for accurate slope and loop-area calculations | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000000) |
| Monotonic Stiffness Test | 27 | If available, record local deformation optically | Video gauge / DIC on specimen or platen markers | `optical_measurement_used`, `optical_file_path` | Crosshead displacement includes frame compliance; optical data improves low-strain stiffness | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000030) |
| Monotonic Stiffness Test | 28 | Note any audible/visible events during loading | Slip, crack, pop, tendon whitening, PETG crack, platen rocking | `event_log` | Sudden events can mark joint failure, not material nonlinearity | (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) |
| Monotonic Stiffness Test | 29 | Compute provisional stiffness values after run | Tangent stiffness from chosen linear window; secant stiffness at fixed strain; effective modulus if desired | `k_tangent_N_mm`, `k_secant_N_mm`, `E_effective_MPa`, `strain_window_used` | Report structural stiffness and be explicit about strain window | (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000038) |
| Monotonic Stiffness Test | 30 | Compute hysteresis metrics after run | Loop area / loading area or equivalent hysteresis ratio | `hysteresis_ratio` | Useful for TPU-dominant response and later cushioning correlation | (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000010) |
| Post-Test | 31 | Photograph specimen immediately after test | Same views as pre-test, include any damaged joint close-ups | image filenames in `photo_post_paths` | Supports diagnosis of slip, delamination, or buckling mode | (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000045) |
| Post-Test | 32 | Inspect joints and members | Check PETG–TPU interfaces, tendon necking, torn anchors, cracked struts, permanent set | `posttest_failure_mode`, `permanent_set_mm`, `notes` | Critical because interface integrity is an experimental unknown | (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034) |
| Post-Test | 33 | Mark specimen disposition | Keep / retest / destructive follow-up / discard | `specimen_disposition` | Maintains traceability through campaign | (pqac-00000045) |
| Data Export | 34 | Export raw CSV immediately | Include at minimum `time_s`, `crosshead_mm`, `force_N` | `csv_file_path` | Minimum machine-data package | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002) |
| Data Export | 35 | Include derived columns if available | `nominal_strain`, `nominal_stress_kPa_or_MPa`, `cycle_index`, `event_flag` | `derived_csv_path` | Simplifies downstream analysis and BO ingestion | (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000023) |
| Data Export | 36 | Save metadata sidecar file | JSON/YAML/CSV row with all specimen + test fields | `metadata_file_path` | Clean handoff to BoTorch/Ax and later statistics | (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000021) |
| Data Export | 37 | Required BO-facing metadata schema | Capture: `specimen_id`, `design_family`, `n_bars`, `cell_type`, `bounding_cube_mm`, `strut_diameter_mm`, `tendon_diameter_mm`, `strut_material`, `tendon_material`, `joint_type`, `relative_density`, `mass_g`, `print_date`, `printer_id`, `nozzle_temp_C`, `bed_temp_C`, `layer_height_mm`, `infill_pct`, `raster_angle_deg`, `build_orientation`, `test_date`, `crosshead_speed_mm_min`, `preload_N`, `k_tangent_N_mm`, `k_secant_N_mm`, `E_effective_MPa`, `peak_force_N`, `strain_at_peak`, `SEA_J_g`, `hysteresis_ratio`, `notes` | All listed fields | These fields connect design, process, and response for surrogate modeling | (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000037) |
| Data Export | 38 | Backup and review before next specimen | Verify raw curve opens, metadata row is complete, images saved, filenames match specimen ID | `qc_checked_by`, `qc_time` | Prevents irreversible data loss during batch testing | (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000037) |


*Table: This table gives a step-by-step first-run quasi-static stiffness protocol for multi-material tensegrity specimens, including pre-test setup, loading sequence, and data capture. It also embeds the minimum metadata schema needed to support later Bayesian optimization of stiffness and energy-absorption responses.*

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a published analogs table for Section 6, listing 10-12 of the closest published papers to the multi-material tensegrity/lattice compression testing campaign. For each paper include columns: Author/Year, Journal/DOI, Specimen Description, Materials, Standard Cited, Machine/Crosshead Speed, Key Stiffness/EA Results, Notable Deviations/Caveats. Include: Bauer et al. 2021 (Advanced Materials, tensegrity metamaterials), Pajunen et al. 2019 (Materials & Design, 3D-printed tensegrity), Lee et al. 2020 (Science Robotics, programmable tensegrity), Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski 2024 (4-strut simplex tensegrity), Bates et al. 2016 (Materials & Design, TPU honeycombs), Rossiter et al. 2020 (truncated octahedron lattice), Arifvianto et al. 2022 (PLA/TPU multi-material), Maskery et al. 2015 (Ti-6Al-4V BCC lattice, Gibson-Ashby), Solyaev et al. 2023 (quasi-cubic lattice Instron 5969), Raghavendra et al. 2021 (cellular materials nominal vs real), Pahari 2024 (multi-material interface DIC), Habib 2024 (3D printed cellular impact protection)."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Author / Year | Journal / DOI | Specimen Description | Materials | Standard Cited | Machine / Crosshead Speed | Key Stiffness / EA Results | Notable Deviations / Caveats |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bauer et al. 2021 | *Advanced Materials* / 10.1002/adma.202005647 | 3D space-tileable tensegrity metamaterials, 6×6×6 cells, truncated-octahedron-derived architecture; compared against octet and Kelvin lattices | IP-Dip polymer via TPP-DLW | No ASTM/ISO mechanical standard stated; custom in situ compression with DIC | Alemnis nanoindenter in SEM/FIB; constant strain rate 0.01 s⁻¹ | Defined E as max linear slope, σy by 0.2% offset, plateau stress averaged 20–40% strain, absorbed energy by stress–strain integral; tensegrity showed up to ~13× energy absorption vs octet experimentally and retained load-bearing to densification, with ηd > 90% | Highly relevant tensegrity analog, but microscale TPP specimens and custom setup differ strongly from FFF macro-specimens; not standard-based (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041) |
| Pajunen et al. 2019 | *Materials & Design* / 10.1016/j.matdes.2019.107966 | 3D-printable tensegrity-inspired unit cells (~48.3 mm tall), fixed-jointed, pin-jointed, and spherically-jointed variants | SLS PA2200 polyamide; cited E ≈ 1.29 GPa, σy ≈ 29.1 MPa | ASTM D638 for constituent tensile characterization; compression itself not tied to a named ASTM standard | Instron E3000; displacement control; crosshead speed not reported in retrieved excerpts | Pin-jointed geometry showed initial stiffness about 10 kPa and buckling near 0.3 strain; modified geometry increased initial stiffness to 48 kPa; normalized strain energy per mass increased ~3× for one redesign and ~1.5× for spherically-jointed design | One of the closest architecture analogs, but constituent material and process differ from PETG/TPU FFF; missing crosshead-speed reporting is a reproducibility gap (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019) |
| Lee et al. 2020 | *Science Robotics* / 10.1126/scirobotics.aay9024 | 3D-printed programmable tensegrity structures for soft robotics; monolithic tendon networks with rigid struts | Multi-material smart-material tensegrity system | No specific ASTM/ISO testing standard recovered in retrieved excerpts | Compression tests reported in paper, but machine/speed details not available in retrieved excerpts | Demonstrated programmable mechanics in printed tensegrity architectures; useful architecture/process analog | Very relevant conceptually for co-printed tensegrity, but retrieved evidence lacks enough test-protocol detail for direct protocol borrowing (paper identified in search results) |
| Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski 2024 | journal not fully resolved in retrieved record / DOI not recovered in retrieved excerpt | Single-cell 4-strut simplex tensegrity-inspired modules, inscribed in 20–50 mm cubes; free upper-base rotation allowed | Multiple AM materials screened; SLA, PolyJet, SLS initially; SLS rejected as too brittle | No explicit ASTM/ISO standard cited in retrieved excerpts | Instron 5567; displacement control at 2 mm/min; force accuracy 0.5 N | Results reported as mean force–displacement curves with SD for groups of seven; strong dependence on parent-material elongation at break and specimen size; observed post-critical strut behavior | Excellent mesoscale tensegrity analog; explicit acknowledgment that manufacturing inaccuracies and free-deformation constraints strongly affect results; no standard cited and no modulus number recovered in excerpt (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045) |
| Bates et al. 2016 | *Materials & Design* / 10.1016/j.matdes.2016.08.062 | FFF TPU hexagonal honeycombs, compressed in different directions, repeated to densification | NinjaFlex and SemiFlex TPU | ASTM D412 for tensile coupons; compression not tied to a named ASTM in retrieved excerpt | Instron 3343 (1 kN) and Shimadzu (10 kN); constant strain rates 0.03, 0.095, 0.3 s⁻¹; minimum 10 Hz acquisition; video gauge used | Tensile low-strain moduli: 26.5 MPa (NinjaFlex) and 89.5 MPa (SemiFlex); study emphasizes stress–strain regions and repeated-energy-absorption behavior | Strong TPU cushioning analog; not tensegrity, but very useful for preconditioning/hysteresis and optical displacement practice; specimen geometry intentionally chosen with L > H to avoid buckling (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000020) |
| Rossiter et al. 2020 | *3D Printing and Additive Manufacturing* / 10.1089/3dp.2019.0030 | Material-extruded truncated-octahedron lattices; factorial study on cell width, strut CSA, orientation, filleting | Nylon via material extrusion | Compression program described, but no named standard recovered in retrieved excerpt | Instron 3366; constant strain rate 1.0 s⁻¹ | Strut CSA, cell width, and their interaction had largest effects on plateau stress and energy capacity | Close topology analog for truncated-octahedral cells, but much higher strain rate than typical quasi-static stiffness tests; likely more useful for later energy-absorption studies than initial stiffness work (search result summary) |
| Arifvianto et al. 2022 | *Progress in Additive Manufacturing* / 10.1007/s40964-022-00295-6 | FFF sandwich-structured PLA/TPU multi-material parts; interface and layered architecture focus | PLA / TPU | Mechanical-property study; specific standard for excerpted hardness/interface observations not recovered here | Machine details not recovered in excerpt used here | Showed weak interfacial bonding, torn interfaces, and TPU delamination-like behavior; raster configuration not strongly significant for hardness in their tested cases | Important multi-material analog for interface failure interpretation, even though geometry is not a tensegrity/lattice cell and loading mode differs (pqac-00000033) |
| Maskery et al. 2015 | *Experimental Mechanics* / 10.1007/s11340-015-0021-5 | BCC Ti-6Al-4V latticed tensile/compression specimens with varying cell size at fixed relative density | SLM Ti-6Al-4V | Gibson–Ashby framework used; machine-compliance considerations discussed; no polymer standard | Instron 5969; detailed speed not recovered in excerpt here | Relative variables defined as E*/Es, ρ*/ρs, σU*/σUs; highlighted modulus drop with increasing cell size and the importance of unit-cell count in gauge region | Not polymer or multi-material, but canonical for nondimensional stiffness scaling and specimen-size effects in lattices; very useful for your reporting framework (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028) |
| Solyaev et al. 2023 | *Scientific Reports* / 10.1038/s41598-023-41614-3 | 3D-printed quasi-cubic polymer lattice metamaterials with asymmetric joints | Polymeric printed lattice | Compression used flat platforms per ASTM E9; compliance correction per ASTM D790; impact per ASTM D6110 | Instron 5969; 1 mm/min; 2.5 kHz acquisition; 50 kN load cell | Compression run to 50% strain or failure; yield from 0.2% offset; toughness from area under stress–strain curve | Very useful practical analog for Instron setup, compliance correction, and reporting conventions, but load cell was oversized for your likely force range (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000014) |
| Raghavendra et al. 2021 | *Forces in Mechanics* / 10.1016/j.finmec.2020.100007 | Regular, irregular, and random AM cellular materials; nominal vs real geometry study with µCT-based models | LB-PBF Ti-6Al-4V cellular specimens | ISO 13314:2011 for compression; ASTM D638 not relevant here | Compression at 1 mm/min; 1 kHz data sampling; LVDT for compression displacement; cyclic loading–unloading used for modulus | Emphasized representative cell count (~8–10 cells in each direction), unloading-based Young’s modulus, and strong influence of as-built porosity on stiffness and yield | Excellent methodological analog for representative specimen size, external displacement sensing, and as-built geometry correction; material/process differ from FFF polymers (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022) |
| Pahari 2024 | journal not fully resolved in retrieved record / DOI not recovered in retrieved excerpt | Multi-material FFF lap-joint/interface study with full-field deformation mapping | PLA, PETG, PETG+CF; interface-focused | Designed around an FRP lap-shear standard; references ASTM D5868 and ISO 21194 in bibliography discussion | Instron ElectroPuls E3000 (3 kN) for shear; 2D DIC with front and side imaging | Main contribution is interface-strain mapping and non-destructive detection of heterogeneous deformation and failure localization | Not a stiffness paper, but among the best analogs for detecting interfacial slip/slip-initiation using DIC rather than mislabeling it as material nonlinearity (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035) |
| Habib 2024 | Thesis / 10.25916/sut.26281492 | 5×5×5 arrays of 10 mm unit cells at 15% relative density for wearable impact protection; multiple lattice topologies | HP PA12 via MJF | ASTM D638-14 for constituent tensile characterization | MTS Criterion Electromechanical Universal Test System Model 43 for tensile coupons with optical extensometer; compression speed not recovered in excerpt | Used quasi-static compression plus FEA to compare topologies for specific energy absorption and transmitted stress; highlighted instability from buckling-dominated topologies | Good application analog for protective cushioning and relative-density-controlled lattice screening; retrieved excerpt lacks compression machine speed/details (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000021) |

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort
        - CASE_CONTROL: Case-Control
        - CASE_ONLY: Case-Only
        - CASE_CROSSOVER: Case-Crossover
        - ECOLOGIC_OR_COMMUNITY: Ecologic or Community
        - FAMILY_BASED: Family-Based
        - DEFINED_POPULATION: Defined Population
        - NATURAL_HISTORY: Natural History
        - OTHER: Other

    DesignMasking:
        - NONE: None (Open Label)
        - SINGLE: Single
        - DOUBLE: Double
        - TRIPLE: Triple
        - QUADRUPLE: Quadruple

    WhoMasked:
        - PARTICIPANT: Participant
        - CARE_PROVIDER: Care Provider
        - INVESTIGATOR: Investigator
        - OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR: Outcomes Assessor

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

List of disease names to search for.
