The excerpt reports that multi-material FFF parts show significant variation in impact and fracture behaviour depending on material pairing and print parameters. PETG's amorphous, ductile nature helps dissipate impact energy via plastic deformation and fibril pull-out, while combinations with more brittle polymers (e.g., PLA) produce hybrid fracture modes and accelerated crack propagation. Printing parameters matter: specimens with ID 100% and RA 90° showed roughly 35–60% higher impact strength than ID 50% and RA 45°, attributed to more uniform interlayer bonds and fewer internal voids. SEM observations revealed common interfacial problems in multimaterial prints—fibril pull-out, microcracks, interlayer gaps, separation zones, and delamination—especially where materials have incompatible thermal/melt behaviour or low surface energy, which favors interface failure and changes in crack path. When material combinations are poorly chosen, fractures often initiate at interfaces and reduce part integrity. These findings are relevant to PETG–TPU interfaces insofar as PETG's ductility and compatibility/melting behaviour, print orientation (raster angle), and infill-related interlayer contact will influence interface bonding and the likelihood of delamination or interfacial failure.

TPU is viscoelastic and shows deformation recovery under cyclic loading; cyclic tests can exhibit hysteresis driven by polymer viscoelasticity and filler–matrix interactions, which can complicate interpretation of load–displacement curves (e.g., hysteresis, energy dissipation). Asymmetric tension–compression connectivity governs deformation delocalization in truss-based metamaterials Valid Text Names: 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 1-2', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 2-4', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 4-5', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 5-8', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 8-9', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 9-10', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 10-10' BibTex: @article{ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity, author = "Ruffini, Franco N. and Rimoli, Julian J.", title = "Asymmetric tension–compression connectivity governs deformation delocalization in truss-based metamaterials", year = "2026", journal = "npj Metamaterials", volume = "2", month = "Mar", doi = "10.1038/s44455-026-00020-1", url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/s44455-026-00020-1" } Abstract: Abstract

Failure in most material systems is characterized by strain localization, where deformation concentrates within a narrow region. Recently, a class of truss-based metamaterials has been shown to undergo severe deformation without exhibiting localization [1]. The mechanisms underlying this unusual delocalized response remain unknown. Here, we employ graph theory to elucidate the origins of this behavior. Each lattice is represented as a pair of graphs—the tension and compression networks—and their topological properties are quantified using graph-theoretic metrics. We find that the onset of localization correlates strongly with connectivity measures of these graphs. Specifically, deformation delocalization arises from an asymmetry in connectivity between these networks: when the tension graph remains more connected than the compression graph, deformation spreads throughout the structure instead of localizing. Connectivity measures such as average global efficiency[2] capture this transition quantitatively. This framework provides design principles for creating materials and metamaterials that intrinsically resist failure localization.

These qualities make them ideal for lightweight, miniaturized and multi-functional structures3–8. However, achieving high enthalpy is challenging, as it requires combining conflicting properties: high stiffness, high strength and large recoverable strain9–11. Here, to address this challenge, we construct high-enthalpy elastic metamaterials from freely rotatable chiral metacells. This deformation mode stores considerable additional energy while having a minimal impact on peak stresses that define material failure. Abstract:
<jats:p>This study introduces a minimalist design strategy to engineer wave propagation in cellularmetamaterials by applying a single-parameter twist to the classical Kelvin unit cell. By breaking the cell’s symmetry while preserving its lattice topology, this geometric modification activates and tunes band-gap frequencies with only a 3% mass increase, thereby obviating increased geometric complexity and significant mass augmentation often required to achieve wave-filtering performance at low frequencies. The proposed strategy relies on complex-valued Bloch–Floquet analysis of quasi-one-dimensional periodic chains (but is not restricted to) that reveals symmetry-breaking triggers activating two distinct wave attenuation mechanisms: wide Bragg-type and narrow polarization-dependent band gaps arising from longitudinal–torsional mode coupling.These findings are substantiated by a physics-driven analytical model that captures the mode coupling-induced avoided crossings and provides key insight into the wave characteristics of twisted architectures. The predictive fidelity of this approach is validated by transmissionmeasurements on SLA three-cell specimens, which reveal up to 20 dB of wave attenuation. Wealso demonstrate that accounting for material viscoelasticity is essential for accurate prediction, as idealized linear-elastic models are insufficient to capture band-gap frequencies in polymer-based chains. Overall, we proved that modest, well-defined modifications to a classical parentgeometry yield advanced wave-filtering performance at low frequencies. This offers a tractableand methodologically complete design strategy for vibration control in lightweight lattices.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000038

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 7-8'.

Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes tensegrity metamaterials designed to produce delocalized deformation, which yields distributed elastic stable buckling (reversible) rather than localized member failure, giving exceptional failure resistance and high energy absorption. Specimens were 3D-printed by two-photon polymerization (TPP-DLW) in IP-Dip (Nanoscribe) on fused silica. Quasi-static compression testing used full stress–strain characterization: E taken as maximum slope of the linear regime, σy from 0.2% offset, plateau strength σp averaged between 20–40% strain, and absorbed energy U as the integral of the stress–strain curve to densification or failure. Internal deformation maps were measured by DIC to quantify delocalization (ηd). Finite-element simulations (ABAQUS, modified RIKS) modeled 6×6×6 elementary-cell tensegrity, octet and iso trusses with small randomized imperfections and matched experimental dimensions; results were reported scale-independent and indicate translatability to metals. Numerically optimized tensegrity showed 3–18× (σ vs U) and 2–7× (E vs U) improvements versus first-order beam lattices, and experiments showed up to 5× higher σ–U combinations, demonstrating that tensegrity architectures outperform many beam-, shell- and hierarchical lightweight designs for reversible, high-energy-absorbing, failure-resistant compression behavior.

## pqac-00000039

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 2-3'.

Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The authors fabricated space-tileable 3D tensegrity metamaterials by recursively reflecting truncated-octahedron elementary cells and 3D-printed them using two-photon polymerization direct laser writing (TPP-DLW). Cells contain tensile members along edges and isolated compressive members inside, satisfying tensegrity topology. Specimens (6×6×6 cells) covered relative densities of 4–12%; truss members were square bars with ≈950 nm edge length and cell sizes 10–20 µm. Mechanical testing used displacement-controlled uniaxial compression with in situ imaging and digital image correlation (DIC) to map local deformation (map element areas a relative to a0). Compared with octet and Kelvin lattices, the tensegrity showed highly uniform, strain-independent deformation and no detectable localized damage up to at least 30% strain. The tensegrity exhibited a fully stable, monotonic stress–strain response with a smooth, elongated post-yield plateau and densification above ε ≈ 62.5%. By contrast, the octet underwent localized damage and system instability at ε ≈ 2.6% and its delocalization efficiency ηd fell to 35%; the Kelvin foam localized above ε ≈ 17% with ηd dropping to 67%. The tensegrity maintained ηd > 90% throughout, linking delocalized deformation to improved energy absorption and failure resistance.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 6-7'.

Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports monotonic compressive testing and finite-element simulations comparing 3D-printed tensegrity lattices to octet and Kelvin continuous-compression architectures at matched density/strength (notably 4% relative density). Experiments and simulations show tensegrity lattices exhibit delocalized deformation, stable stress–strain responses, and greatly enhanced damage resistance: the tensegrity retained load-bearing capacity up to densification (ε = 62.5%), and at εc = 70% the octet had only 7% of its initial stiffness versus 70% for the tensegrity. Although the octet’s initial stiffness/strength were higher (≈14× and 9×), tensegrity absorbed far more energy before failure (≈13× vs octet and ≈2× vs Kelvin in experiments). Strain energy U was computed as the area under stress–strain curves up to failure/densification. Simulations reproduced experiments, showed localization and unstable stress drops in octet/Kelvin, and enabled numerical optimization of tensile/compressive member cross-sections to double tensegrity performance and further increase absorbed energy (up to 26× and 4× vs octet/Kelvin; down to very low densities predicted energy-absorption gains up to 225×). Fabrication used TPP-DLW polymer printing for 2–5% relative density samples.

The authors fabricated tensegrity, octet and Kelvin lattice specimens by two-photon polymerization direct laser writing (TPP-DLW) using IP-Dip polymer. Specimens (6×6×6 cells) were printed at 10 µm s−1, with bars hatched from seven print lines; laser power and hatching distance were tuned (7.275–8.625 mW, 60–90 nm) to produce square-shaped bar cross sections. Post-processing included PGMEA and isopropanol baths and critical-point drying. Relative densities from ≈4% to 12% were achieved by changing elementary cell size (tensegrity cell sizes 18.1–10.6 µm for ≈4–12% density). SEM characterization measured member cross-section heights and widths (tensegrity ~1047 ± 86 nm by 832 ± 14 nm; octet ~1113 ± 40 by 847 ± 25 nm). The tensegrity geometry was parametrically optimized (tensile/compressive member edge lengths set to 1300 and 450 nm) to maximize strength, stiffness and absorbed strain energy while holding density constant. Finite-element simulations used a nonlinear material model representative of IP-Dip. ## pqac-00000046

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 29-34'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt cites ASTM E111-04 (Standard test method for Young’s modulus, tangent modulus, and chord modulus) and ASTM E83-06 (verification and classification of extensometer systems), indicating the study references the formal standards for modulus determination and extensometer verification. Relevant methodological research is cited: Graham & Adler (2011) on determining slope and quality of fit for the linear part of a test record, and Scibetta & Schuurmans (2004) on an algorithm to determine the initial linear portion of a force–displacement record—both directly related to toe correction and selection of tangent/secant regions. Figures report measured modulus and 0.2% offset yield strength as a function of number/usage of extensometers, highlighting the influence of extensometer configuration on modulus determination. Another figure notes lubricant effects on stress–strain behavior, which can affect initial contact/toe behavior. While the excerpt references standards and studies relevant to tangent/secant modulus, toe correction, and extensometer practices, it does not present a detailed machine load-frame compliance correction protocol in these pages.


---

## pqac-00000047

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 24-26'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt describes a reanalysis of compression stress-strain curves (per ASTM E111) to obtain consistent elastic modulus values (EGA) using a Scibetta–Schuurmans based nine-step procedure. Laboratories often used ASTM E83 Class B-2 extensometers, and E9 Section 9.2 permits B-2 when yield strength is primary; ASTM E111 would require a Class B-1 for modulus as the primary parameter. The nine steps include: locating the knee of the curve (points e1 at s1 = 0.05 max(s), eo=e1 with so=0.2 max(s), and finding (et,st) tangent through (eo,so)); truncating and normalizing data at (et,st); checking digital resolution (with a rule that no more than 25% of points should have zero change); applying the Scibetta–Schuurmans algorithm to find the optimal fit window (considering all subsets with at least 20% of data and selecting lowest residual std. dev.); checking noise (standard error in strain or stress ≤ 0.01); extending the fit to include points within one standard error; refitting to get EGA; checking residual curvature (slope in outer quartiles ≤ 0.05) and ensuring the optimal fit stress range > 0.4st. Quality metrics are defined for digital resolution, noise, curvature, and fit range. The accepted aluminum modulus used for error assessment was EaccAl = 75.2 GPa and the absolute error is defined as ∆EGA = |EaccAl − EGA|.


---

## pqac-00000048

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 6-11'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

This interlaboratory compression study followed ASTM E9 and required fixture qualification per E9 Section 6.6. Participants used at least one extensometer (gauge lengths reported in Table 3, e.g. G = 25.4 mm or 12.7 mm), ran tests at a nominal strain rate of 0.005 min−1, and intentionally did not report strain from actuator displacement. Laboratories used a variety of fixturing/alignment approaches (sub-presses, precision-ground sub-presses, adjustable platens, two-opposed extensometers) to control alignment and reduce fixturing effects. Electronic stress-strain traces were collected and returned. For ‘toe’ correction the organizers (or analysts) shifted each stress-strain curve along the strain axis so that a linear fit to the stress-strain data in the range 50–175 MPa intercepted the origin — effectively removing initial offset before determining modulus. These details imply recommended practice for tangent/secant modulus determination: use extensometer-measured strain (not actuator displacement), collect high-resolution stress-strain traces, qualify fixtures per E9, control alignment (sub-press/precision platens), and apply a linear-fit-based toe correction over an appropriate stress range prior to modulus extraction. The excerpt does not provide a step-by-step machine compliance correction protocol, but fixture qualification and avoidance of actuator-displacement strain measurement are emphasized.

## pqac-00000049

From text 'potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 21-24'.

Petrina C. Potts, Li Ma, Stephen M. Graham, and Matthew A. Adler. Repeatability and reproducibility of compression strength measurements conducted according to astm e9. ArXiv, Sep 2010. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.tn.1679, doi:10.6028/nist.tn.1679. This article has 17 citations.

The excerpt references ASTM E111 as the standard for validating compression test fixtures for elastic modulus: laboratories should measure aluminum 2024-T4 per E111 and obtain measurements on five consecutive specimens within 5% of E = 73.8 GPa. This interlaboratory study of ASTM E9 compression testing reports key points relevant to measuring elastic modulus and yield strength in compression. Participants commonly used extensometers attached to the specimen; using diametrically opposed extensometers (vs a single extensometer) substantially improved precision. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Phase | Step | Checklist item | Target / setting | Record in metadata / file | Why / note | Citation |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-Test | 1 | Verify specimen has been conditioned before test | 48 h at 23 °C, 50 % RH | `conditioning_time_h`, `conditioning_temp_C`, `conditioning_RH_pct` | Reduces moisture/history variability in PETG/TPU; aligns with AM polymer coupon practice | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000031) |
| Pre-Test | 2 | Inspect specimen visually before handling | No obvious warp, cracked struts, delaminated tendons, detached joints | `pretest_visual_status`, `notes` | Reject obviously defective prints before loading | (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000033) |
| Pre-Test | 3 | Assign and confirm unique specimen ID | Use permanent ID on bag + worksheet + CSV | `specimen_id` | Prevents data/design mismatch in later BO loop | (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000037) |
| Pre-Test | 4 | Measure mass | 0.01 g scale; 2 repeated readings if difference >0.02 g, take third and average | `mass_g` | Needed for relative density checks and SEA later | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000022) |
| Pre-Test | 5 | Measure overall geometry | Calipers, 0.01 mm resolution; measure height and two orthogonal widths at 3 locations each | `height_mm`, `width_x_mm`, `width_y_mm`, `bounding_cube_mm` | Use measured dimensions, not CAD only | (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022) |
| Pre-Test | 6 | Measure key feature sizes if accessible | Strut diameter and tendon diameter at 3 representative locations | `strut_diameter_mm`, `tendon_diameter_mm` | As-built dimensions can differ from nominal and affect stiffness | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000022) |
| Pre-Test | 7 | Photograph specimen before test | All faces + top/bottom + isometric, with ruler/scale bar and specimen ID visible | image filenames in `photo_pre_paths` | Supports later failure/joint-slip interpretation | (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032) |
| Pre-Test | 8 | Verify required print metadata is complete | Confirm print log is attached | `design_family`, `n_bars`, `cell_type`, `strut_material`, `tendon_material`, `joint_type`, `relative_density`, `print_date`, `printer_id`, `nozzle_temp_C`, `bed_temp_C`, `layer_height_mm`, `infill_pct`, `raster_angle_deg`, `build_orientation` | Essential for AM reproducibility/reporting | (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000031) |
| Mounting | 9 | Select load cell and confirm zero/load range | Prefer smallest verified cell that keeps peak load in useful range; if only available, use 5 kN and verify low-load resolution | `load_cell_kN`, `load_cell_serial`, `E4_class_if_known` | Low-load tendon-dominated response is sensitive to poor load resolution | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004) |
| Mounting | 10 | Confirm platen condition | Clean flat platens; remove debris; inspect for nicks | `platen_type`, `platen_surface_condition` | Surface condition affects initial contact stiffness | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000050) |
| Mounting | 11 | Decide whether to use PTFE / low-friction film | Use PTFE film only if barreling/friction suspected; keep choice fixed within a batch | `interface_film_used`, `film_type` | Friction/lubrication changes apparent modulus and yield | (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000048) |
| Mounting | 12 | Center specimen on lower platen | Align projected center of specimen with platen centerline | `mounting_centered_yes_no` | Reduces bending/eccentric loading | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000051) |
| Mounting | 13 | Check parallelism / alignment | Bring upper platen close without contact; verify specimen top is visually parallel; adjust if needed | `alignment_checked_yes_no` | Non-axial loading biases stiffness | (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000051) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 14 | Start data acquisition before contact | Record from before first contact | raw file name in `raw_data_path` | Preserves toe/contact region for later correction | (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000046) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 15 | Approach slowly to contact | Crosshead speed 0.5 mm/min until preload threshold reached | `contact_find_speed_mm_min` | Gentle seating limits impact/contact artifact | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 16 | Set preload / contact criterion | Detect 0.5–1.0 N sustained preload | `preload_N` | Defines test zero consistently for soft specimens | (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000052) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 17 | Hold briefly after preload | 3–5 s hold after preload before zeroing displacement | `preload_hold_s` | Lets load settle before zeroing | (pqac-00000052) |
| Alignment / Contact-Find | 18 | Zero displacement at preload | Zero crosshead position at preload; if DIC/video extensometry is used, also define local zero | `zero_method` | Needed for repeatable structural stiffness extraction | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000052) |
| Preconditioning | 19 | Run preconditioning cycles | 5 cycles to 5 % nominal strain at 1 mm/min | `preconditioning_cycles`, `preconditioning_strain_pct`, `preconditioning_speed_mm_min` | TPU and elastomeric systems show first-cycle softening/hysteresis/history effects | (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) |
| Preconditioning | 20 | Pause between cycles | 30 s between cycles | `preconditioning_pause_s` | Improves comparability of cyclic response | (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012) |
| Preconditioning | 21 | Watch live force–displacement trace during cycling | Look for settling after first cycle and any sudden drops/clicks | `preconditioning_observation`, `notes` | Helps identify joint slip versus normal Mullins-like behavior | (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036) |
| Preconditioning | 22 | Stop and flag if damage occurs during preconditioning | Abort if visible joint tearing, tendon detachment, or force drop >20 % at same displacement | `abort_reason` if applicable | First stiffness run should not consume specimen in preconditioning | (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000045) |

{"answer": "# Technical Brief: Instron Stiffness Testing Protocol for Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity-Inspired Unit Cells

**Program:** BYU Mentored Research Grant (PIs Hill & Baird) — `vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization`, Issue #49
**Scope:** First-round quasi-static stiffness characterization of PETG + TPU 85A co-printed tensegrity-inspired specimens on a screw-driven Instron load frame.

---

## 1. Applicable ASTM / ISO Standards

No single standard was written for multi-material, mechanism-dominated tensegrity-inspired cellular specimens. The testing campaign must therefore assemble a standards portfolio, cite each one for a specific sub-task, and disclose deviations. The following table maps each standard to your specimen class, identifies normative vs. informative roles, and flags the adaptation gap.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Recommended primary citation stack for an ASME JMD / IDETC paper:**
ASTM D638 + ASTM D412 for material cards; ASTM D1621 or ASTM C365 (adapted, deviations disclosed) for unit-cell compression; ASTM E111 for modulus extraction; ASTM E9 for fixture/alignment practice; ISO/ASTM 52900 + 52921 + ASTM F2971 for AM reporting. ISO 13314, while written for porous metals, provides excellent methodological language for cellular-specimen testing including representative cell counts and cyclic unloading modulus determination (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000017).

**Most-cited published examples following these standards for similar geometries:**
- ASTM D638 for AM polymer coupons: Ahmed et al. (2023) for PLA tensile at 5 mm/min on Instron 5585 (pqac-00000017); Habib (2024) used ASTM D638-14 Type I for HP PA12 (pqac-00000005).
- ASTM D412 for TPU tensile: Bates et al. (2016) applied D412 for NinjaFlex/SemiFlex coupons, obtaining low-strain moduli of 26.5 and 89.5 MPa respectively (pqac-00000020).
- ASTM C365 for sandwich-core compression: Ye et al. (2019) and Dikshit et al. (2016) both used ASTM C365 for 3D-printed lattice core compression.
- ASTM E9 / ASTM D790 for fixture and compliance: Solyaev et al. (2023) performed compliance correction per ASTM D790 on an Instron 5969 (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000014).
- ISO 13314 for cellular compression: Raghavendra et al. (2021) followed ISO 13314:2011 at 1 mm/min with 1 kHz acquisition and LVDT displacement sensing (pqac-00000000).

---

## 2. Best Practices / Pitfalls for the Actual Instron Test

### 2.1 Crosshead Speed and Strain Rate
A crosshead speed of **1 mm/min** is the most common quasi-static rate for lattice/cellular compression in the published analog set (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000016). For a 25–50 mm specimen this yields a nominal strain rate of 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ to 6.7 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Report both the commanded crosshead speed and the nominal engineering strain rate (crosshead speed / initial specimen height). If using DIC-derived local strain, report that separately. Bates et al. (2016) tested TPU honeycombs at higher strain rates (0.03–0.3 s⁻¹), which is relevant for later energy-absorption studies but not first-round stiffness (pqac-00000001).

### 2.2 Platen Choice
Use **flat, hardened steel platens** per ASTM E9 fixture practice (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048). Consider PTFE anti-friction film between platen and specimen if barreling or friction-induced stiffening is suspected; keep the choice fixed within a batch. The NIST interlaboratory study found that lubrication vs. no lubrication changed measured modulus by approximately 5.7% and yield strength by 3.1% in metal compression (pqac-00000051). For tensegrity cells where the top face may not be flat, a **thin compliant shim** (silicone sheet, ~1 mm) can improve contact uniformity, but this must be documented and the shim compliance subtracted. Spherically-seated platens are an option for alignment but introduce a rotational degree of freedom that may activate the tensegrity mechanism prematurely; use with caution and document.

### 2.3 Machine Compliance Correction
This is **critical** for sub-mm deformations of soft cellular specimens. Crosshead displacement includes load-string compliance (load cell, platens, couplings) that cannot be distinguished from specimen deformation without correction (pqac-00000052). The recommended protocol:
1. Run a platen-to-platen (no specimen) compression to the expected peak load, recording force vs. crosshead displacement.
2. Fit a linear compliance curve C_machine = Δδ/ΔF (mm/N).
3. Subtract C_machine × F(t) from the measured crosshead displacement at each time point.
4. Alternatively, and preferably, use a **non-contact extensometer** (DIC or video gauge) to measure specimen deformation directly, bypassing compliance entirely.

Solyaev et al. (2023) performed compliance correction per ASTM D790 and noted it was important for accurate modulus extraction from lattice tests on an Instron 5969 (pqac-00000002). The NIST study found that actuator-displacement-based stress was ~1.4% higher than extensometer-based measures even after correction (pqac-00000049). For your TPU-dominated specimens at low loads, compliance errors can exceed 50% of apparent deformation; DIC or a clip-on displacement transducer on the platens is strongly recommended.

### 2.4 Preload / Contact-Find and Toe Correction
Apply a preload of **0.5–1.0 N** at a slow approach speed (0.5 mm/min) to establish contact (pqac-00000048). Zero the displacement reference at this preload. For toe-region removal, the NIST ASTM E9 study shifted stress-strain curves so that a linear fit in the range 50–175 MPa (for aluminum) intercepted the origin (pqac-00000048). For your low-force polymeric cells, apply an analogous procedure: identify the initial linear region of the force-displacement curve, extend the linear fit back to zero force, and shift the displacement origin accordingly, per the intent of ASTM E111 (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047).

### 2.5 Non-Contact Extensometry
Bates et al. (2016) used a **video gauge with speckle-pattern markers** on the compression platens to verify crosshead-derived positional measurements (pqac-00000001). Pahari (2024) applied **2D DIC** with simultaneous front and side imaging to detect interfacial strain concentrations in multi-material FFF parts (pqac-00000032). For your specimens, a camera-based approach is ideal: apply speckle or fiducial markers to the top and bottom platens (or directly on the specimen if it has a flat PETG face) and compute the relative displacement at ≥10 Hz. This eliminates frame compliance from the stiffness calculation and provides strain-field data useful for detecting joint slip.

### 2.6 Conditioning: Mullins Effect in TPU
TPU exhibits a complex cyclic response that differs from classical Mullins softening in crosslinked rubbers. Scetta et al. (2021) demonstrated that soft TPU shows large hysteresis on the first load-unload cycle, pronounced softening after the first loading, marked residual deformation, and — importantly — a **stiffening** effect (not just softening) under step-cyclic loading at strains above ~1.5 Hencky strain, attributed to hard-domain fragmentation and additional physical crosslinking (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). Holzweber et al. (2018) explicitly applied "pre-cycles to avoid the Mullins- or softening effect" and noted that hysteresis decreases with increasing cycle count (pqac-00000010). Zhou et al. (2025) used an energy-ratio metric W₄/W₁ (fourth-cycle loading energy over first-cycle) to quantify Mullins-related softening, with lower ratios indicating stronger preconditioning damage (pqac-00000011).

**Recommendation:** Run **5 preconditioning cycles** to 5% nominal strain at 1 mm/min with 30 s pause between cycles. Compare the loading stiffness of cycles 1 and 5 to quantify conditioning magnitude. Report W₅/W₁ and note any irreversible residual strain. Do not precondition to more than 5% strain on a stiffness test — larger strains risk activating tensegrity buckling mechanisms that should be reserved for the energy-absorption campaign.

**Humidity:** PETG is hygroscopic — "absorbed water chemically attacks the polyester chains via hydrolysis" (pqac-00000031). TPU is also moisture-sensitive, with absorbed moisture affecting melt viscosity and mechanical properties (pqac-00000036). **Dry all filaments** before printing (60°C for PETG, 50°C for TPU, 4+ h) and condition finished specimens at 23 ± 2°C, 50 ± 5% RH for ≥48 h before testing (pqac-00000004).

### 2.7 Definition of "Stiffness" to Report
Report at minimum:
- **Structural stiffness k** = dF/dδ (N/mm) — the tangent of the force-displacement curve in the initial linear region after toe correction. Specify the displacement or strain window used (e.g., 1–5% nominal strain).
- **Secant structural stiffness** k_sec at a specified strain level (e.g., at 5% strain) — useful for comparing specimens with different toe-region behaviors.
- **Effective modulus** E_eff = k × h₀ / A₀ (MPa), where h₀ is the initial specimen height and A₀ is the projected bounding-box cross-sectional area. This is an apparent material-like property; it is not a true material modulus but is useful for comparison.
- **Non-dimensionalized relative modulus** E*/E_s = E_eff / E_solid and **relative density** ρ*/ρ_s = (mass / bounding volume) / ρ_solid, plotted in Gibson-Ashby fashion.

For the Gibson-Ashby framework, the canonical scaling is E*/E_s = C₁(ρ*/ρ_s)^n, where n ≈ 2 for bending-dominated open-cell structures and n ≈ 1 for stretching-dominated architectures (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027). The prefactor C₁ "includes all of the geometric constants of proportionality" and depends on unit-cell topology, cell size, stress type, and global shape (pqac-00000023). Tensegrity structures involve a mix of tension (stretching in tendons) and compression (strut buckling), so expect n between 1 and 2; fitting n from your data is itself a scientific contribution.

Bauer et al. (2021) defined E as the maximum slope of the linear regime, σ_y from a 0.2% offset, plateau stress σ_p averaged between 20–40% strain, and absorbed energy U as the integral of stress-strain to densification (pqac-00000038). This reporting framework is directly applicable to your later energy-absorption tests.

### 2.8 Replicates and Statistics
**Minimum n = 5** replicates per design variant for stiffness. Report mean ± SD and 95% CI. The ASTM E9 interlaboratory study found within-lab repeatability of ~1.1% CV and between-lab reproducibility of ~2.0% CV for yield strength of well-machined metal specimens (pqac-00000053); for FFF cellular parts expect substantially higher variability (5–15% CV). Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski (2024) tested groups of seven and reported mean curves with standard deviation bands (pqac-00000016); this is a good minimum. Produce extra samples to discard obviously defective prints (pqac-00000045). For later failure-related quantities (strength, SEA), report Weibull parameters if the dataset is large enough (≥15 specimens).

### 2.9 Build-Parameter Documentation per ASTM F2971 / ISO/ASTM 52921
For each specimen, record and report: build orientation (Z-up vs. XY-flat, per ISO/ASTM 52921 coordinate system), layer height (0.2 mm), nozzle diameter (0.4 mm), number of perimeters (≥3 for TPU tendons), infill pattern and density (100% for structural members), raster angle, nozzle temperature (by material), bed temperature, print speed, and any post-processing (none for initial tests) (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000031). This information is normative for peer review and essential for the BO loop.

---

## 3. Concrete First-Test Protocol (Checklist)

The following checklist can be handed directly to the undergraduate operator. It covers every step from pre-test conditioning through data export, and includes the metadata schema designed for downstream Bayesian optimization.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Specimen ID / Metadata Schema for BO

The metadata schema embedded in the checklist above captures all fields needed for a BoTorch/Ax Gaussian process surrogate to fit stiffness and SEA simultaneously. The design-space variables (inputs to the GP) should include at minimum: `design_family`, `n_bars`, `cell_type`, `strut_diameter_mm`, `tendon_diameter_mm`, `joint_type`, `relative_density`, and `build_orientation`. The response variables (outputs) should include: `k_tangent_N_mm`, `k_secant_N_mm`, `E_effective_MPa`, `hysteresis_ratio`, and (later) `SEA_J_g` and `peak_force_N`. Including `mass_g`, `bounding_cube_mm`, and printing parameters as contextual features allows the GP to account for process variability.

---

## 4. Stiffness-Specific vs. Strength/Energy-Absorption Test Design

The issue title is *stiffness testing*, and the differences from energy-absorption testing are critical:

| Parameter | Stiffness Test (current) | Energy-Absorption Test (later) |
|---|---|---|
| **Load limit** | 15–20% nominal strain (well below densification) | Full densification (60–80% strain) or until failure |
| **Strain window for metric extraction** | 1–5% strain for tangent stiffness; 0–10% for secant | Full curve: plateau stress (20–40% strain), densification onset, area under curve |
| **Preconditioning** | 5 cycles to 5% strain; establishes stable baseline | May include 5 cycles to full target strain; Mullins damage is intentional and itself a metric |
| **Replicate count** | n ≥ 5 per design; focus on precision of mean stiffness | n ≥ 5 for mean SEA; n ≥ 15 for Weibull failure statistics |
| **Reportable metrics** | k_tangent, k_secant, E_effective, E*/E_s, hysteresis ratio | Peak F, plateau σ, SEA (J/g), volumetric EA (J/cm³), compaction efficiency η, transmitted force |
| **Specimen reuse** | Specimen should be reusable (no damage at 15–20% strain) | Specimen may be consumed / damaged |

**Recommendation:** Measure stiffness in a **separate dedicated test campaign** rather than extracting it exclusively from the loading branch of energy-absorption tests. Reasons: (a) stiffness is sensitive to toe-region artifacts that are less critical for EA integral calculations; (b) the low-strain regime is where machine compliance errors are largest; (c) preconditioning for stiffness should be limited to small strains to avoid Mullins-altered response; (d) dedicated stiffness tests preserve specimens for potential re-testing or microscopy. However, also extract the **unloading tangent stiffness** from the first unloading cycle of EA tests (analogous to ISO 13314's cyclic unloading method) as a secondary stiffness metric for cross-validation (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000038).

---

## 5. Multi-Material FFF-Specific Considerations for Stiffness Data Quality

### 5.1 Layer-Stack Orientation Effect
FFF parts are inherently anisotropic. For PETG, tensile properties are strongest along the raster direction and weakest across layers (Z-direction), with modulus reductions of 15–40% reported for Z-built vs. XY-built specimens depending on material and parameters (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000037). **Recommendation:** Test struts printed in at least two orientations — (a) struts parallel to build direction (Z) and (b) struts perpendicular to build direction (XY) — using standalone coupon tests per ASTM D695/D638. For the full tensegrity cell, document the build orientation of the complete assembly and note which strut axis is closest to the build Z-axis.

### 5.2 PETG–TPU Interface Integrity and Joint-Slippage Detection
Multi-material FFF interfaces are weak zones. Arifvianto et al. (2022) found that PLA/TPU interfaces showed poor adhesion with torn/delaminated regions and TPU fibers lying over PLA rather than bonding (pqac-00000033). Dağlı (2025) reported SEM-observed microcracks, interlayer gaps, and delamination at multi-material boundaries, with fractures often initiating at interfaces (pqac-00000034). PETG–TPU peer-reviewed interface strength data does not exist in the literature surveyed.

**How to detect joint slippage in load-displacement data:**
- **Sudden force drops** (>10% at constant displacement rate) that are not associated with visible buckling indicate joint failure (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000033).
- **Slope changes** in the loading curve that cannot be attributed to known geometric nonlinearity (e.g., tensegrity mechanism engagement) may indicate progressive slip.
- **DIC** at the interface region is the most reliable detection method. Pahari (2024) demonstrated 2D DIC with simultaneous front and side imaging to capture heterogeneous deformation at multi-material boundaries in FFF parts (pqac-00000032).
- **Post-test inspection** of joint regions under magnification (10×–20× stereo microscope) looking for whitening, necking, gap opening, or fibrillation.

### 5.3 Mass / Dimensional Check Protocol
- Mass: 0.01 g precision balance; average two readings.
- Dimensions: digital calipers, 0.01 mm resolution; measure height and two orthogonal widths at three locations each and report mean ± range.
- If available, CT or structured-light scan to compare as-built vs. CAD geometry and compute actual relative density. Raghavendra et al. (2021) used µCT to quantify morphological deviations and found ~5% lower porosity in built vs. designed specimens, which materially affected stiffness predictions (pqac-00000022).

### 5.4 Aging / Batch Effects and Control Specimens
Print a batch of **control specimens** (a single, simple design variant — e.g., 3-bar prism in PETG+TPU) at the start of the campaign. Retest one control specimen every N = 10 test specimens (or once per test session, whichever is more frequent) to monitor for:
- Machine drift (load-cell calibration shift, platen wear).
- Material aging (PETG hydrolysis, TPU moisture uptake, UV exposure if stored near windows).
- Print-batch variability (filament lot, nozzle wear).

Track control-specimen stiffness on a control chart. If the control shifts by >2σ from the initial baseline, halt testing and investigate. This matches the campaign protocol described in the `idetc-abstract.tex` framework.

---

## 6. Closest Published Analogs

The following table summarizes the most directly relevant published studies, prioritized by similarity to your PETG/TPU FFF tensegrity-inspired specimens.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

**Key observations across the analog set:**
- No published study has tested multi-material PETG + TPU tensegrity-inspired cells. Your work is novel in this material combination and architecture family.
- The closest tensegrity architecture analogs (Bauer et al. 2021; Pajunen et al. 2019; Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski 2024) used single-material prints (IP-Dip polymer, PA2200, or PolyJet resins) rather than multi-material FFF (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).
- The closest material/process analogs (Bates et al. 2016; Arifvianto et al. 2022) tested TPU or PLA/TPU multi-material but not tensegrity architectures (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000033).
- Notably, **none of the tensegrity papers cited a named ASTM/ISO compression standard** — they all used custom compression protocols. This is a gap your paper can address by explicitly citing ASTM D1621 or C365 (adapted) and disclosing deviations.

---

## 7. Equipment-Specific Recommendations

### 7.1 Load Cell Selection
Your available 5 kN load cell is appropriate but may be at the upper limit. For tensegrity specimens of 5–30 g at 15–20% strain, expected peak forces will be in the range of approximately 1–200 N (based on Pajunen et al.'s initial stiffness of ~10–48 kPa for ~48 mm specimens giving forces of ~10–50 N, and your stiffer PETG struts potentially reaching higher values) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000019). The Instron 5 kN cell has accuracy ±0.5% down to 1/1000 of capacity (per Solyaev et al. on the 5969 platform), meaning ±0.025 N at 5 N and ±2.5 N at 500 N (pqac-00000002). At forces below ~5 N, the signal-to-noise ratio will be poor. If you find that peak forces consistently fall below 50 N, consider requesting or borrowing a **500 N or 1 kN load cell** for better resolution in the tendon-dominated low-strain regime. Bates et al. (2016) used a 1 kN load cell on an Instron 3343 for TPU honeycombs, which is a good precedent for soft cellular specimens (pqac-00000001).

### 7.2 Load-Cell Verification
Verify the load cell per **ASTM E4** (Force Verification for Testing Machines) before beginning the campaign. The standard requires verification at ≥5 points across the range and ±1% accuracy for Class A verification.

### 7.3 Data-Acquisition Rate
Acquire at **≥10 Hz** for quasi-static tests at 1 mm/min (pqac-00000001). Solyaev et al. (2023) used 2.5 kHz on an Instron 5969 (pqac-00000002); Raghavendra et al. (2021) used 1 kHz (pqac-00000000). Higher rates are beneficial for capturing any sudden events (joint slip, strut snap) but generate larger files. A practical recommendation is **50–100 Hz** — high enough to resolve transient events without excessive data volume.

### 7.4 Instron Platform Notes
- **Instron 5965** (5 kN maximum): Excellent choice if available; matched to your expected force range.
- **Instron 5969** (50 kN maximum): Workable but the 5 kN cell operates in the lower end of the frame capacity. Solyaev et al. (2023) successfully used this platform with a 50 kN cell for polymer lattices (pqac-00000002), but your forces will be much lower.
- **ElectroPuls E3000** (3 kN dynamic): Better suited for later cyclic/fatigue work or if you need precise displacement control at low forces. Pahari (2024) used this platform for interface shear tests (pqac-00000032).
- **MTS Insight**: Comparable to the Instron 59xx series; follow the same protocols.

---

## 8. Open Questions / Things the Lab Should Decide Before the First Test

1. **Platen interface:** Bare steel, PTFE film, or compliant shim? Run a quick pilot (3 specimens, one condition) comparing bare vs. PTFE before committing to a batch protocol.

2. **Preload threshold:** 0.5 N or 1.0 N? For very soft TPU-dominated cells, even 0.5 N may cause measurable deformation. Start with 0.5 N and verify it produces a clean toe-to-linear transition.

3. **Strain limit for stiffness test:** 15% or 20%? Test one sacrificial specimen to full densification to identify where the tensegrity mechanism engages (buckling plateau onset) and set the stiffness-test limit well below that transition.

4. **DIC availability:** Can a camera be set up to view the specimen during loading? Even a smartphone at 30 fps with fiducial markers provides useful backup displacement data. If a proper DIC system (e.g., GOM, VIC-2D, or open-source ncorr) is available, use it from day one.

5. **Load-cell swap:** Will a smaller load cell (500 N or 1 kN) be available or borrowable? If so, it is worth running a comparison test to quantify resolution improvement.

6. **Control-specimen design:** Finalize which single design variant serves as the batch control. Ideally choose the simplest cell (3-bar prism) with the most robust joints, so control-specimen failures are informative rather than routine.

7. **Joint-type priority for first batch:** The repo mentions anchor-bulb, dovetail, and TPU-rebar joint variants. Decide whether the first test batch sweeps all three joint types or fixes one and sweeps architecture.

8. **Temperature and humidity logging:** Is a lab datalogger running continuously? If not, record ambient temperature and humidity at the start and end of each test session. Both PETG and TPU are sensitive to moisture (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036).

9. **Filament drying protocol and verification:** Confirm that PETG and TPU filaments are dried before printing. PETG dries at 60–65°C for 4+ h; TPU at 50°C for 4+ h. Print a test specimen immediately after drying to establish the baseline.

10. **Post-test specimen disposition:** Will tested stiffness specimens be retained for later energy-absorption tests (possible if undamaged at 15–20% strain), or dedicated only to stiffness? Retaining them allows paired stiffness → EA data on the same specimen, which strengthens the BO surrogate model.

11. **Strain-window definition for k_tangent:** Fix the strain window (e.g., 1–5%, or 2–8%) before batch testing so that all specimens are compared on the same basis. The Scibetta-Schuurmans algorithm used in the NIST E9 study recommends that the fit range cover at least 40% of the elastic-region stress range for reliable modulus estimation (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000053).

12. **Compression direction for tensegrity prisms:** Define whether loading is axial (along the prism axis) or transverse. For Snelson-class 3-bar prisms, axial loading activates the tensegrity mechanism; transverse may collapse joints differently. Document and fix the loading direction per design family.

---

## References to Key Standards (for convenience)

- ASTM D695: Standard Test Method for Compressive Properties of Rigid Plastics
- ASTM D1621: Standard Test Method for Compressive Properties of Rigid Cellular Plastics
- ASTM D3574: Standard Test Methods for Flexible Cellular Materials
- ASTM D638: Standard Test Method for Tensile Properties of Plastics
- ASTM D412: Standard Test Methods for Vulcanized Rubber and Thermoplastic Elastomers—Tension
- ASTM C365/C365M: Standard Test Method for Flatwise Compressive Properties of Sandwich Cores
- ASTM E111: Standard Test Method for Young's Modulus, Tangent Modulus, and Chord Modulus
- ASTM E9: Standard Test Methods of Compression Testing of Metallic Materials at Room Temperature
- ASTM E4: Standard Practices for Force Verification of Testing Machines
- ASTM F2971: Standard Practice for Reporting Data for Test Specimens Prepared by Additive Manufacturing
- ISO 13314: Mechanical testing of metals — Ductility testing — Compression test for porous and cellular metals
- ISO/ASTM 52900: Additive manufacturing — General principles — Fundamentals and vocabulary
- ISO/ASTM 52921: Additive manufacturing — Standard terminology — Coordinate systems and test methodologies
- ISO 604: Plastics — Determination of compressive properties
- ISO 527: Plastics — Determination of tensile properties
- ISO 37: Rubber, vulcanized or thermoplastic — Determination of tensile stress-strain properties"}

function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Technical Brief: Instron Stiffness Testing Protocol for Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity-Inspired Unit Cells

**Program:** BYU Mentored Research Grant (PIs Hill & Baird) — `vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization`, Issue #49
**Scope:** First-round quasi-static stiffness characterization of PETG + TPU 85A co-printed tensegrity-inspired specimens on a screw-driven Instron load frame.

---

## 1. Applicable ASTM / ISO Standards

No single standard was written for multi-material, mechanism-dominated tensegrity-inspired cellular specimens. The testing campaign must therefore assemble a standards portfolio, cite each one for a specific sub-task, and disclose deviations. The following table maps each standard to your specimen class, identifies normative vs. informative roles, and flags the adaptation gap.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Recommended primary citation stack for an ASME JMD / IDETC paper:**
ASTM D638 + ASTM D412 for material cards; ASTM D1621 or ASTM C365 (adapted, deviations disclosed) for unit-cell compression; ASTM E111 for modulus extraction; ASTM E9 for fixture/alignment practice; ISO/ASTM 52900 + 52921 + ASTM F2971 for AM reporting. ISO 13314, while written for porous metals, provides excellent methodological language for cellular-specimen testing including representative cell counts and cyclic unloading modulus determination (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000017).

**Most-cited published examples following these standards for similar geometries:**
- ASTM D638 for AM polymer coupons: Ahmed et al. (2023) for PLA tensile at 5 mm/min on Instron 5585 (pqac-00000017); Habib (2024) used ASTM D638-14 Type I for HP PA12 (pqac-00000005).
- ASTM D412 for TPU tensile: Bates et al. (2016) applied D412 for NinjaFlex/SemiFlex coupons, obtaining low-strain moduli of 26.5 and 89.5 MPa respectively (pqac-00000020).
- ASTM C365 for sandwich-core compression: Ye et al. (2019) and Dikshit et al. (2016) both used ASTM C365 for 3D-printed lattice core compression.
- ASTM E9 / ASTM D790 for fixture and compliance: Solyaev et al. (2023) performed compliance correction per ASTM D790 on an Instron 5969 (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000014).
- ISO 13314 for cellular compression: Raghavendra et al. (2021) followed ISO 13314:2011 at 1 mm/min with 1 kHz acquisition and LVDT displacement sensing (pqac-00000000).

---

## 2. Best Practices / Pitfalls for the Actual Instron Test

### 2.1 Crosshead Speed and Strain Rate
A crosshead speed of **1 mm/min** is the most common quasi-static rate for lattice/cellular compression in the published analog set (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000016). For a 25–50 mm specimen this yields a nominal strain rate of 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ to 6.7 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Report both the commanded crosshead speed and the nominal engineering strain rate (crosshead speed / initial specimen height). If using DIC-derived local strain, report that separately. Bates et al. (2016) tested TPU honeycombs at higher strain rates (0.03–0.3 s⁻¹), which is relevant for later energy-absorption studies but not first-round stiffness (pqac-00000001).

### 2.2 Platen Choice
Use **flat, hardened steel platens** per ASTM E9 fixture practice (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048). Consider PTFE anti-friction film between platen and specimen if barreling or friction-induced stiffening is suspected; keep the choice fixed within a batch. The NIST interlaboratory study found that lubrication vs. no lubrication changed measured modulus by approximately 5.7% and yield strength by 3.1% in metal compression (pqac-00000051). For tensegrity cells where the top face may not be flat, a **thin compliant shim** (silicone sheet, ~1 mm) can improve contact uniformity, but this must be documented and the shim compliance subtracted. Spherically-seated platens are an option for alignment but introduce a rotational degree of freedom that may activate the tensegrity mechanism prematurely; use with caution and document.

### 2.3 Machine Compliance Correction
This is **critical** for sub-mm deformations of soft cellular specimens. Crosshead displacement includes load-string compliance (load cell, platens, couplings) that cannot be distinguished from specimen deformation without correction (pqac-00000052). The recommended protocol:
1. Run a platen-to-platen (no specimen) compression to the expected peak load, recording force vs. crosshead displacement.
2. Fit a linear compliance curve C_machine = Δδ/ΔF (mm/N).
3. Subtract C_machine × F(t) from the measured crosshead displacement at each time point.
4. Alternatively, and preferably, use a **non-contact extensometer** (DIC or video gauge) to measure specimen deformation directly, bypassing compliance entirely.

Solyaev et al. (2023) performed compliance correction per ASTM D790 and noted it was important for accurate modulus extraction from lattice tests on an Instron 5969 (pqac-00000002). The NIST study found that actuator-displacement-based stress was ~1.4% higher than extensometer-based measures even after correction (pqac-00000049). For your TPU-dominated specimens at low loads, compliance errors can exceed 50% of apparent deformation; DIC or a clip-on displacement transducer on the platens is strongly recommended.

### 2.4 Preload / Contact-Find and Toe Correction
Apply a preload of **0.5–1.0 N** at a slow approach speed (0.5 mm/min) to establish contact (pqac-00000048). Zero the displacement reference at this preload. For toe-region removal, the NIST ASTM E9 study shifted stress-strain curves so that a linear fit in the range 50–175 MPa (for aluminum) intercepted the origin (pqac-00000048). For your low-force polymeric cells, apply an analogous procedure: identify the initial linear region of the force-displacement curve, extend the linear fit back to zero force, and shift the displacement origin accordingly, per the intent of ASTM E111 (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047).

### 2.5 Non-Contact Extensometry
Bates et al. (2016) used a **video gauge with speckle-pattern markers** on the compression platens to verify crosshead-derived positional measurements (pqac-00000001). Pahari (2024) applied **2D DIC** with simultaneous front and side imaging to detect interfacial strain concentrations in multi-material FFF parts (pqac-00000032). For your specimens, a camera-based approach is ideal: apply speckle or fiducial markers to the top and bottom platens (or directly on the specimen if it has a flat PETG face) and compute the relative displacement at ≥10 Hz. This eliminates frame compliance from the stiffness calculation and provides strain-field data useful for detecting joint slip.

### 2.6 Conditioning: Mullins Effect in TPU
TPU exhibits a complex cyclic response that differs from classical Mullins softening in crosslinked rubbers. Scetta et al. (2021) demonstrated that soft TPU shows large hysteresis on the first load-unload cycle, pronounced softening after the first loading, marked residual deformation, and — importantly — a **stiffening** effect (not just softening) under step-cyclic loading at strains above ~1.5 Hencky strain, attributed to hard-domain fragmentation and additional physical crosslinking (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). Holzweber et al. (2018) explicitly applied "pre-cycles to avoid the Mullins- or softening effect" and noted that hysteresis decreases with increasing cycle count (pqac-00000010). Zhou et al. (2025) used an energy-ratio metric W₄/W₁ (fourth-cycle loading energy over first-cycle) to quantify Mullins-related softening, with lower ratios indicating stronger preconditioning damage (pqac-00000011).

**Recommendation:** Run **5 preconditioning cycles** to 5% nominal strain at 1 mm/min with 30 s pause between cycles. Compare the loading stiffness of cycles 1 and 5 to quantify conditioning magnitude. Report W₅/W₁ and note any irreversible residual strain. Do not precondition to more than 5% strain on a stiffness test — larger strains risk activating tensegrity buckling mechanisms that should be reserved for the energy-absorption campaign.

**Humidity:** PETG is hygroscopic — "absorbed water chemically attacks the polyester chains via hydrolysis" (pqac-00000031). TPU is also moisture-sensitive, with absorbed moisture affecting melt viscosity and mechanical properties (pqac-00000036). **Dry all filaments** before printing (60°C for PETG, 50°C for TPU, 4+ h) and condition finished specimens at 23 ± 2°C, 50 ± 5% RH for ≥48 h before testing (pqac-00000004).

### 2.7 Definition of "Stiffness" to Report
Report at minimum:
- **Structural stiffness k** = dF/dδ (N/mm) — the tangent of the force-displacement curve in the initial linear region after toe correction. Specify the displacement or strain window used (e.g., 1–5% nominal strain).
- **Secant structural stiffness** k_sec at a specified strain level (e.g., at 5% strain) — useful for comparing specimens with different toe-region behaviors.
- **Effective modulus** E_eff = k × h₀ / A₀ (MPa), where h₀ is the initial specimen height and A₀ is the projected bounding-box cross-sectional area. This is an apparent material-like property; it is not a true material modulus but is useful for comparison.
- **Non-dimensionalized relative modulus** E*/E_s = E_eff / E_solid and **relative density** ρ*/ρ_s = (mass / bounding volume) / ρ_solid, plotted in Gibson-Ashby fashion.

For the Gibson-Ashby framework, the canonical scaling is E*/E_s = C₁(ρ*/ρ_s)^n, where n ≈ 2 for bending-dominated open-cell structures and n ≈ 1 for stretching-dominated architectures (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027). The prefactor C₁ "includes all of the geometric constants of proportionality" and depends on unit-cell topology, cell size, stress type, and global shape (pqac-00000023). Tensegrity structures involve a mix of tension (stretching in tendons) and compression (strut buckling), so expect n between 1 and 2; fitting n from your data is itself a scientific contribution.

Bauer et al. (2021) defined E as the maximum slope of the linear regime, σ_y from a 0.2% offset, plateau stress σ_p averaged between 20–40% strain, and absorbed energy U as the integral of stress-strain to densification (pqac-00000038). This reporting framework is directly applicable to your later energy-absorption tests.

### 2.8 Replicates and Statistics
**Minimum n = 5** replicates per design variant for stiffness. Report mean ± SD and 95% CI. The ASTM E9 interlaboratory study found within-lab repeatability of ~1.1% CV and between-lab reproducibility of ~2.0% CV for yield strength of well-machined metal specimens (pqac-00000053); for FFF cellular parts expect substantially higher variability (5–15% CV). Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski (2024) tested groups of seven and reported mean curves with standard deviation bands (pqac-00000016); this is a good minimum. Produce extra samples to discard obviously defective prints (pqac-00000045). For later failure-related quantities (strength, SEA), report Weibull parameters if the dataset is large enough (≥15 specimens).

### 2.9 Build-Parameter Documentation per ASTM F2971 / ISO/ASTM 52921
For each specimen, record and report: build orientation (Z-up vs. XY-flat, per ISO/ASTM 52921 coordinate system), layer height (0.2 mm), nozzle diameter (0.4 mm), number of perimeters (≥3 for TPU tendons), infill pattern and density (100% for structural members), raster angle, nozzle temperature (by material), bed temperature, print speed, and any post-processing (none for initial tests) (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000031). This information is normative for peer review and essential for the BO loop.

---

## 3. Concrete First-Test Protocol (Checklist)

The following checklist can be handed directly to the undergraduate operator. It covers every step from pre-test conditioning through data export, and includes the metadata schema designed for downstream Bayesian optimization.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Specimen ID / Metadata Schema for BO

The metadata schema embedded in the checklist above captures all fields needed for a BoTorch/Ax Gaussian process surrogate to fit stiffness and SEA simultaneously. The design-space variables (inputs to the GP) should include at minimum: `design_family`, `n_bars`, `cell_type`, `strut_diameter_mm`, `tendon_diameter_mm`, `joint_type`, `relative_density`, and `build_orientation`. The response variables (outputs) should include: `k_tangent_N_mm`, `k_secant_N_mm`, `E_effective_MPa`, `hysteresis_ratio`, and (later) `SEA_J_g` and `peak_force_N`. Including `mass_g`, `bounding_cube_mm`, and printing parameters as contextual features allows the GP to account for process variability.

---

## 4. Stiffness-Specific vs. Strength/Energy-Absorption Test Design

The issue title is *stiffness testing*, and the differences from energy-absorption testing are critical:

| Parameter | Stiffness Test (current) | Energy-Absorption Test (later) |
|---|---|---|
| **Load limit** | 15–20% nominal strain (well below densification) | Full densification (60–80% strain) or until failure |
| **Strain window for metric extraction** | 1–5% strain for tangent stiffness; 0–10% for secant | Full curve: plateau stress (20–40% strain), densification onset, area under curve |
| **Preconditioning** | 5 cycles to 5% strain; establishes stable baseline | May include 5 cycles to full target strain; Mullins damage is intentional and itself a metric |
| **Replicate count** | n ≥ 5 per design; focus on precision of mean stiffness | n ≥ 5 for mean SEA; n ≥ 15 for Weibull failure statistics |
| **Reportable metrics** | k_tangent, k_secant, E_effective, E*/E_s, hysteresis ratio | Peak F, plateau σ, SEA (J/g), volumetric EA (J/cm³), compaction efficiency η, transmitted force |
| **Specimen reuse** | Specimen should be reusable (no damage at 15–20% strain) | Specimen may be consumed / damaged |

**Recommendation:** Measure stiffness in a **separate dedicated test campaign** rather than extracting it exclusively from the loading branch of energy-absorption tests. Reasons: (a) stiffness is sensitive to toe-region artifacts that are less critical for EA integral calculations; (b) the low-strain regime is where machine compliance errors are largest; (c) preconditioning for stiffness should be limited to small strains to avoid Mullins-altered response; (d) dedicated stiffness tests preserve specimens for potential re-testing or microscopy. However, also extract the **unloading tangent stiffness** from the first unloading cycle of EA tests (analogous to ISO 13314's cyclic unloading method) as a secondary stiffness metric for cross-validation (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000038).

---

## 5. Multi-Material FFF-Specific Considerations for Stiffness Data Quality

### 5.1 Layer-Stack Orientation Effect
FFF parts are inherently anisotropic. For PETG, tensile properties are strongest along the raster direction and weakest across layers (Z-direction), with modulus reductions of 15–40% reported for Z-built vs. XY-built specimens depending on material and parameters (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000037). **Recommendation:** Test struts printed in at least two orientations — (a) struts parallel to build direction (Z) and (b) struts perpendicular to build direction (XY) — using standalone coupon tests per ASTM D695/D638. For the full tensegrity cell, document the build orientation of the complete assembly and note which strut axis is closest to the build Z-axis.

### 5.2 PETG–TPU Interface Integrity and Joint-Slippage Detection
Multi-material FFF interfaces are weak zones. Arifvianto et al. (2022) found that PLA/TPU interfaces showed poor adhesion with torn/delaminated regions and TPU fibers lying over PLA rather than bonding (pqac-00000033). Dağlı (2025) reported SEM-observed microcracks, interlayer gaps, and delamination at multi-material boundaries, with fractures often initiating at interfaces (pqac-00000034). PETG–TPU peer-reviewed interface strength data does not exist in the literature surveyed.

**How to detect joint slippage in load-displacement data:**
- **Sudden force drops** (>10% at constant displacement rate) that are not associated with visible buckling indicate joint failure (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000033).
- **Slope changes** in the loading curve that cannot be attributed to known geometric nonlinearity (e.g., tensegrity mechanism engagement) may indicate progressive slip.
- **DIC** at the interface region is the most reliable detection method. Pahari (2024) demonstrated 2D DIC with simultaneous front and side imaging to capture heterogeneous deformation at multi-material boundaries in FFF parts (pqac-00000032).
- **Post-test inspection** of joint regions under magnification (10×–20× stereo microscope) looking for whitening, necking, gap opening, or fibrillation.

### 5.3 Mass / Dimensional Check Protocol
- Mass: 0.01 g precision balance; average two readings.
- Dimensions: digital calipers, 0.01 mm resolution; measure height and two orthogonal widths at three locations each and report mean ± range.
- If available, CT or structured-light scan to compare as-built vs. CAD geometry and compute actual relative density. Raghavendra et al. (2021) used µCT to quantify morphological deviations and found ~5% lower porosity in built vs. designed specimens, which materially affected stiffness predictions (pqac-00000022).

### 5.4 Aging / Batch Effects and Control Specimens
Print a batch of **control specimens** (a single, simple design variant — e.g., 3-bar prism in PETG+TPU) at the start of the campaign. Retest one control specimen every N = 10 test specimens (or once per test session, whichever is more frequent) to monitor for:
- Machine drift (load-cell calibration shift, platen wear).
- Material aging (PETG hydrolysis, TPU moisture uptake, UV exposure if stored near windows).
- Print-batch variability (filament lot, nozzle wear).

Track control-specimen stiffness on a control chart. If the control shifts by >2σ from the initial baseline, halt testing and investigate. This matches the campaign protocol described in the `idetc-abstract.tex` framework.

---

## 6. Closest Published Analogs

The following table summarizes the most directly relevant published studies, prioritized by similarity to your PETG/TPU FFF tensegrity-inspired specimens.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

**Key observations across the analog set:**
- No published study has tested multi-material PETG + TPU tensegrity-inspired cells. Your work is novel in this material combination and architecture family.
- The closest tensegrity architecture analogs (Bauer et al. 2021; Pajunen et al. 2019; Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski 2024) used single-material prints (IP-Dip polymer, PA2200, or PolyJet resins) rather than multi-material FFF (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).
- The closest material/process analogs (Bates et al. 2016; Arifvianto et al. 2022) tested TPU or PLA/TPU multi-material but not tensegrity architectures (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000033).
- Notably, **none of the tensegrity papers cited a named ASTM/ISO compression standard** — they all used custom compression protocols. This is a gap your paper can address by explicitly citing ASTM D1621 or C365 (adapted) and disclosing deviations.

---

## 7. Equipment-Specific Recommendations

### 7.1 Load Cell Selection
Your available 5 kN load cell is appropriate but may be at the upper limit. For tensegrity specimens of 5–30 g at 15–20% strain, expected peak forces will be in the range of approximately 1–200 N (based on Pajunen et al.'s initial stiffness of ~10–48 kPa for ~48 mm specimens giving forces of ~10–50 N, and your stiffer PETG struts potentially reaching higher values) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000019). The Instron 5 kN cell has accuracy ±0.5% down to 1/1000 of capacity (per Solyaev et al. on the 5969 platform), meaning ±0.025 N at 5 N and ±2.5 N at 500 N (pqac-00000002). At forces below ~5 N, the signal-to-noise ratio will be poor. If you find that peak forces consistently fall below 50 N, consider requesting or borrowing a **500 N or 1 kN load cell** for better resolution in the tendon-dominated low-strain regime. Bates et al. (2016) used a 1 kN load cell on an Instron 3343 for TPU honeycombs, which is a good precedent for soft cellular specimens (pqac-00000001).

### 7.2 Load-Cell Verification
Verify the load cell per **ASTM E4** (Force Verification for Testing Machines) before beginning the campaign. The standard requires verification at ≥5 points across the range and ±1% accuracy for Class A verification.

### 7.3 Data-Acquisition Rate
Acquire at **≥10 Hz** for quasi-static tests at 1 mm/min (pqac-00000001). Solyaev et al. (2023) used 2.5 kHz on an Instron 5969 (pqac-00000002); Raghavendra et al. (2021) used 1 kHz (pqac-00000000). Higher rates are beneficial for capturing any sudden events (joint slip, strut snap) but generate larger files. A practical recommendation is **50–100 Hz** — high enough to resolve transient events without excessive data volume.

### 7.4 Instron Platform Notes
- **Instron 5965** (5 kN maximum): Excellent choice if available; matched to your expected force range.
- **Instron 5969** (50 kN maximum): Workable but the 5 kN cell operates in the lower end of the frame capacity. Solyaev et al. (2023) successfully used this platform with a 50 kN cell for polymer lattices (pqac-00000002), but your forces will be much lower.
- **ElectroPuls E3000** (3 kN dynamic): Better suited for later cyclic/fatigue work or if you need precise displacement control at low forces. Pahari (2024) used this platform for interface shear tests (pqac-00000032).
- **MTS Insight**: Comparable to the Instron 59xx series; follow the same protocols.

---

## 8. Open Questions / Things the Lab Should Decide Before the First Test

1. **Platen interface:** Bare steel, PTFE film, or compliant shim? Run a quick pilot (3 specimens, one condition) comparing bare vs. PTFE before committing to a batch protocol.

2. **Preload threshold:** 0.5 N or 1.0 N? For very soft TPU-dominated cells, even 0.5 N may cause measurable deformation. Start with 0.5 N and verify it produces a clean toe-to-linear transition.

3. **Strain limit for stiffness test:** 15% or 20%? Test one sacrificial specimen to full densification to identify where the tensegrity mechanism engages (buckling plateau onset) and set the stiffness-test limit well below that transition.

4. **DIC availability:** Can a camera be set up to view the specimen during loading? Even a smartphone at 30 fps with fiducial markers provides useful backup displacement data. If a proper DIC system (e.g., GOM, VIC-2D, or open-source ncorr) is available, use it from day one.

5. **Load-cell swap:** Will a smaller load cell (500 N or 1 kN) be available or borrowable? If so, it is worth running a comparison test to quantify resolution improvement.

6. **Control-specimen design:** Finalize which single design variant serves as the batch control. Ideally choose the simplest cell (3-bar prism) with the most robust joints, so control-specimen failures are informative rather than routine.

7. **Joint-type priority for first batch:** The repo mentions anchor-bulb, dovetail, and TPU-rebar joint variants. Decide whether the first test batch sweeps all three joint types or fixes one and sweeps architecture.

8. **Temperature and humidity logging:** Is a lab datalogger running continuously? If not, record ambient temperature and humidity at the start and end of each test session. Both PETG and TPU are sensitive to moisture (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036).

9. **Filament drying protocol and verification:** Confirm that PETG and TPU filaments are dried before printing. PETG dries at 60–65°C for 4+ h; TPU at 50°C for 4+ h. Print a test specimen immediately after drying to establish the baseline.

10. **Post-test specimen disposition:** Will tested stiffness specimens be retained for later energy-absorption tests (possible if undamaged at 15–20% strain), or dedicated only to stiffness? Retaining them allows paired stiffness → EA data on the same specimen, which strengthens the BO surrogate model.

11. **Strain-window definition for k_tangent:** Fix the strain window (e.g., 1–5%, or 2–8%) before batch testing so that all specimens are compared on the same basis. The Scibetta-Schuurmans algorithm used in the NIST E9 study recommends that the fit range cover at least 40% of the elastic-region stress range for reliable modulus estimation (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000053).

12. **Compression direction for tensegrity prisms:** Define whether loading is axial (along the prism axis) or transverse. For Snelson-class 3-bar prisms, axial loading activates the tensegrity mechanism; transverse may collapse joints differently. Document and fix the loading direction per design family.

---

## References to Key Standards (for convenience)

- ASTM D695: Standard Test Method for Compressive Properties of Rigid Plastics
- ASTM D1621: Standard Test Method for Compressive Properties of Rigid Cellular Plastics
- ASTM D3574: Standard Test Methods for Flexible Cellular Materials
- ASTM D638: Standard Test Method for Tensile Properties of Plastics
- ASTM D412: Standard Test Methods for Vulcanized Rubber and Thermoplastic Elastomers—Tension
- ASTM C365/C365M: Standard Test Method for Flatwise Compressive Properties of Sandwich Cores
- ASTM E111: Standard Test Method for Young's Modulus, Tangent Modulus, and Chord Modulus
- ASTM E9: Standard Test Methods of Compression Testing of Metallic Materials at Room Temperature
- ASTM E4: Standard Practices for Force Verification of Testing Machines
- ASTM F2971: Standard Practice for Reporting Data for Test Specimens Prepared by Additive Manufacturing
- ISO 13314: Mechanical testing of metals — Ductility testing — Compression test for porous and cellular metals
- ISO/ASTM 52900: Additive manufacturing — General principles — Fundamentals and vocabulary
- ISO/ASTM 52921: Additive manufacturing — Standard terminology — Coordinate systems and test methodologies
- ISO 604: Plastics — Determination of compressive properties
- ISO 527: Plastics — Determination of tensile properties
- ISO 37: Rubber, vulcanized or thermoplastic — Determination of tensile stress-strain properties"}

Mentored Research Grant; PIs Hill & Baird; repo
``vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization``; tracking issue #49). The
overall campaign is a closed-loop **design -> print -> test -> Bayesian
optimization** workflow targeting energy-absorption / cushioning

**What we want from this query (be specific and prescriptive):**

1. **Applicable ASTM / ISO standards** for stiffness characterization of

   standard and our 3D-printed cellular tensegrity-inspired specimens (i.e.
