# Technical Brief: Instron Stiffness Testing Protocol for Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity-Inspired Unit Cells

**Program:** BYU Mentored Research Grant (PIs Hill & Baird) — `vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization`, Issue #49
**Scope:** First-round quasi-static stiffness characterization of PETG + TPU 85A co-printed tensegrity-inspired specimens on a screw-driven Instron load frame.

---

## 1. Applicable ASTM / ISO Standards

No single standard was written for multi-material, mechanism-dominated tensegrity-inspired cellular specimens. The testing campaign must therefore assemble a standards portfolio, cite each one for a specific sub-task, and disclose deviations. The following table maps each standard to your specimen class, identifies normative vs. informative roles, and flags the adaptation gap.

| Standard Number | Title/Scope | What It Measures | Specimen Geometry Requirements | Crosshead Speed / Strain Rate | Gap vs. Tensegrity Specimens | Normative vs. Informative for AM-tensegrity paper |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ASTM D695 | Compressive Properties of Rigid Plastics | Compressive strength, yield, strain at yield, modulus/apparent compressive behavior of rigid plastics | Standard coupon geometry for rigid plastics; intended for bulk, homogeneous specimens rather than open cellular architectures | Method-defined constant crosshead speed tied to specimen geometry/material response; report nominal strain rate and machine used | Good for PETG/PLA bulk coupons only; not directly valid for unit-cell architectures, tendon-dominated compliance, or jointed multi-material specimens. Use as constituent-material bracket, not structural-cell standard | **Normative** for PETG/PLA material-card compression coupons; **informative only** for whole tensegrity cells |
| ISO 604 | Plastics — Determination of Compressive Properties | Compressive stress-strain response and modulus of plastics | Prismatic/cylindrical bulk-plastic specimens with prescribed dimensions and end parallelism; homogeneous material assumption | Constant compression rate specified by standard by specimen type/material | Same gap as D695: appropriate for printed PETG/PLA coupons, not for sparse multi-material cells with large void fraction and mechanism-driven deformation | **Normative** for bulk plastic coupons; **informative only** for unit cells |
| ASTM D1621 | Compressive Properties of Rigid Cellular Plastics | Compressive stress-strain, strength, and apparent modulus of rigid foams/cellular plastics | Minimum specimen commonly interpreted as ~25.4 mm cube in practice for cellular materials; full specimen should be representative through thickness | Constant rate of crosshead motion selected to achieve specified nominal strain-rate regime for foams | Closest analog for single-cell or tiled rigid-dominant lattice/cellular specimens, but your specimens are open, architected, anisotropic, and multi-material rather than stochastic rigid foam. Must report architecture, loading direction, contact area definition, relative density, and any departures from cube geometry | **Normative-adjacent / preferred primary citation** for quasi-static compression of rigid-dominant cellular specimens if adapted and deviations disclosed |
| ASTM D3574 | Flexible Cellular Materials — Slab, Bonded, and Molded Urethane Foams | Flexible foam compression force-deflection, hysteresis, support factor, fatigue, and related cushioning metrics depending on test | Foam blocks/slabs with dimensions tied to specific subtests; intended for flexible foam products rather than architected open cells | Crosshead speed depends on subtest (typically force-deflection/compression-set style procedures with prescribed rates) | Useful analog for TPU-dominant cushioning response and hysteresis, but not directly for discrete tensegrity/lattice cells with rigid struts, nonuniform contact, and joint-slip risk. Must specify which subtest is adapted | **Informative**, especially for later cushioning/energy-absorption phases |
| ASTM D7726 | Standard Test Method for the Effect of Compression on High-Visibility/Protective Padding Materials (protective-material compression analog) | Compression behavior of protective padding/material systems under prescribed loading histories | Product-like padding specimens; geometry depends on protective material format | Standard-specified loading protocol for protective materials; report full test history | Potentially useful for application framing (protective gear), but not geometry-faithful for unit cells. Better for benchmarking later pad-level assemblies than early unit cells | **Informative** |
| ASTM F1614 | Test Method for Shock-Attenuating Properties of Materials Systems for Athletic Footwear / impact-attenuating systems | Shock attenuation / impact response of cushioning materials | Product/material-system specimens sized for impact apparatus, not quasi-static cell coupons | Impact protocol rather than quasi-static crosshead rate | Relevant to later impact/drop-weight campaign and protective-gear motivation, not first-round stiffness tests | **Informative** for roadmap; not primary for current quasi-static stiffness tests |

**Recommended primary citation stack for an ASME JMD / IDETC paper:**

**Most-cited published examples following these standards for similar geometries:**

For a 25–50 mm specimen this yields a nominal strain rate of 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ to 6.7 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Report both the commanded crosshead speed and the nominal engineering strain rate (crosshead speed / initial specimen height). If using DIC-derived local strain, report that separately. Bates et al. (2016) tested TPU honeycombs at higher strain rates (0.03–0.3 s⁻¹), which is relevant for later energy-absorption studies but not first-round stiffness (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 7-10).

### 2.2 Platen Choice
Use **flat, hardened steel platens** per ASTM E9 fixture practice (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11, potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 6-11). Consider PTFE anti-friction film between platen and specimen if barreling or friction-induced stiffening is suspected; keep the choice fixed within a batch. The NIST interlaboratory study found that lubrication vs. no lubrication changed measured modulus by approximately 5.7% and yield strength by 3.1% in metal compression (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 18-21). For tensegrity cells where the top face may not be flat, a **thin compliant shim** (silicone sheet, ~1 mm) can improve contact uniformity, but this must be documented and the shim compliance subtracted. Spherically-seated platens are an option for alignment but introduce a rotational degree of freedom that may activate the tensegrity mechanism prematurely; use with caution and document.

### 2.3 Machine Compliance Correction
This is **critical** for sub-mm deformations of soft cellular specimens. Crosshead displacement includes load-string compliance (load cell, platens, couplings) that cannot be distinguished from specimen deformation without correction (biesiekierski2020mechanicaltestingof pages 13-16). The recommended protocol:
1. Run a platen-to-platen (no specimen) compression to the expected peak load, recording force vs. crosshead displacement.
2. Fit a linear compliance curve C_machine = Δδ/ΔF (mm/N).
3. Subtract C_machine × F(t) from the measured crosshead displacement at each time point.
4. Alternatively, and preferably, use a **non-contact extensometer** (DIC or video gauge) to measure specimen deformation directly, bypassing compliance entirely.

Solyaev et al. (2023) performed compliance correction per ASTM D790 and noted it was important for accurate modulus extraction from lattice tests on an Instron 5969 (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11). The NIST study found that actuator-displacement-based stress was ~1.4% higher than extensometer-based measures even after correction (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 21-24). For your TPU-dominated specimens at low loads, compliance errors can exceed 50% of apparent deformation; DIC or a clip-on displacement transducer on the platens is strongly recommended.

### 2.4 Preload / Contact-Find and Toe Correction
Apply a preload of **0.5–1.0 N** at a slow approach speed (0.5 mm/min) to establish contact (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 6-11). Zero the displacement reference at this preload. For toe-region removal, the NIST ASTM E9 study shifted stress-strain curves so that a linear fit in the range 50–175 MPa (for aluminum) intercepted the origin (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 6-11). For your low-force polymeric cells, apply an analogous procedure: identify the initial linear region of the force-displacement curve, extend the linear fit back to zero force, and shift the displacement origin accordingly, per the intent of ASTM E111 (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 29-34, potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 24-26).

### 2.5 Non-Contact Extensometry
Bates et al. (2016) used a **video gauge with speckle-pattern markers** on the compression platens to verify crosshead-derived positional measurements (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 7-10). Pahari (2024) applied **2D DIC** with simultaneous front and side imaging to detect interfacial strain concentrations in multi-material FFF parts (pahari2024analysisofthe pages 65-70). For your specimens, a camera-based approach is ideal: apply speckle or fiducial markers to the top and bottom platens (or directly on the specimen if it has a flat PETG face) and compute the relative displacement at ≥10 Hz. This eliminates frame compliance from the stiffness calculation and provides strain-field data useful for detecting joint slip.

### 2.6 Conditioning: Mullins Effect in TPU
TPU exhibits a complex cyclic response that differs from classical Mullins softening in crosslinked rubbers. Scetta et al. (2021) demonstrated that soft TPU shows large hysteresis on the first load-unload cycle, pronounced softening after the first loading, marked residual deformation, and — importantly — a **stiffening** effect (not just softening) under step-cyclic loading at strains above ~1.5 Hencky strain, attributed to hard-domain fragmentation and additional physical crosslinking (scetta2021straininducedstrengthening pages 6-12, scetta2021straininducedstrengthening pages 1-6, scetta2021straininducedstrengthening pages 12-17). Holzweber et al. (2018) explicitly applied "pre-cycles to avoid the Mullins- or softening effect" and noted that hysteresis decreases with increasing cycle count (holzweber2018characterizationandmodeling pages 4-6). Zhou et al. (2025) used an energy-ratio metric W₄/W₁ (fourth-cycle loading energy over first-cycle) to quantify Mullins-related softening, with lower ratios indicating stronger preconditioning damage (zhou2025enhancingtheenergy pages 12-15).

**Recommendation:** Run **5 preconditioning cycles** to 5% nominal strain at 1 mm/min with 30 s pause between cycles. Compare the loading stiffness of cycles 1 and 5 to quantify conditioning magnitude. Report W₅/W₁ and note any irreversible residual strain. Do not precondition to more than 5% strain on a stiffness test — larger strains risk activating tensegrity buckling mechanisms that should be reserved for the energy-absorption campaign.

**Humidity:** PETG is hygroscopic — "absorbed water chemically attacks the polyester chains via hydrolysis" (lesniowski2025enhancingtheperformance pages 16-18). TPU is also moisture-sensitive, with absorbed moisture affecting melt viscosity and mechanical properties (lopes2024interfaceboundarymechanical pages 33-37). **Dry all filaments** before printing (60°C for PETG, 50°C for TPU, 4+ h) and condition finished specimens at 23 ± 2°C, 50 ± 5% RH for ≥48 h before testing (zhang20213dprintingof pages 44-52).

### 2.7 Definition of "Stiffness" to Report
Report at minimum:
- **Structural stiffness k** = dF/dδ (N/mm) — the tangent of the force-displacement curve in the initial linear region after toe correction. Specify the displacement or strain window used (e.g., 1–5% nominal strain).
- **Secant structural stiffness** k_sec at a specified strain level (e.g., at 5% strain) — useful for comparing specimens with different toe-region behaviors.
- **Effective modulus** E_eff = k × h₀ / A₀ (MPa), where h₀ is the initial specimen height and A₀ is the projected bounding-box cross-sectional area. This is an apparent material-like property; it is not a true material modulus but is useful for comparison.
- **Non-dimensionalized relative modulus** E*/E_s = E_eff / E_solid and **relative density** ρ*/ρ_s = (mass / bounding volume) / ρ_solid, plotted in Gibson-Ashby fashion.

For the Gibson-Ashby framework, the canonical scaling is E*/E_s = C₁(ρ*/ρ_s)^n, where n ≈ 2 for bending-dominated open-cell structures and n ≈ 1 for stretching-dominated architectures (maskery2015mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-4, roberts2002elasticpropertiesof pages 3-6, maskery2017aninvestigationinto pages 1-3, roberts2001elasticmoduliof pages 1-3). The prefactor C₁ "includes all of the geometric constants of proportionality" and depends on unit-cell topology, cell size, stress type, and global shape (maskery2015mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-4). Tensegrity structures involve a mix of tension (stretching in tendons) and compression (strut buckling), so expect n between 1 and 2; fitting n from your data is itself a scientific contribution.

Bauer et al. (2021) defined E as the maximum slope of the linear regime, σ_y from a 0.2% offset, plateau stress σ_p averaged between 20–40% strain, and absorbed energy U as the integral of stress-strain to densification (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 7-8). This reporting framework is directly applicable to your later energy-absorption tests.

### 2.8 Replicates and Statistics
**Minimum n = 5** replicates per design variant for stiffness. Report mean ± SD and 95% CI. The ASTM E9 interlaboratory study found within-lab repeatability of ~1.1% CV and between-lab reproducibility of ~2.0% CV for yield strength of well-machined metal specimens (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 26-29); for FFF cellular parts expect substantially higher variability (5–15% CV). Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski (2024) tested groups of seven and reported mean curves with standard deviation bands (sabounizawadzka2024experimentalinvestigationson pages 6-11); this is a good minimum. Produce extra samples to discard obviously defective prints (sabounizawadzka2024experimentalinvestigationsona pages 11-13). For later failure-related quantities (strength, SEA), report Weibull parameters if the dataset is large enough (≥15 specimens).

### 2.9 Build-Parameter Documentation per ASTM F2971 / ISO/ASTM 52921
For each specimen, record and report: build orientation (Z-up vs. XY-flat, per ISO/ASTM 52921 coordinate system), layer height (0.2 mm), nozzle diameter (0.4 mm), number of perimeters (≥3 for TPU tendons), infill pattern and density (100% for structural members), raster angle, nozzle temperature (by material), bed temperature, print speed, and any post-processing (none for initial tests) (daglı2025mechanicalcharacterizationand pages 4-7, lesniowski2025enhancingtheperformance pages 16-18). This information is normative for peer review and essential for the BO loop.

## 4. Stiffness-Specific vs. Strength/Energy-Absorption Test Design

The issue title is *stiffness testing*, and the differences from energy-absorption testing are critical:

| Parameter | Stiffness Test (current) | Energy-Absorption Test (later) |
|---|---|---|
| **Load limit** | 15–20% nominal strain (well below densification) | Full densification (60–80% strain) or until failure |
| **Strain window for metric extraction** | 1–5% strain for tangent stiffness; 0–10% for secant | Full curve: plateau stress (20–40% strain), densification onset, area under curve |
| **Preconditioning** | 5 cycles to 5% strain; establishes stable baseline | May include 5 cycles to full target strain; Mullins damage is intentional and itself a metric |
| **Replicate count** | n ≥ 5 per design; focus on precision of mean stiffness | n ≥ 5 for mean SEA; n ≥ 15 for Weibull failure statistics |
| **Reportable metrics** | k_tangent, k_secant, E_effective, E*/E_s, hysteresis ratio | Peak F, plateau σ, SEA (J/g), volumetric EA (J/cm³), compaction efficiency η, transmitted force |
| **Specimen reuse** | Specimen should be reusable (no damage at 15–20% strain) | Specimen may be consumed / damaged |

**Recommendation:** Measure stiffness in a **separate dedicated test campaign** rather than extracting it exclusively from the loading branch of energy-absorption tests. Reasons: (a) stiffness is sensitive to toe-region artifacts that are less critical for EA integral calculations; (b) the low-strain regime is where machine compliance errors are largest; (c) preconditioning for stiffness should be limited to small strains to avoid Mullins-altered response; (d) dedicated stiffness tests preserve specimens for potential re-testing or microscopy. However, also extract the **unloading tangent stiffness** from the first unloading cycle of EA tests (analogous to ISO 13314's cyclic unloading method) as a secondary stiffness metric for cross-validation (raghavendra2021uniaxialstaticmechanical pages 5-7, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 7-8).

## 5. Multi-Material FFF-Specific Considerations for Stiffness Data Quality

### 5.1 Layer-Stack Orientation Effect
FFF parts are inherently anisotropic. For PETG, tensile properties are strongest along the raster direction and weakest across layers (Z-direction), with modulus reductions of 15–40% reported for Z-built vs. XY-built specimens depending on material and parameters (lesniowski2025enhancingtheperformance pages 16-18, daglı2025mechanicalcharacterizationand pages 4-7). **Recommendation:** Test struts printed in at least two orientations — (a) struts parallel to build direction (Z) and (b) struts perpendicular to build direction (XY) — using standalone coupon tests per ASTM D695/D638. For the full tensegrity cell, document the build orientation of the complete assembly and note which strut axis is closest to the build Z-axis.

### 5.2 PETG–TPU Interface Integrity and Joint-Slippage Detection
Multi-material FFF interfaces are weak zones. Arifvianto et al. (2022) found that PLA/TPU interfaces showed poor adhesion with torn/delaminated regions and TPU fibers lying over PLA rather than bonding (arifvianto2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 6-8). Dağlı (2025) reported SEM-observed microcracks, interlayer gaps, and delamination at multi-material boundaries, with fractures often initiating at interfaces (daglı2025mechanicalcharacterizationand pages 11-14). PETG–TPU peer-reviewed interface strength data does not exist in the literature surveyed.

**How to detect joint slippage in load-displacement data:**
- **Sudden force drops** (>10% at constant displacement rate) that are not associated with visible buckling indicate joint failure (daglı2025mechanicalcharacterizationand pages 11-14, arifvianto2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 6-8).
- **Slope changes** in the loading curve that cannot be attributed to known geometric nonlinearity (e.g., tensegrity mechanism engagement) may indicate progressive slip.
- **DIC** at the interface region is the most reliable detection method. Pahari (2024) demonstrated 2D DIC with simultaneous front and side imaging to capture heterogeneous deformation at multi-material boundaries in FFF parts (pahari2024analysisofthe pages 65-70).
- **Post-test inspection** of joint regions under magnification (10×–20× stereo microscope) looking for whitening, necking, gap opening, or fibrillation.

### 5.3 Mass / Dimensional Check Protocol
- Mass: 0.01 g precision balance; average two readings.
- Dimensions: digital calipers, 0.01 mm resolution; measure height and two orthogonal widths at three locations each and report mean ± range.
- If available, CT or structured-light scan to compare as-built vs. CAD geometry and compute actual relative density. Raghavendra et al. (2021) used µCT to quantify morphological deviations and found ~5% lower porosity in built vs. designed specimens, which materially affected stiffness predictions (raghavendra2021uniaxialstaticmechanical pages 13-17).

### 5.4 Aging / Batch Effects and Control Specimens
Print a batch of **control specimens** (a single, simple design variant — e.g., 3-bar prism in PETG+TPU) at the start of the campaign. Retest one control specimen every N = 10 test specimens (or once per test session, whichever is more frequent) to monitor for:
- Machine drift (load-cell calibration shift, platen wear).
- Material aging (PETG hydrolysis, TPU moisture uptake, UV exposure if stored near windows).
- Print-batch variability (filament lot, nozzle wear).

Track control-specimen stiffness on a control chart. If the control shifts by >2σ from the initial baseline, halt testing and investigate. This matches the campaign protocol described in the `idetc-abstract.tex` framework.

## 7. Equipment-Specific Recommendations

### 7.1 Load Cell Selection
Your available 5 kN load cell is appropriate but may be at the upper limit. For tensegrity specimens of 5–30 g at 15–20% strain, expected peak forces will be in the range of approximately 1–200 N (based on Pajunen et al.'s initial stiffness of ~10–48 kPa for ~48 mm specimens giving forces of ~10–50 N, and your stiffer PETG struts potentially reaching higher values) (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 3-4, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 4-5). The Instron 5 kN cell has accuracy ±0.5% down to 1/1000 of capacity (per Solyaev et al. on the 5969 platform), meaning ±0.025 N at 5 N and ±2.5 N at 500 N (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11). At forces below ~5 N, the signal-to-noise ratio will be poor. If you find that peak forces consistently fall below 50 N, consider requesting or borrowing a **500 N or 1 kN load cell** for better resolution in the tendon-dominated low-strain regime. Bates et al. (2016) used a 1 kN load cell on an Instron 3343 for TPU honeycombs, which is a good precedent for soft cellular specimens (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 7-10).

### 7.2 Load-Cell Verification
Verify the load cell per **ASTM E4** (Force Verification for Testing Machines) before beginning the campaign. The standard requires verification at ≥5 points across the range and ±1% accuracy for Class A verification.

### 7.3 Data-Acquisition Rate
Acquire at **≥10 Hz** for quasi-static tests at 1 mm/min (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 7-10). Solyaev et al. (2023) used 2.5 kHz on an Instron 5969 (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11); Raghavendra et al. (2021) used 1 kHz (raghavendra2021uniaxialstaticmechanical pages 5-7). Higher rates are beneficial for capturing any sudden events (joint slip, strut snap) but generate larger files. A practical recommendation is **50–100 Hz** — high enough to resolve transient events without excessive data volume.

### 7.4 Instron Platform Notes
- **Instron 5965** (5 kN maximum): Excellent choice if available; matched to your expected force range.
- **Instron 5969** (50 kN maximum): Workable but the 5 kN cell operates in the lower end of the frame capacity. Solyaev et al. (2023) successfully used this platform with a 50 kN cell for polymer lattices (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11), but your forces will be much lower.
- **ElectroPuls E3000** (3 kN dynamic): Better suited for later cyclic/fatigue work or if you need precise displacement control at low forces. Pahari (2024) used this platform for interface shear tests (pahari2024analysisofthe pages 65-70).
- **MTS Insight**: Comparable to the Instron 59xx series; follow the same protocols.

---

## 8. Open Questions / Things the Lab Should Decide Before the First Test

1. **Platen interface:** Bare steel, PTFE film, or compliant shim? Run a quick pilot (3 specimens, one condition) comparing bare vs. PTFE before committing to a batch protocol.

2. **Preload threshold:** 0.5 N or 1.0 N? For very soft TPU-dominated cells, even 0.5 N may cause measurable deformation. Start with 0.5 N and verify it produces a clean toe-to-linear transition.

3. **Strain limit for stiffness test:** 15% or 20%? Test one sacrificial specimen to full densification to identify where the tensegrity mechanism engages (buckling plateau onset) and set the stiffness-test limit well below that transition.

4. **DIC availability:** Can a camera be set up to view the specimen during loading? Even a smartphone at 30 fps with fiducial markers provides useful backup displacement data. If a proper DIC system (e.g., GOM, VIC-2D, or open-source ncorr) is available, use it from day one.

5. **Load-cell swap:** Will a smaller load cell (500 N or 1 kN) be available or borrowable? If so, it is worth running a comparison test to quantify resolution improvement.

6. **Control-specimen design:** Finalize which single design variant serves as the batch control. Ideally choose the simplest cell (3-bar prism) with the most robust joints, so control-specimen failures are informative rather than routine.

7. **Joint-type priority for first batch:** The repo mentions anchor-bulb, dovetail, and TPU-rebar joint variants. Decide whether the first test batch sweeps all three joint types or fixes one and sweeps architecture.

8. **Temperature and humidity logging:** Is a lab datalogger running continuously? If not, record ambient temperature and humidity at the start and end of each test session. Both PETG and TPU are sensitive to moisture (lesniowski2025enhancingtheperformance pages 16-18, lopes2024interfaceboundarymechanical pages 33-37).

9. **Filament drying protocol and verification:** Confirm that PETG and TPU filaments are dried before printing. PETG dries at 60–65°C for 4+ h; TPU at 50°C for 4+ h. Print a test specimen immediately after drying to establish the baseline.

10. **Post-test specimen disposition:** Will tested stiffness specimens be retained for later energy-absorption tests (possible if undamaged at 15–20% strain), or dedicated only to stiffness? Retaining them allows paired stiffness → EA data on the same specimen, which strengthens the BO surrogate model.

11. **Strain-window definition for k_tangent:** Fix the strain window (e.g., 1–5%, or 2–8%) before batch testing so that all specimens are compared on the same basis. The Scibetta-Schuurmans algorithm used in the NIST E9 study recommends that the fit range cover at least 40% of the elastic-region stress range for reliable modulus estimation (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 24-26, potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 26-29).

12. **Compression direction for tensegrity prisms:** Define whether loading is axial (along the prism axis) or transverse. For Snelson-class 3-bar prisms, axial loading activates the tensegrity mechanism; transverse may collapse joints differently. Document and fix the loading direction per design family.

## 2. Best Practices / Pitfalls for the Actual Instron Test

### 2.1 Crosshead Speed and Strain Rate
A crosshead speed of **1 mm/min** is the most common quasi-static rate for lattice/cellular compression in the published analog set (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000016). For a 25–50 mm specimen this yields a nominal strain rate of 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ to 6.7 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Report both the commanded crosshead speed and the nominal engineering strain rate (crosshead speed / initial specimen height). If using DIC-derived local strain, report that separately. Bates et al. (2016) tested TPU honeycombs at higher strain rates (0.03–0.3 s⁻¹), which is relevant for later energy-absorption studies but not first-round stiffness (pqac-00000001).

### 2.2 Platen Choice
Use **flat, hardened steel platens** per ASTM E9 fixture practice (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000048). Consider PTFE anti-friction film between platen and specimen if barreling or friction-induced stiffening is suspected; keep the choice fixed within a batch. The NIST interlaboratory study found that lubrication vs. no lubrication changed measured modulus by approximately 5.7% and yield strength by 3.1% in metal compression (pqac-00000051). For tensegrity cells where the top face may not be flat, a **thin compliant shim** (silicone sheet, ~1 mm) can improve contact uniformity, but this must be documented and the shim compliance subtracted. Spherically-seated platens are an option for alignment but introduce a rotational degree of freedom that may activate the tensegrity mechanism prematurely; use with caution and document.

### 2.3 Machine Compliance Correction
This is **critical** for sub-mm deformations of soft cellular specimens. Crosshead displacement includes load-string compliance (load cell, platens, couplings) that cannot be distinguished from specimen deformation without correction (pqac-00000052). The recommended protocol:
1. Run a platen-to-platen (no specimen) compression to the expected peak load, recording force vs. crosshead displacement.
2. Fit a linear compliance curve C_machine = Δδ/ΔF (mm/N).
3. Subtract C_machine × F(t) from the measured crosshead displacement at each time point.
4. Alternatively, and preferably, use a **non-contact extensometer** (DIC or video gauge) to measure specimen deformation directly, bypassing compliance entirely.

Solyaev et al. (2023) performed compliance correction per ASTM D790 and noted it was important for accurate modulus extraction from lattice tests on an Instron 5969 (pqac-00000002). The NIST study found that actuator-displacement-based stress was ~1.4% higher than extensometer-based measures even after correction (pqac-00000049). For your TPU-dominated specimens at low loads, compliance errors can exceed 50% of apparent deformation; DIC or a clip-on displacement transducer on the platens is strongly recommended.

### 2.4 Preload / Contact-Find and Toe Correction
Apply a preload of **0.5–1.0 N** at a slow approach speed (0.5 mm/min) to establish contact (pqac-00000048). Zero the displacement reference at this preload. For toe-region removal, the NIST ASTM E9 study shifted stress-strain curves so that a linear fit in the range 50–175 MPa (for aluminum) intercepted the origin (pqac-00000048). For your low-force polymeric cells, apply an analogous procedure: identify the initial linear region of the force-displacement curve, extend the linear fit back to zero force, and shift the displacement origin accordingly, per the intent of ASTM E111 (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047).

### 2.5 Non-Contact Extensometry
Bates et al. (2016) used a **video gauge with speckle-pattern markers** on the compression platens to verify crosshead-derived positional measurements (pqac-00000001). Pahari (2024) applied **2D DIC** with simultaneous front and side imaging to detect interfacial strain concentrations in multi-material FFF parts (pqac-00000032). For your specimens, a camera-based approach is ideal: apply speckle or fiducial markers to the top and bottom platens (or directly on the specimen if it has a flat PETG face) and compute the relative displacement at ≥10 Hz. This eliminates frame compliance from the stiffness calculation and provides strain-field data useful for detecting joint slip.

### 2.6 Conditioning: Mullins Effect in TPU
TPU exhibits a complex cyclic response that differs from classical Mullins softening in crosslinked rubbers. Scetta et al. (2021) demonstrated that soft TPU shows large hysteresis on the first load-unload cycle, pronounced softening after the first loading, marked residual deformation, and — importantly — a **stiffening** effect (not just softening) under step-cyclic loading at strains above ~1.5 Hencky strain, attributed to hard-domain fragmentation and additional physical crosslinking (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008). Holzweber et al. (2018) explicitly applied "pre-cycles to avoid the Mullins- or softening effect" and noted that hysteresis decreases with increasing cycle count (pqac-00000010). Zhou et al. (2025) used an energy-ratio metric W₄/W₁ (fourth-cycle loading energy over first-cycle) to quantify Mullins-related softening, with lower ratios indicating stronger preconditioning damage (pqac-00000011).

**Recommendation:** Run **5 preconditioning cycles** to 5% nominal strain at 1 mm/min with 30 s pause between cycles. Compare the loading stiffness of cycles 1 and 5 to quantify conditioning magnitude. Report W₅/W₁ and note any irreversible residual strain. Do not precondition to more than 5% strain on a stiffness test — larger strains risk activating tensegrity buckling mechanisms that should be reserved for the energy-absorption campaign.

**Humidity:** PETG is hygroscopic — "absorbed water chemically attacks the polyester chains via hydrolysis" (pqac-00000031). TPU is also moisture-sensitive, with absorbed moisture affecting melt viscosity and mechanical properties (pqac-00000036). **Dry all filaments** before printing (60°C for PETG, 50°C for TPU, 4+ h) and condition finished specimens at 23 ± 2°C, 50 ± 5% RH for ≥48 h before testing (pqac-00000004).

### 2.7 Definition of "Stiffness" to Report
Report at minimum:
- **Structural stiffness k** = dF/dδ (N/mm) — the tangent of the force-displacement curve in the initial linear region after toe correction. Specify the displacement or strain window used (e.g., 1–5% nominal strain).
- **Secant structural stiffness** k_sec at a specified strain level (e.g., at 5% strain) — useful for comparing specimens with different toe-region behaviors.
- **Effective modulus** E_eff = k × h₀ / A₀ (MPa), where h₀ is the initial specimen height and A₀ is the projected bounding-box cross-sectional area. This is an apparent material-like property; it is not a true material modulus but is useful for comparison.
- **Non-dimensionalized relative modulus** E*/E_s = E_eff / E_solid and **relative density** ρ*/ρ_s = (mass / bounding volume) / ρ_solid, plotted in Gibson-Ashby fashion.

For the Gibson-Ashby framework, the canonical scaling is E*/E_s = C₁(ρ*/ρ_s)^n, where n ≈ 2 for bending-dominated open-cell structures and n ≈ 1 for stretching-dominated architectures (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027). The prefactor C₁ "includes all of the geometric constants of proportionality" and depends on unit-cell topology, cell size, stress type, and global shape (pqac-00000023). Tensegrity structures involve a mix of tension (stretching in tendons) and compression (strut buckling), so expect n between 1 and 2; fitting n from your data is itself a scientific contribution.

Bauer et al. (2021) defined E as the maximum slope of the linear regime, σ_y from a 0.2% offset, plateau stress σ_p averaged between 20–40% strain, and absorbed energy U as the integral of stress-strain to densification (pqac-00000038). This reporting framework is directly applicable to your later energy-absorption tests.

### 2.8 Replicates and Statistics
**Minimum n = 5** replicates per design variant for stiffness. Report mean ± SD and 95% CI. The ASTM E9 interlaboratory study found within-lab repeatability of ~1.1% CV and between-lab reproducibility of ~2.0% CV for yield strength of well-machined metal specimens (pqac-00000053); for FFF cellular parts expect substantially higher variability (5–15% CV). Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski (2024) tested groups of seven and reported mean curves with standard deviation bands (pqac-00000016); this is a good minimum. Produce extra samples to discard obviously defective prints (pqac-00000045). For later failure-related quantities (strength, SEA), report Weibull parameters if the dataset is large enough (≥15 specimens).

### 2.9 Build-Parameter Documentation per ASTM F2971 / ISO/ASTM 52921
For each specimen, record and report: build orientation (Z-up vs. XY-flat, per ISO/ASTM 52921 coordinate system), layer height (0.2 mm), nozzle diameter (0.4 mm), number of perimeters (≥3 for TPU tendons), infill pattern and density (100% for structural members), raster angle, nozzle temperature (by material), bed temperature, print speed, and any post-processing (none for initial tests) (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000031). This information is normative for peer review and essential for the BO loop.

## 4. Stiffness-Specific vs. Strength/Energy-Absorption Test Design

The issue title is *stiffness testing*, and the differences from energy-absorption testing are critical:

| Parameter | Stiffness Test (current) | Energy-Absorption Test (later) |
|---|---|---|
| **Load limit** | 15–20% nominal strain (well below densification) | Full densification (60–80% strain) or until failure |
| **Strain window for metric extraction** | 1–5% strain for tangent stiffness; 0–10% for secant | Full curve: plateau stress (20–40% strain), densification onset, area under curve |
| **Preconditioning** | 5 cycles to 5% strain; establishes stable baseline | May include 5 cycles to full target strain; Mullins damage is intentional and itself a metric |
| **Replicate count** | n ≥ 5 per design; focus on precision of mean stiffness | n ≥ 5 for mean SEA; n ≥ 15 for Weibull failure statistics |
| **Reportable metrics** | k_tangent, k_secant, E_effective, E*/E_s, hysteresis ratio | Peak F, plateau σ, SEA (J/g), volumetric EA (J/cm³), compaction efficiency η, transmitted force |
| **Specimen reuse** | Specimen should be reusable (no damage at 15–20% strain) | Specimen may be consumed / damaged |

**Recommendation:** Measure stiffness in a **separate dedicated test campaign** rather than extracting it exclusively from the loading branch of energy-absorption tests. Reasons: (a) stiffness is sensitive to toe-region artifacts that are less critical for EA integral calculations; (b) the low-strain regime is where machine compliance errors are largest; (c) preconditioning for stiffness should be limited to small strains to avoid Mullins-altered response; (d) dedicated stiffness tests preserve specimens for potential re-testing or microscopy. However, also extract the **unloading tangent stiffness** from the first unloading cycle of EA tests (analogous to ISO 13314's cyclic unloading method) as a secondary stiffness metric for cross-validation (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000038).

## 5. Multi-Material FFF-Specific Considerations for Stiffness Data Quality

### 5.1 Layer-Stack Orientation Effect
FFF parts are inherently anisotropic. For PETG, tensile properties are strongest along the raster direction and weakest across layers (Z-direction), with modulus reductions of 15–40% reported for Z-built vs. XY-built specimens depending on material and parameters (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000037). **Recommendation:** Test struts printed in at least two orientations — (a) struts parallel to build direction (Z) and (b) struts perpendicular to build direction (XY) — using standalone coupon tests per ASTM D695/D638. For the full tensegrity cell, document the build orientation of the complete assembly and note which strut axis is closest to the build Z-axis.

### 5.2 PETG–TPU Interface Integrity and Joint-Slippage Detection
Multi-material FFF interfaces are weak zones. Arifvianto et al. (2022) found that PLA/TPU interfaces showed poor adhesion with torn/delaminated regions and TPU fibers lying over PLA rather than bonding (pqac-00000033). Dağlı (2025) reported SEM-observed microcracks, interlayer gaps, and delamination at multi-material boundaries, with fractures often initiating at interfaces (pqac-00000034). PETG–TPU peer-reviewed interface strength data does not exist in the literature surveyed.

**How to detect joint slippage in load-displacement data:**
- **Sudden force drops** (>10% at constant displacement rate) that are not associated with visible buckling indicate joint failure (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000033).
- **Slope changes** in the loading curve that cannot be attributed to known geometric nonlinearity (e.g., tensegrity mechanism engagement) may indicate progressive slip.
- **DIC** at the interface region is the most reliable detection method. Pahari (2024) demonstrated 2D DIC with simultaneous front and side imaging to capture heterogeneous deformation at multi-material boundaries in FFF parts (pqac-00000032).
- **Post-test inspection** of joint regions under magnification (10×–20× stereo microscope) looking for whitening, necking, gap opening, or fibrillation.

### 5.3 Mass / Dimensional Check Protocol
- Mass: 0.01 g precision balance; average two readings.
- Dimensions: digital calipers, 0.01 mm resolution; measure height and two orthogonal widths at three locations each and report mean ± range.
- If available, CT or structured-light scan to compare as-built vs. CAD geometry and compute actual relative density. Raghavendra et al. (2021) used µCT to quantify morphological deviations and found ~5% lower porosity in built vs. designed specimens, which materially affected stiffness predictions (pqac-00000022).

### 5.4 Aging / Batch Effects and Control Specimens
Print a batch of **control specimens** (a single, simple design variant — e.g., 3-bar prism in PETG+TPU) at the start of the campaign. Retest one control specimen every N = 10 test specimens (or once per test session, whichever is more frequent) to monitor for:
- Machine drift (load-cell calibration shift, platen wear).
- Material aging (PETG hydrolysis, TPU moisture uptake, UV exposure if stored near windows).
- Print-batch variability (filament lot, nozzle wear).

Track control-specimen stiffness on a control chart. If the control shifts by >2σ from the initial baseline, halt testing and investigate. This matches the campaign protocol described in the `idetc-abstract.tex` framework.

*Table: This table summarizes the closest published experimental analogs to the planned multi-material tensegrity/lattice Instron campaign. It is useful for borrowing test parameters, identifying reporting norms, and modeling justified deviations from standards.*

**Key observations across the analog set:**
- No published study has tested multi-material PETG + TPU tensegrity-inspired cells. Your work is novel in this material combination and architecture family.
- The closest tensegrity architecture analogs (Bauer et al. 2021; Pajunen et al. 2019; Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski 2024) used single-material prints (IP-Dip polymer, PA2200, or PolyJet resins) rather than multi-material FFF (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).
- The closest material/process analogs (Bates et al. 2016; Arifvianto et al. 2022) tested TPU or PLA/TPU multi-material but not tensegrity architectures (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000033).
- Notably, **none of the tensegrity papers cited a named ASTM/ISO compression standard** — they all used custom compression protocols. This is a gap your paper can address by explicitly citing ASTM D1621 or C365 (adapted) and disclosing deviations.

---

## 7. Equipment-Specific Recommendations

### 7.1 Load Cell Selection
Your available 5 kN load cell is appropriate but may be at the upper limit. For tensegrity specimens of 5–30 g at 15–20% strain, expected peak forces will be in the range of approximately 1–200 N (based on Pajunen et al.'s initial stiffness of ~10–48 kPa for ~48 mm specimens giving forces of ~10–50 N, and your stiffer PETG struts potentially reaching higher values) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000019). The Instron 5 kN cell has accuracy ±0.5% down to 1/1000 of capacity (per Solyaev et al. on the 5969 platform), meaning ±0.025 N at 5 N and ±2.5 N at 500 N (pqac-00000002). At forces below ~5 N, the signal-to-noise ratio will be poor. If you find that peak forces consistently fall below 50 N, consider requesting or borrowing a **500 N or 1 kN load cell** for better resolution in the tendon-dominated low-strain regime. Bates et al. (2016) used a 1 kN load cell on an Instron 3343 for TPU honeycombs, which is a good precedent for soft cellular specimens (pqac-00000001).

### 7.2 Load-Cell Verification
Verify the load cell per **ASTM E4** (Force Verification for Testing Machines) before beginning the campaign. The standard requires verification at ≥5 points across the range and ±1% accuracy for Class A verification.

### 7.3 Data-Acquisition Rate
Acquire at **≥10 Hz** for quasi-static tests at 1 mm/min (pqac-00000001). Solyaev et al. (2023) used 2.5 kHz on an Instron 5969 (pqac-00000002); Raghavendra et al. (2021) used 1 kHz (pqac-00000000). Higher rates are beneficial for capturing any sudden events (joint slip, strut snap) but generate larger files. A practical recommendation is **50–100 Hz** — high enough to resolve transient events without excessive data volume.

### 7.4 Instron Platform Notes
- **Instron 5965** (5 kN maximum): Excellent choice if available; matched to your expected force range.
- **Instron 5969** (50 kN maximum): Workable but the 5 kN cell operates in the lower end of the frame capacity. Solyaev et al. (2023) successfully used this platform with a 50 kN cell for polymer lattices (pqac-00000002), but your forces will be much lower.
- **ElectroPuls E3000** (3 kN dynamic): Better suited for later cyclic/fatigue work or if you need precise displacement control at low forces. Pahari (2024) used this platform for interface shear tests (pqac-00000032).
- **MTS Insight**: Comparable to the Instron 59xx series; follow the same protocols.

---

## 8. Open Questions / Things the Lab Should Decide Before the First Test

1. **Platen interface:** Bare steel, PTFE film, or compliant shim? Run a quick pilot (3 specimens, one condition) comparing bare vs. PTFE before committing to a batch protocol.

2. **Preload threshold:** 0.5 N or 1.0 N? For very soft TPU-dominated cells, even 0.5 N may cause measurable deformation. Start with 0.5 N and verify it produces a clean toe-to-linear transition.

3. **Strain limit for stiffness test:** 15% or 20%? Test one sacrificial specimen to full densification to identify where the tensegrity mechanism engages (buckling plateau onset) and set the stiffness-test limit well below that transition.

4. **DIC availability:** Can a camera be set up to view the specimen during loading? Even a smartphone at 30 fps with fiducial markers provides useful backup displacement data. If a proper DIC system (e.g., GOM, VIC-2D, or open-source ncorr) is available, use it from day one.

5. **Load-cell swap:** Will a smaller load cell (500 N or 1 kN) be available or borrowable? If so, it is worth running a comparison test to quantify resolution improvement.

6. **Control-specimen design:** Finalize which single design variant serves as the batch control. Ideally choose the simplest cell (3-bar prism) with the most robust joints, so control-specimen failures are informative rather than routine.

7. **Joint-type priority for first batch:** The repo mentions anchor-bulb, dovetail, and TPU-rebar joint variants. Decide whether the first test batch sweeps all three joint types or fixes one and sweeps architecture.

8. **Temperature and humidity logging:** Is a lab datalogger running continuously? If not, record ambient temperature and humidity at the start and end of each test session. Both PETG and TPU are sensitive to moisture (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036).

9. **Filament drying protocol and verification:** Confirm that PETG and TPU filaments are dried before printing. PETG dries at 60–65°C for 4+ h; TPU at 50°C for 4+ h. Print a test specimen immediately after drying to establish the baseline.

10. **Post-test specimen disposition:** Will tested stiffness specimens be retained for later energy-absorption tests (possible if undamaged at 15–20% strain), or dedicated only to stiffness? Retaining them allows paired stiffness → EA data on the same specimen, which strengthens the BO surrogate model.

11. **Strain-window definition for k_tangent:** Fix the strain window (e.g., 1–5%, or 2–8%) before batch testing so that all specimens are compared on the same basis. The Scibetta-Schuurmans algorithm used in the NIST E9 study recommends that the fit range cover at least 40% of the elastic-region stress range for reliable modulus estimation (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000053).

12. **Compression direction for tensegrity prisms:** Define whether loading is axial (along the prism axis) or transverse. For Snelson-class 3-bar prisms, axial loading activates the tensegrity mechanism; transverse may collapse joints differently. Document and fix the loading direction per design family.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports the authors' compression test procedure for 3D-printed lattice specimens. Compression testing used flat platforms per ASTM E9. Load/deflection curves were recorded until 50% compressive deformation or specimen failure. Deformation was evaluated as the relative change of specimen height from crosshead displacements with correction for equipment compliance. Engineering stress was computed using the initial lattice core cross-sectional area A = H b, and yield strength was taken from the engineering stress–strain curve using a 0.2% strain offset. Quasi-static crosshead speed used in all static tests was 1 mm/min; the applied force for bending was taken within the linear elastic range (deflections ≤ 1 mm). Tests were performed at room temperature (22 ± 1 °C). contexts.context: The excerpt states there is no single specific standard for compression testing of additively manufactured TPMS/cellular hybrid materials, so ASTM D3574 (a foam test standard) was adopted because of similarity to EPS. ASTM D3574 cites a preferred specimen dimension of 50 x 50 x 25 mm but does not mandate a minimum; the authors selected a 50 x 50 x 50 mm cube due to machine/printing/foaming constraints and printed seven specimens per configuration. ASTM D3574 requires the crosshead displacement rate equal to 10% of sample thickness per minute. For the authors' 50 mm thickness this gives 5 mm/min crosshead speed and an implied strain rate of 0.0016 s^-1. The paper also notes that the AM material (acrylonitrile styrene acrylate) was characterized under compression per ASTM D1621. Tests were performed in the build direction (perpendicular to the layer). contexts.context: This paper describes compression testing of 3D-printable tensegrity-inspired unit cells and reports practical specimen geometry and testing setup details. The authors used a unit height of 48.3 mm and member diameters (cables 1.37 mm, struts 3.05 mm, ds/dc = 2.23) chosen to permit elastic buckling, verified by the Euler–Johnson relation (variables L, q, E, sy specified). Samples were printed in PA2200 by SLS; SLS yields parts with no support, no post-curing, and consistent constitutive properties. Compression experiments were performed in displacement control, with samples loaded on the top face; the top and bottom faces were allowed to rotate during compression due to face-node asymmetry. To better approximate pin-jointed behavior, the authors scaled the geometry and/or inserted spherical joints to maintain nodal locations and cable lengths. Finite-element models used 3D stress quadratic tetrahedral elements (C3D10) and kinematic coupling of reference points to face nodes to allow rotation. Stress–strain responses comparing pin-jointed and fixed-jointed designs showed distinct buckling versus rupture behaviors, underscoring the importance of joint design and setup when interpreting stiffness and buckling results.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes compression testing of 3D-printed cellular specimens on an Instron (3343, 1 kN) and a Shimadzu (10 kN). Unconstrained samples were compressed between flat steel plates to full densification and unloaded at the same rates; cycles were repeated five times to assess durability. Tests used constant strain rates (0.03, 0.095, 0.3 s-1) and a minimum data capture rate of 10 Hz with acquisition via Bluehill/Trapezium X. Deformation was recorded with a video gauge using a speckle pattern on the platen to verify positional measurements from the test frame. Nominal strain was obtained from change in deflection at the sample–plate interface and nominal stress from force divided by the initial projected area (D x L); stress–strain curves were post-processed in MATLAB to extract energy-absorption metrics. Geometric choices (make L larger than H) avoided global buckling. The text also highlights manufacturing variability (over-extrusion, nozzle choice, Bowden vs direct drive) affecting wall thickness and density — relevant when interpreting stiffness and repeatability in compression tests.

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on compression testing of 3D-printed TPU hexagonal cellular arrays and provides guidance on specimen design, test objectives, and how to interpret results. It stresses that compressive behaviour has three regions—linear elasticity, plateau and densification—and that energy absorption is the area under the stress–strain curve, with a long flat plateau desirable for efficient, near-constant-load absorption. Test specimens were oriented and assembled so they could be compressed in defined directions ("designed to be compressed in the transverse direction" and "in the ribbon direction"), and samples were intentionally designed with a larger length than height (L > H) to avoid global buckling and reduce free-boundary effects. The mechanical testing program aimed to establish durability through repeated compressions to densification. The paper also documents specimen preparation and quality control: FFF printing on an Ultimaker Original, DSC to set melt temperature, and optimization of extrusion rate, layer height and print-head speed to minimise void fraction; tensile tests followed ASTM D412. The excerpt therefore supplies geometry and test-goal guidance, deformation-region interpretation, and specimen-quality controls but does not provide Instron-specific protocols (e.g. compliance correction procedures, platen fixturing details, or explicit crosshead speeds).

snippets: In order to assess the energy absorbing potential of the 3D printed structures, it is necessary to understand their compressive behaviour.
three deformation regions can be observed: linear elasticity, plateau and densification.
The energy absorbed by a cellular structure during a compression is simply the area under the stress strain curve, up to the strain, ε, to which it is compressed.

Since very little energy is absorbed in the linear region, it is a long flat plateau that is desired for an efficient energy absorbing structure, such that compressive energy can be absorbed at a near constant load.

Samples were designed to have a larger length, L compared to height, H in order to avoid global buckling of the sample in compression and reduce the effects of the vertical free boundaries on the global compressive behaviour.

contexts.context: Relevant experimental details: tensile experiments used a universal Instron 100kN Tester (5982) fitted with a 5kN load cell; crosshead displacement rate was 5 mm/min (per ASTM); strain was measured with a 25 mm extensometer. Specimens were supported with four laser-cut acrylic tabs glued with epoxy resin (allowed to cure 48 hours) and positioned using tab holders to ensure identical effective length. All samples were climate-conditioned in chambers at 23°C and 50% RH for over 48 hours before testing. Video capture (smartphone) was used during tests. Printing and specimen-prep notes that affect mechanical behaviour: overall print speed 900 mm/min (first layer at 50%), nozzle temp 215°C, bed 80°C, and outline/solid infill underspeed set to 90% to improve surface finish and reduce printer vibration. Trial-print adjustments (extrusion multipliers for PLA/TPU) were required to ensure bonding and correct feature thickness. These details inform selection of load cell capacity, use of local strain measurement (extensometer), specimen mounting/alignment practices, environmental preconditioning, test speed selection, and consideration of printed-bonding quality when designing compression test protocols for 3D printed lattice/tensegrity parts.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents compression and tensile testing practices used for LB-PBF Ti6Al4V cellular specimens. Compression testing followed ISO 13314:2011; tests were performed at room temperature with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min and 1 kHz data sampling. Displacement for compression was measured with an LVDT (extensometer used for tensile tests). Young’s modulus via the unloading method was obtained from cyclic loading-unloading tests (cycles between ~20–70% of the yield load). Specimen geometry for compression used cylindrical samples (~15 mm diameter, 16 mm length); at least 8–10 unit cells were included in each direction to ensure representativity. Two sets of five specimens per topology were produced. Authors used µCT to quantify as-built morphological deviations and porosity, and porosity was also measured by dry-weight/density methods. The text notes alignment issues in compression (asymmetric behavior from inclined loading) and that tensile tests provided better alignment for stiffness estimation. Manufacturing details (Ti6Al4V powder 15–45 μm, EOS machine, 400 W laser, 60 μm layer) and heat treatment to stabilize microstructure are also reported. These elements inform protocols for platen/setup, alignment, compliance correction via external displacement sensors, cyclic preconditioning, and representative specimen design.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes experimental compression and impact testing practices for 3D-printable tensegrity-inspired structures that can inform Instron compression testing. Samples were mounted on a glass sheet acting as a stiff surface extension for the force sensor, with a thin liquid layer of acetone applied to reduce friction. The setup allowed natural rotation of the sample by running a guiding metal rod through the structure center. Reaction forces were measured beneath the glass-mounted sample; displacements of top nodes were captured using a high-speed camera (1000 fps) with optical markers. Multiple samples were tested due to manufacturing variability. Tests compressed samples up to 0.48 strain (densification when struts touch). The paper contrasts modeling approaches: beam-element models are much faster than full 3D stress simulations, facilitating geometry/diameter iteration. It also notes that prestress states (pin-jointed prestressed vs spherically-jointed non-prestressed) govern buckling behavior, relevant when designing preconditioning or stiffness measurement protocols. These specifics point to best practices for reducing platen friction, ensuring rigid load-paths to sensors, permitting rotational degrees of freedom, using optical tracking, and accounting for sample variability.
contexts.question: What are the best practices for compression testing of 3D printed tensegrity structures and lattice structures on an Instron machine? Include machine compliance correction, crosshead speed, platen setup, preconditioning, and stiffness measurement protocols.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes quasi-static compression test practice for 3D-printed lattice specimens using an Instron 5969. Key instrument parameters: a 50 kN load cell (measurement accuracy ±0.5% down to 1/1000 of capacity) and 2.5 kHz acquisition. Crosshead speed for quasi-static tests was 1 mm/min. Compression used flat platforms per ASTM E9, with load/deflection recorded until 50% compressive strain or failure. Deformations were evaluated from crosshead displacement as relative height change, with correction for equipment compliance (compliance correction performed according to ASTM D790). Engineering stress was computed using initial lattice core area (A = Hb) and yield strength taken from a 0.2% strain offset. Toughness was estimated as area under stress–strain curves. Simulation/testing considerations include using small fillets at strut intersections equal to printing resolution (50 µm) for mesh/geometry fidelity and considering a contact/friction coefficient of 0.2. The excerpt does not discuss preconditioning, explicit platen alignment procedures, preload cycles, or specific stiffness-measurement protocols beyond deriving apparent modulus from stress–strain data and machine compliance correction.
contexts.question: What are the best practices for compression testing of 3D printed tensegrity structures and lattice structures on an Instron machine? Include machine compliance correction, crosshead speed, platen setup, preconditioning, and stiffness measurement protocols.

snippets: Static tests were performed by using Instron 5969 universal testing machine with force sensor 2580-203 (load cell capacity 50 kN, measurement accuracy ± 0.5% of reading down to 1/1000 of load cell capacity, data acquisition rate 2.5 kHz).
Crosshead speed in all quasi-static tests was 1 mm/min.
The compression tests were performed using flat platforms (ASTM E9).
Load/deflection curves were registered until the 50% of compressive deformations of the specimen or until its failure (if the ultimate deformations were less then 50%).
The deformations were evaluated as the relative change of specimen height under compression through the crosshead displacements and taking into account correction for the equipment compliance.
Compliance correction of the testing machine was performed according to ASTM D790.
The yield strength was estimated from engineering stress/strain curve using 0,2% strain offset.
The engineering stress in the cross section of specimens was evaluated as the ratio of the registered load to the initial area of the lattice core ( A = Hb ).
The toughness U in the quasi-static compression tests was estimated as the area under obtained stress-strain curves.
To provide the mesh independent solutions we added small fillets at the intersections of all struts in 3d models. Radius of the fillets was equal to the resolution of 3D printing (50 µm).
The friction coefficient was 0.2.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes quasi-static uniaxial compressive testing of 3D printed polymeric lattice structures designed to a uniform relative density (15%). Specimens were 5x5x5 arrays of unit cells (10x10x10 mm each) with varying unit-cell topology to produce different deformation mechanisms (bending, stretching, buckling). Full-scale nonlinear FEA was used to simulate compressive behaviour and experiments were used for validation. Lattices were fabricated using HP Multi Jet Fusion (MJF) in HP PA12, a process noted for good dimensional accuracy and near-isotropic mechanical properties. Material characterisation for HP PA12 was performed using four Type I tensile specimens printed on the HP Jet Fusion 4200 and tested in accordance with ASTM D638-14 with an optical extensometer. The text also highlights that vertical struts prone to buckling cause instability and undulating stress in the plateau region, which is undesirable for energy absorption. These details inform test planning: specimen geometry and relative density control, the need to characterise base material per ASTM standards, awareness of buckling/instability in compression, and that MJF parts show reduced anisotropy compared with other printing methods.

contexts.context: The paper focuses on comprehensive mechanical characterization of TPU including time-, rate-, temperature- and hysteresis-dependencies and translates these into hyperelastic material models for FE and lifetime estimations. It explicitly treats both monotonic and cyclic loading and documents experimental protocols relevant to cyclic behavior: uniaxial tensile tests with DIC for local strains (not run to failure for strains >500%), planar/pure-shear and compression tests, DTMA sinusoidal testing to obtain viscoelastic moduli and tanδ over frequency/temperature, and fatigue testing on Diabolo specimens at RT and 5 Hz. A stepwise relaxation compression protocol is described where specimens were loaded in steps (1.5 mm increments to -6 mm) with 120 s holds to record stress relaxation; during unloading "five hysteresis between -1.5 mm and 3 mm were implemented." The methodology also covers determining local-strain-based Wöhler curves (LSWC). While the excerpt does not explicitly name the Mullins effect or prescribe preconditioning cycles, the documented hysteresis loops, relaxation holds, DTMA sinusoidal cycles, and fatigue/hysteresis test details constitute relevant protocols and measurements that could be used to study Mullins-type softening or cyclic stabilization in TPU.

contexts.context: The paper studies cyclic uniaxial tension on three commercial Elastollan™ TPU and quantifies structural changes under cyclic loading. Contrary to the classical Mullins behavior in chemically crosslinked filled rubbers, the authors observe a "stiffening effect after conditioning in step cyclic loading" for these soft TPUs. However, their step-strain cyclic tests at 23°C also show "Large hysteresis between the first load-unload cycle," "Very pronounced softening after the first loading, and recovery of the monotonic test behavior envelope only when the material is stretched to higher values than those previously applied (Mullins effect)," and "Marked residual deformation." The residual stretch is linked to the lack of chemical crosslinks and "plastic deformation of the hard domains following the application of large strains." The authors propose a mechanism where "fragmentation of hard domains, naturally present in TPU, in smaller but more numerous sub-units" creates additional physical crosslinking, producing persistent self-reinforcement analogous to strain-induced crystallization (notably observed in TPU_XTAL). They reference a methodology that uses "two damage parameters: one to account for the reduction in linear modulus and the other to account for the change in the onset of strain hardening in large strain" to separate small-strain modulus changes from large-strain behavior.
contexts.question: Mullins effect in thermoplastic polyurethane TPU: preconditioning cycles, softening vs stiffening, cyclic loading protocol for mechanical testing

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses Mullins-like behavior and strong residual deformation in thermoplastic polyurethanes (TPU) caused by lack of chemical crosslinks and plastic deformation of hard domains. All TPUs showed a similar fraction of residual stretch for a given maximum applied stretch, whereas crosslinked SBR has much lower residual stretch. The authors emphasize that engineering stress–strain curves can misleadingly suggest cyclic softening in TPU because they ignore accumulated residual strain; true stress vs. Hencky strain representation should be used instead. Their cyclic protocol evaluates linear modulus Ek from unloading slopes and compares Ek to the pristine modulus E0 to quantify damage. They shift each unloading curve to the origin to compensate residual strain and build a master curve by superposition (least-squares fit to the first unloading curve) to obtain a rescaling factor α and define large- and small-strain damage metrics. Experimentally, TPU materials typically show initial softening (damage increases) with increasing max Hencky strain followed, beyond ~1.5 Hencky strain, by stiffening (damage decreases and can become negative, especially at 60°C and for TPU_XTAL). SBR, by contrast, shows monotonic softening and lower residual plasticity.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses how TPUs show Mullins-like behavior under cyclic loading: cyclic deformation induces mechanical hysteresis, stress softening, and permanent changes such as residual plastic strain and reduced small-strain modulus and maximum extensibility. These effects stem from strain-dependent changes to the hard-domain morphology and the lack of chemical crosslinks, which also leads to creep and viscoplastic deformation under repeated stretch. The authors note that when TPUs are cyclically loaded to the same maximum stretch, the stress–stretch response evolves with cycle number but eventually reaches a steady-state. Because of TPU creep and viscoplasticity, standard fracture/fatigue protocols used for crosslinked rubbers need modification; the paper proposes a fracture-mechanics-based methodology with additional treatments to account for TPU creep. The text also references the common rubber practice of preconditioning (pre-straining) unnotched samples for thousands of cycles to obtain stable energy-release-rate calculations, implying that preconditioning until a steady-state response is a relevant step for cyclic testing of TPU.

contexts.context: The excerpt contrasts standard preconditioning protocols used for filled rubbers with the challenges encountered when applying them to thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). For filled rubbers, pre-straining (thousands of cycles at larger stretches) is commonly used to remove transient Mullins damage so that a stable energy release rate G(λ) can be evaluated. However, TPUs "typically show significant residual deformation when unloaded," and this residual (plastic) stretch accumulates with cycling, altering the stress–stretch response and making the effective energy release rate depend on both maximum stretch and cycle number, i.e. G(λ,n). Allowing full unloading to the original reference (λmin = 1) can cause buckling during unloading and additional damage. Standard pre-conditioning would require very large stretches for TPU (risking damage) and even modest preconditioning to λp slightly above the test stretch makes the calculated G dependent on λp: G(λ,λp). Therefore, conventional preconditioning to remove Mullins-like transients is not directly transferable to TPU; specific cyclic loading protocols and definitions of reference state are needed to obtain reproducible crack propagation/fatigue data.

snippets: A common approach to calculate G(λ) in filled rubbers is to pre-strain (or precondition) the unnotched sample for some thousands of cycles at higher values of λ than those used in fatigue testing and then to evaluate G(λ) by cyclically straining the accommodated sample at different values of increasing stretch.
In this way, most of transient effects related to Mullins damage in the first cycles are avoided in the calculation of the relevant G for long term cyclic fatigue.
Applying this method to TPUs without modification creates several challenges that are the focus of this paper.
The first issue is that TPUs typically show significant residual deformation when unloaded.

While the sample is cyclically loaded at a constant maximum applied stretch, the residual deformation increases during cycles, and hence the stress-stretch curve is modified and the actual energy release rate seen by the crack is not constant.
Unlike conventional rubbers, the applied energy release rate G is a function of both the maximum applied stretch and the number of cycles (n): G(λ,n).

if the sample is allowed to unload up to λmin = 1, calculated using the initial height h0 of the pristine sample, the residual plastic stretch causes an extensive buckling during unloading cycles that may induce additional undesirable damage in the sample.
The well-established pre-conditioning procedure cannot be easily implemented to eliminate transient effects, since it would involve very large stretch that are likely to damage the sample.

Also, if the sample is preconditioned to a stretch λp that is only slightly larger than the cyclic stretch λ to be tested, the values of the energy release rate will depend on this maximum stretch: G(λ,λp) applied during the preconditioning.
Defining in which conditions should the cyclic load be applied in TPU to obtain reliable and reproducible crack propagation data is precisely the objective of this work.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) exhibits a Mullins-type softening during early cyclic loading: "In the first couples of cycles, the drop of the reachable load is significantly higher than in the stationary section" and "This phenomena is referred to as the softening behavior and can be detected in most of the TPUs." To mitigate this, the authors applied preconditioning: "To avoid the Mullins- or softening effect some pre cycles were defined." Cyclic testing was displacement-controlled with measurements of Fmax/Fmin, cycles-to-failure (Nf), and local strain determined via FE and a calibration curve. contexts.context: The excerpt describes how the Mullins effect in TPU under cyclic compression is quantified using an energy-ratio metric W4/W1 (fourth-cycle loading energy divided by first-cycle loading energy) following Rey et al. This metric (0 < W4/W1 ≤ 1) isolates Mullins-induced softening by negating residual-strain contributions and decoupling viscoelastic dissipation, with lower ratios indicating stronger Mullins softening from irreversible microstructural damage occurring during preconditioning. The authors use at least four loading cycles (compare first and fourth) as part of the cyclic protocol to capture preconditioning behavior. They also analyze hysteresis loss (ΔW/W) from loading–unloading loops to quantify energy dissipation, noting that in these CF/TPU systems the TPU matrix remains the dominant dissipation source, making hysteresis relatively insensitive to fiber content. Neat TPU shows ultra-low residual strain and near-perfect elastic recovery; adding fibers raises residual strain (due to chain disruption and localized damage) though residual stress remained below ~7% and overall elasticity remained good. These points inform cyclic testing protocols: perform multiple preconditioning cycles (≥4), track W1 vs W4 and hysteresis loop areas, and measure residual strain to distinguish Mullins softening from viscoelastic effects.

snippets: To characterize the evolution of the Mullins effect in polyurethane elastomers under cyclic compression, we adopt the energy ratio metric established by Rey et al., defining the ratio of fourth-cycle loading energy W4 to first-cycle loading energy W1 [40].
This approach isolates Mullins-induced damage by negating residual strain contributions and decoupling viscoelastic dissipation (Figure 11b).
The metric inherently satisfies 0 < W4/W1 ≤ 1, where lower values signify stronger Mullins softening, indicating greater irreversible microstructural damage during preconditioning.
The residual (Figure 10) strain (quantifying permanent deformation after unloading) exhibits a pronounced minimum at neat TPU [39], significantly lower than all other compositions.
This ultra-low value signifies near-perfect elastic recovery.
Hysteresis loss is the ratio of the energy dissipation ∆W generated during a loading and unloading cycle to the required energy W for loading [39].
As shown in Figure 11a, the apparent insensitivity of hysteresis loss to fiber content stems from the TPU matrix remaining the dominant dissipation source.

Similarly, the significant insensitivity of the first and fourth losses to fiber content in combination with hysteresis loss analysis is due to the fact that TPU matrix remains the main source of dissipation.
Although the residual stress only increased but remained below 7%, the material still exhibited good elasticity and low cyclic damage.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes compression/energy-absorption testing of 3D-printed polymeric lattice structures rather than tensegrity per se, but provides several relevant experimental details. Parts were printed in polyamide 12 (HP PA12) using Multi Jet Fusion on an HP Jet Fusion 4200. Lattices were built from 10 x 10 x 10 mm unit cells assembled into 5 x 5 x 5 lattices with a constant relative density of 15%. Six unit-cell topologies were studied (circular, octagonal, strengthened octagonal, Kelvin/tetrakaidecahedron, rhombicuboctahedron, cube) with circular struts. Material characterization included four tensile Type I specimens built and tested according to ASTM D638-14. Tensile tests were performed on an MTS Criterion Electromechanical Universal Test System (Model 43) with a 50 kN load cell and an optical extensometer at room temperature. The study used full-scale nonlinear FEA to simulate compressive behaviour and performed experimental compressive tests to validate the models, aiming to identify lattices with the highest specific energy absorption at the lowest transmitted stress. Impact strength of the specimens were found by using Charpy impact testing equipment (ASTM D6110).

compliance correction of the testing machine was performed according to ASTM D790.

The toughness U in the quasi-static compression tests was estimated as the area under obtained stress-strain curves.
The engineering stress in the cross section of specimens was evaluated as the ratio of the registered load to the initial area of the lattice core cross section ( A = Hb ).

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes porosity (and thus relative density) as the primary control on stiffness and strength for additively manufactured cellular materials. Experiment, CAD and µCT-derived FE models show a clear trend: stiffness increases as porosity decreases. Small porosity differences (~5% lower porosity in experimental samples versus µCT models) materially increase stiffness and yield strength, explaining why experimental 0.2% yield strengths (60–100 MPa) exceed CAD-as-designed predictions (20–30 MPa). The authors find tensile testing gives the most consistent Young’s modulus (smallest monotonic vs. cyclic differences) and therefore use tensile data and µCT-based FE models for comparisons. They note modeling choices (multi-linear isotropic material model and bulk material data) can slightly affect FE results but that porosity differences dominate. Failure locations depend on topology (cubic-regular: mid-strut; cubic-irregular: junctions and struts; trabecular: junctions), which can influence effective mechanical scaling. The manuscript states the next step is to apply the Gibson–Ashby model using Young’s modulus values from experimental, CAD and µCT sources to relate stiffness to relative density.

contexts.context: The excerpt defines nondimensional (relative) variables used in Gibson–Ashby scaling: relative density ρ* = ρlatt./ρsol., relative modulus E* = Elatt./Esol., and relative ultimate strength σU* = σUlatt./σUsol. Gibson and Ashby propose the semi-empirical scaling E* = C1 ρ*^m, where for open, bending-dominated cells (e.g. BCC) m = 2. The prefactor C1 “includes all of the geometric constants of proportionality” and therefore must subsume nearly all geometric information except relative density; the authors stress C1 depends on unit cell type, global shape, stress type and cell size. For strength and fracture properties, Gibson–Ashby relations also include cell-size dependence via a Weibull-like parameter mw: mw governs size sensitivity (e.g. mw = 6 implies cell-size independence for fracture toughness, mw > 6 gives toughness increasing with cell size). The excerpt cites an experimental example (Young’s modulus dropping from ≈306 to 241 MPa when cell size increased from 2 to 8 mm) and shows Table 1 listing unit cell widths and number of cells in gauge volumes—highlighting that reporting cell size and number of cells (or gauge dimensions) is important when comparing nondimensional stiffness across specimens.
