contexts.context: The excerpt reviews theoretical, semi-empirical, and numerical (FEM) approaches for predicting elastic properties of cellular solids and explicitly cites the Gibson–Ashby open-cell scaling as a commonly used result. It emphasizes that Young’s modulus and other properties can be cast as simple two-parameter relations in the low-density limit, and that deformation mechanism controls the density exponent: bending-dominated foams typically show a quadratic dependence of modulus on relative density, while stretch- or straight-through-strut geometries produce an approximately linear dependence. The prefactor (C) and exact exponent depend on microstructure, beam cross-section and connectivity; Poisson’s ratio and bulk behaviour can vary with orientation and model (e.g., tetrakaidecahedral models show near-incompressible behaviour at low density). The paper uses FEM on several statistical microstructure models to quantify finite-density effects, isotropic disorder, and to provide benchmarks for comparing experiments and theory. Normalizing stiffness by the solid-phase modulus and using relative density are the implied nondimensional parameters for comparing across different specimens and models.

contexts.context: The excerpt reviews the Gibson–Ashby (G&A) power-law for porous materials, expressing the effective Young’s modulus as a nondimensional ratio (E*/Es) that scales with relative density (rho*/rho_s) to a power n. It reiterates the classical interpretation that bending-dominated lattices follow a quadratic scaling (n ≈ 2) while stretching-dominated lattices scale linearly (n ≈ 1). The paper presents a modified scaling law for gyroid-based nanoporous materials that explicitly includes separate terms/constants accounting for bending and stretching contributions (i.e., a mixed-mode power-law form). Prior MD-based fits (Sun et al.) produced constants indicating comparable bending and stretching contributions for NP gold. The authors emphasize that at nanoscale the simple G&A assumption (properties independent of structural parameters) breaks down: ligament aspect ratio, node-to-ligament volume ratio, network connectivity, surface effects, and ligament length scales influence stiffness. The gyroid model shows a transition from bending-stretching to stretching-dominant behavior as relative density increases. These points support using nondimensional ratios (E*/Es, rho*/rho_s) while recognizing additional nondimensional geometry/size parameters (ligament aspect ratio, node geometry, surface-to-volume related terms) are needed to compare stiffness across specimen sizes and architectures.

contexts.context: The paper uses the standard Gibson–Ashby style scaling E/Es = C p^n (with p = ρ/ρs the reduced density) as a non-dimensional representation of stiffness. Es and ρs are the Young’s modulus and density of the solid skeleton, so stiffness and density are non-dimensionalized by the base solid properties. The constants C and n depend on microstructure; n typically lies between 1 and 4, with closed-cell foams often showing 1 < n < 2. Mechanisms map to exponents: edge-bending gives n = 2, cell-wall bending n = 3 (Gibson–Ashby), and cell-wall stretching n = 1; experimental and model disorder can shift effective n above the ideal periodic-model value (e.g., tetrakaidecahedral models give n ≈ 1, but disorder increases density dependence). The authors compute E and Poisson’s ratio for isotropic random models (Voronoi tessellations and level-cut Gaussian random fields) using FEM over scales ≈100 cells, and report FEM numerical errors ≲10%. For comparing specimens of different sizes or materials, use E/Es versus p = ρ/ρs and fit a power law E/Es = C p^n (typically in the low-density limit) to obtain size- and microstructure-independent non-dimensional stiffness.

contexts.context: The paper uses finite-element models of closed-cell cellular solids and describes stiffness scaling using the non-dimensional form E/Es = C(ρ/ρs)^n, which the authors also use to extrapolate beyond computational density limits. Exponent n depends strongly on microstructure: Voronoi tessellations gave n = 1.19, the closed-cell Gaussian random field (curved walls) gave n ≈ 1.5, and when >70% of cell faces are removed edge-bending dominates with n = 2. The semi-empirical closed-cell theory (plate-stretching plus edge-bending) was found inapplicable for the models studied, sometimes violating Hashin–Shtrikman bounds due to low edge fractions. Decomposition into simple bending (n=2) and stretching (n=1) components failed because mechanisms interact non-linearly; hence best represented by a non-integer power law. Results were obtained with νs = 0.2 and the Young’s modulus varies only ~2% for 0 < νs < 0.5, so solid Poisson’s ratio has little effect. FEM results have ~10% uncertainty from resolution. These points support using dimensionless ratios (E/Es, ρ/ρs) to compare specimens of different size and material, but C and n must be determined for the microstructure in question.

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on TPU in FFF and contains several points relevant to interface bonding, build orientation and interpreting mechanical tests. It notes that there is limited research specifically on interlayer and multi-material raster bonding in FFF TPU parts. TPU is viscoelastic and shows deformation recovery under cyclic loading; cyclic tests can exhibit hysteresis driven by polymer viscoelasticity and filler–matrix interactions, which can complicate interpretation of load–displacement curves (e.g., hysteresis, energy dissipation). Process factors affecting bonding and mechanical performance include infill percentage and pattern (higher infill increases stiffness/strength; concentric 20% showed VPF-like compression), air gap (reported as more important than raster angle/temperature for tensile strength), raster orientation (0° may be optimal in some studies), extrusion temperature (200 °C recommended in one study), and nozzle height (lower height increases packing density, reduces voids, and via a squeezing effect promotes molecular diffusion and bonding). Printing issues—filament buckling, moisture sensitivity, and filler-induced brittleness or irregular deposition—can reduce repeatability and impair interface quality. The excerpt does not discuss PETG or PETG–TPU interfaces specifically.

contexts.context: The excerpt summarizes PETG mechanical and processing characteristics that are relevant when considering PETG interfaces in FFF parts. Reported bulk properties include ultimate tensile strength of 25–54 MPa and Young’s modulus of 906–2280 MPa, with toughness and impact resistance higher than PLA but modest elongation. In printed parts, performance under bending and load is strongly influenced by internal architecture: "build orientation, infill pattern and density" and by interlayer phenomena such as "micro-delaminations and void deformation," meaning interfacial adhesion and deposition strategy critically affect joint strength. Processing windows that favor strong interlayer bonding are given: nozzle 215–235 °C, bed 70–90 °C, and moderate speeds (commonly 30–50 mm/s), plus careful retraction tuning to avoid stringing/oozing. PETG is hygroscopic; "absorbed water chemically attacks the polyester chains via hydrolysis," so filament drying is important to avoid covert loss of strength. Thermal limits are indicated by a Tg of ~67.5–77.3 °C, implying softening/creep risk near these temperatures. The excerpt does not discuss TPU, PETG–TPU multi-material bonding specifics, or methods for detecting joint failure or slippage in load–displacement curves.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that multi-material FFF parts show significant variation in impact and fracture behaviour depending on material pairing and print parameters. PETG's amorphous, ductile nature helps dissipate impact energy via plastic deformation and fibril pull-out, while combinations with more brittle polymers (e.g., PLA) produce hybrid fracture modes and accelerated crack propagation. Printing parameters matter: specimens with ID 100% and RA 90° showed roughly 35–60% higher impact strength than ID 50% and RA 45°, attributed to more uniform interlayer bonds and fewer internal voids. SEM observations revealed common interfacial problems in multimaterial prints—fibril pull-out, microcracks, interlayer gaps, separation zones, and delamination—especially where materials have incompatible thermal/melt behaviour or low surface energy, which favors interface failure and changes in crack path. When material combinations are poorly chosen, fractures often initiate at interfaces and reduce part integrity. These findings are relevant to PETG–TPU interfaces insofar as PETG's ductility and compatibility/melting behaviour, print orientation (raster angle), and infill-related interlayer contact will influence interface bonding and the likelihood of delamination or interfacial failure.

contexts.context: The excerpt introduces space-tilable tensegrity metamaterials that delocalize deformation by introducing discontinuities in their compression members. Architecturally, recursive reflections of a truncated-octahedron cell produce 2×2×2 supercells containing isolated compressive-member loops that do not form continuous load paths through a 6×6×6-cell metamaterial. Measured and simulated uniaxial compression responses show a compression discontinuity that prevents localized failure propagation and yields a homogeneous, delocalized deformation distribution. The authors report up to a 25-fold increase in deformability and orders-of-magnitude higher energy absorption without failure compared to same-strength state-of-the-art lattice architectures. The paper frames delocalization as a route to avoid system-level instability (identified by the first negative-stiffness event) that typically leads to catastrophic collapse in stretching-dominated lattices under load-controlled conditions. contexts.context: The excerpt describes tensegrity metamaterials designed to produce delocalized deformation, which yields distributed elastic stable buckling (reversible) rather than localized member failure, giving exceptional failure resistance and high energy absorption. Specimens were 3D-printed by two-photon polymerization (TPP-DLW) in IP-Dip (Nanoscribe) on fused silica. Quasi-static compression testing used full stress–strain characterization: E taken as maximum slope of the linear regime, σy from 0.2% offset, plateau strength σp averaged between 20–40% strain, and absorbed energy U as the integral of the stress–strain curve to densification or failure. Internal deformation maps were measured by DIC to quantify delocalization (ηd). Finite-element simulations (ABAQUS, modified RIKS) modeled 6×6×6 elementary-cell tensegrity, octet and iso trusses with small randomized imperfections and matched experimental dimensions; results were reported scale-independent and indicate translatability to metals. Numerically optimized tensegrity showed 3–18× (σ vs U) and 2–7× (E vs U) improvements versus first-order beam lattices, and experiments showed up to 5× higher σ–U combinations, demonstrating that tensegrity architectures outperform many beam-, shell- and hierarchical lightweight designs for reversible, high-energy-absorbing, failure-resistant compression behavior.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports experimental uniaxial compression testing on 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired modules. Tests were run in two series: the first screened AM technologies and parent materials; the second analyzed parent-material influence and scale effects. Three AM methods were evaluated (SLA, SLS, PolyJet); SLS was rejected for brittle material behavior. Modules corresponded to cells inscribed in cubes with edge lengths from 20 to 50 mm (limited by manufacturer capabilities). The authors emphasize that elongation at break of the parent material strongly affects sample ductility: higher elongation at break produces more ductile module response. Manufacturing inaccuracies substantially alter mechanical behaviour; the authors recommend printing extra samples to discard geometrically defective parts. Mean force–displacement curves with standard deviation (for module s3) demonstrate reproducible manufacturing. Observations highlight the need to allow free deformation consistent with the infinitesimal mechanism of tensegrity modules and note post-critical strut behaviour. Future work will target local strut stability and theoretical models with rigid joints. The excerpt cites Bauer et al. but contains no details on their delocalized-deformation/energy-absorption findings or explicit energy-absorption metrics for comparison.

contexts.context: The authors fabricated space-tileable 3D tensegrity metamaterials by recursively reflecting truncated-octahedron elementary cells and 3D-printed them using two-photon polymerization direct laser writing (TPP-DLW). Cells contain tensile members along edges and isolated compressive members inside, satisfying tensegrity topology. Specimens (6×6×6 cells) covered relative densities of 4–12%; truss members were square bars with ≈950 nm edge length and cell sizes 10–20 µm. Mechanical testing used displacement-controlled uniaxial compression with in situ imaging and digital image correlation (DIC) to map local deformation (map element areas a relative to a0). Compared with octet and Kelvin lattices, the tensegrity showed highly uniform, strain-independent deformation and no detectable localized damage up to at least 30% strain. The tensegrity exhibited a fully stable, monotonic stress–strain response with a smooth, elongated post-yield plateau and densification above ε ≈ 62.5%. By contrast, the octet underwent localized damage and system instability at ε ≈ 2.6% and its delocalization efficiency ηd fell to 35%; the Kelvin foam localized above ε ≈ 17% with ηd dropping to 67%. The tensegrity maintained ηd > 90% throughout, linking delocalized deformation to improved energy absorption and failure resistance.

contexts.context: The excerpt cites Bauer et al. (2021) on tensegrity metamaterials but does not report their experimental results. Instead, it provides finite-element simulation and quasi-static compression methodology used for 3D-printed lattice specimens that may be applicable to compression testing of tensegrity systems. The authors used ANSYS Transient Structural in quasi-static mode with geometric nonlinearity, added small fillets at strut intersections sized to 3D-printing resolution (50 µm) to ensure mesh-independent results, and applied local mesh refinement in fillet zones. Element types were TET10 and HEX20. Specimens were placed between two rigid plates with a friction coefficient of 0.2; a plasticity model with isotropic hardening was used. Simulations ran to a mean compressive strain of ε = 0.15 (plate displacement = 0.15 of initial height). They evaluated stress triaxiality (σh/σe) to assess hydrostatic vs. deviatoric stress states, noting high positive triaxiality indicates propensity for brittle fracture. Data are stated to be included in the manuscript and SI. The excerpt therefore offers testing/simulation protocol details but not Bauer et al.'s specific compression results.

contexts.context: The authors fabricated tensegrity, octet and Kelvin lattice specimens by two-photon polymerization direct laser writing (TPP-DLW) using IP-Dip polymer. Specimens (6×6×6 cells) were printed at 10 µm s−1, with bars hatched from seven print lines; laser power and hatching distance were tuned (7.275–8.625 mW, 60–90 nm) to produce square-shaped bar cross sections. Post-processing included PGMEA and isopropanol baths and critical-point drying. Relative densities from ≈4% to 12% were achieved by changing elementary cell size (tensegrity cell sizes 18.1–10.6 µm for ≈4–12% density). SEM characterization measured member cross-section heights and widths (tensegrity ~1047 ± 86 nm by 832 ± 14 nm; octet ~1113 ± 40 by 847 ± 25 nm). The tensegrity geometry was parametrically optimized (tensile/compressive member edge lengths set to 1300 and 450 nm) to maximize strength, stiffness and absorbed strain energy while holding density constant. Finite-element simulations used a nonlinear material model representative of IP-Dip. Mechanical testing: uniaxial in situ compression inside an SEM/FIB chamber with an Alemnis nanoindenter at a constant strain rate of 0.01 s−1.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports monotonic compressive testing and finite-element simulations comparing 3D-printed tensegrity lattices to octet and Kelvin continuous-compression architectures at matched density/strength (notably 4% relative density). Experiments and simulations show tensegrity lattices exhibit delocalized deformation, stable stress–strain responses, and greatly enhanced damage resistance: the tensegrity retained load-bearing capacity up to densification (ε = 62.5%), and at εc = 70% the octet had only 7% of its initial stiffness versus 70% for the tensegrity. Although the octet’s initial stiffness/strength were higher (≈14× and 9×), tensegrity absorbed far more energy before failure (≈13× vs octet and ≈2× vs Kelvin in experiments). Strain energy U was computed as the area under stress–strain curves up to failure/densification. Simulations reproduced experiments, showed localization and unstable stress drops in octet/Kelvin, and enabled numerical optimization of tensile/compressive member cross-sections to double tensegrity performance and further increase absorbed energy (up to 26× and 4× vs octet/Kelvin; down to very low densities predicted energy-absorption gains up to 225×). Fabrication used TPP-DLW polymer printing for 2–5% relative density samples.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports uniaxial compression testing of 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired single-cell modules carried out in two series. The first series screened additive-manufacturing methods and parent materials: SLA, SLS and PolyJet were evaluated and SLS was rejected because the material was brittle. The second series examined parent-material influence and scale effects using four module sizes (inscribed in cubes 20–50 mm edge). Results include mean force–displacement curves with standard deviations (Fig. 10) showing manufacturing reproducibility for modules s3. Key findings: parent-material elongation-at-break strongly affects ductile vs brittle behaviour; geometric/production defects significantly degrade mechanical response; ensuring free deformation consistent with the infinitesimal mechanism is crucial to observe tensegrity behaviour; post-critical buckling/behaviour of struts was observed. Limitations: tested modules are medium-scale due to manufacturing/test constraints (real metamaterials would be micro/nano scale). Recommendations include producing extra samples to discard defective prints and future work on local strut stability and theoretical models including rigid joints, plus testing other module types and larger supercells/lattices.

contexts.context: This interlaboratory study of ASTM E9 compression testing reports key points relevant to measuring elastic modulus and yield strength in compression. Participants commonly used extensometers attached to the specimen; using diametrically opposed extensometers (vs a single extensometer) substantially improved precision. The authors reanalyzed modulus from stress–strain data with a technique that selects an optimal fit range and applies quality checks, and they found modulus error increases markedly when the fit range drops below about 40% of the stress range. ASTM E9 includes requirements for calibrating and qualifying the testing machine and extensometers and for aligning fixtures/specimens, but the standard does not require an extensometer in contact with the specimen—many implementations instead infer strain from actuator displacement. The study also found that whether specimen ends were lubricated affected measured yield and modulus values, and a finite-element analysis could not fully explain that discrepancy. The report’s results were incorporated into E9’s precision/bias statement (2009).

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a reanalysis of compression stress-strain curves (per ASTM E111) to obtain consistent elastic modulus values (EGA) using a Scibetta–Schuurmans based nine-step procedure. Laboratories often used ASTM E83 Class B-2 extensometers, and E9 Section 9.2 permits B-2 when yield strength is primary; ASTM E111 would require a Class B-1 for modulus as the primary parameter. The nine steps include: locating the knee of the curve (points e1 at s1 = 0.05 max(s), eo=e1 with so=0.2 max(s), and finding (et,st) tangent through (eo,so)); truncating and normalizing data at (et,st); checking digital resolution (with a rule that no more than 25% of points should have zero change); applying the Scibetta–Schuurmans algorithm to find the optimal fit window (considering all subsets with at least 20% of data and selecting lowest residual std. dev.); checking noise (standard error in strain or stress ≤ 0.01); extending the fit to include points within one standard error; refitting to get EGA; checking residual curvature (slope in outer quartiles ≤ 0.05) and ensuring the optimal fit stress range > 0.4st. Quality metrics are defined for digital resolution, noise, curvature, and fit range. The accepted aluminum modulus used for error assessment was EaccAl = 75.2 GPa and the absolute error is defined as ∆EGA = |EaccAl − EGA|.

contexts.context: This interlaboratory compression study followed ASTM E9 and required fixture qualification per E9 Section 6.6. Participants used at least one extensometer (gauge lengths reported in Table 3, e.g. G = 25.4 mm or 12.7 mm), ran tests at a nominal strain rate of 0.005 min−1, and intentionally did not report strain from actuator displacement. Laboratories used a variety of fixturing/alignment approaches (sub-presses, precision-ground sub-presses, adjustable platens, two-opposed extensometers) to control alignment and reduce fixturing effects. Electronic stress-strain traces were collected and returned. For ‘toe’ correction the organizers (or analysts) shifted each stress-strain curve along the strain axis so that a linear fit to the stress-strain data in the range 50–175 MPa intercepted the origin — effectively removing initial offset before determining modulus. These details imply recommended practice for tangent/secant modulus determination: use extensometer-measured strain (not actuator displacement), collect high-resolution stress-strain traces, qualify fixtures per E9, control alignment (sub-press/precision platens), and apply a linear-fit-based toe correction over an appropriate stress range prior to modulus extraction. The excerpt does not provide a step-by-step machine compliance correction protocol, but fixture qualification and avoidance of actuator-displacement strain measurement are emphasized.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe ASTM E111 toe-correction algorithms or a machine/frame compliance correction protocol directly, but it provides relevant observations about factors that affect measured modulus and yield on compression stress–strain data. Labs that used two-opposed extensometers reported modulus values closest to the accepted value; two extensometers "will tend to average the effect of non-axial loading" and reduce bias from bending. By contrast, single-extensometer setups often produced lab means systematically above or below the grand average, implicating compression-fixture alignment rather than specimen machining as the source of non-axiality. The fixed geometric relation between extensometer and loading fixturing can cause consistent over- or under-estimation of strain when bending is present. Lubrication of specimen ends also affected results: unlubricated labs reported average YS ~10.6 MPa (3.1%) lower and E ~4.1 GPa (5.7%) smaller. The paper also supplies standard definitions and formulas for repeatability (within-lab) and reproducibility (between-lab) standard deviations (sr, sR) and coefficients of variation, useful for quantifying variability before/after any toe or compliance corrections. Overall, the text supports using dual extensometers, careful alignment and lubrication control and statistical characterization, but does not give toe-correction or load-frame compliance procedures.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that accurate strain measurement is essential to determine modulus (E), elongation and other mechanical properties. It warns that using crosshead displacement (displacement sensor divided by gauge length) is the least accurate because the integrated displacement sensor cannot distinguish sample deformation from load-frame distortion; that distortion depends on the geometry and stiffness of both the test frame and the sample. This underscores the need to account for machine compliance when determining elastic moduli. Alternative measurement options discussed include bonded strain gauges (limited to small strains and single use), clip-on extensometers ("substantially more accurate and precise than bonded foil gauges" and reusable, but may distort small samples or be damaged), and non-contact digital image methods (DIC) which allow the camera to be separated from the specimen and map strain fields but are sensitive to optical issues. The excerpt also cites ASTM E8M strain-rate recommendations for tensile testing and provides true-compression conversions (σ0 = -σ(1-ε) and ε0 = -ln(1-ε)). The text does not give ASTM E111-specific tangent/secant modulus procedures, a toe-correction algorithm for compression curves, or a step-by-step machine compliance correction protocol, but it provides the measurement-method and correction context relevant to implementing those procedures (i.e., use of local extensometry or DIC to avoid frame compliance errors and conversion to true stress/strain for compression).

contexts.context: This excerpt (ASTM E9 compression interlaboratory study) discusses procedures and quality metrics for estimating elastic modulus from compression stress–strain curves. It recommends checking curvature by examining residual slope in the outer quartiles: if that slope exceeds 5% of the optimal-region slope the fit is excessive. More importantly, the size of the final fit range (Rf) is the strongest predictor of modulus quality; a minimum Rf ≥ 0.4 (40% of the elastic-region stress range) is used, and tests with Rf < 0.4 show ≈2.5× larger mean modulus error (4.88 vs. 1.95 GPa). Linear regression showed no relation between residual-slope magnitude and modulus error. For strain measurement, using two diametrically opposed extensometers can improve precision by over two times. The study also reports repeatability and reproducibility for yield strength measured per ASTM E9 (~1.1% and ~2.0% of the mean, respectively). These points inform fit selection, fit-range limits, and extensometer practice for reliable modulus estimation in compression testing, though the excerpt does not describe ASTM E111-specific tangent/secant definitions, toe-correction, or machine compliance correction protocols.

snippets: If the slope of the residuals vs. strain in the outer quartiles is greater than 5 % of the slope in the optimal region, the curvature of the fit is deemed excessive.
All but one of the tests fall inside the ±5 % limits.
Figure 20 plots the absolute modulus error, Eq. 10, against the fraction of the range of original stress data. The dashed line is the boundary of the minimum acceptable limit Rf ≥0.4.
The absolute modulus error, Eq. 10, increases as the size of the fit region decreases, as expected, and the boundary between the two regions lies at the chosen final fit range minimum Rf = 0.4.
The mean error for tests with fit region Rf < 0.4 is 2.5 times larger (4.88 GPa vs. 1.95 GPa) than that from the acceptable region.

Of the quality metrics, the size of the final fit range is the best predictor of overall quality of the modulus measurement, and the level chosen, Rf ≥0.4, is a good metric for identifying potential problems with modulus measurement.
Using two diametrally opposed extensometers instead of a single extensometer can improve the precision of the strain measurement by more than two times, Figure 10
The repeatability of yield strength determined from compression tests conducted according to ASTM E9 can be expected to be about 1.1 % of the mean value, cvr= 0.011 , Figure 6 and Table 5.
The reproducibility of yield strength determined from compression tests conducted according to ASTM E9 can be expected to be about 2 % of the mean value, cvR= 0.020 , Figure 6 and Table 5.
In addition, linear regression of the absolute modulus error against the absolute value of the residual slope reveals no relationship.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We are kicking off the **first round of Instron stiffness tests** for a
multi-material 3D-printed *tensegrity-inspired* unit-cell program (BYU
Mentored Research Grant; PIs Hill & Baird; repo
``vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization``; tracking issue #49). The
overall campaign is a closed-loop **design -> print -> test -> Bayesian
optimization** workflow targeting energy-absorption / cushioning
applications (impact-protective gear, packaging, planetary-lander egg-drop
analog). Initial tests are *quasi-static* on an Instron-class screw-driven
load frame; later phases add drop-weight impact and (potentially) wave
propagation.

**Specimens (initial batch):**
* Architecture: Snelson-class 3-bar / 6-bar tensegrity prisms and
  tensegrity-inspired truncated-octa / icosa unit cells, single cell and
  small (2x2x2) tilings. Bounding cube ~25-50 mm, mass ~5-30 g.
* Materials: rigid struts in **PETG** (E ~= 2 GPa, sigma_b ~= 50 MPa,
  rho ~= 1.27 g/cc) — also PLA as a baseline; tension elements in **TPU 85A**
  (NinjaFlex-class, secant E ~= 12 MPa, sigma_b ~= 26 MPa, strain-to-break
  ~600 %, rho ~= 1.20 g/cc). Co-printed multi-material on a Bambu H2D dual-
  toolhead FFF system (0.4 mm nozzle, layer 0.2 mm, 3-perimeter min on TPU
  tendons -> minimum tendon Ø 1.2 mm, strut Ø ≥ 2.0 mm).
* Joinery between PETG and TPU follows the joint-design study in this repo
  (anchor-bulb / dovetail / TPU-rebar variants); peer-reviewed PETG–TPU
  interface strength data does **not** exist, so joint integrity is itself
  an experimental unknown.

**What we want from this query (be specific and prescriptive):**

1. **Applicable ASTM / ISO standards** for stiffness characterization of
   this exact specimen class.  For each, please give the standard number,
   title, what it actually measures, sample-geometry requirements,
   strain-rate / crosshead-speed requirements, and the *gap* between the
   standard and our 3D-printed cellular tensegrity-inspired specimens (i.e.
   what we have to adapt or report as a deviation).  Please cover at minimum:
     * **Bulk plastic compression** (ASTM D695, ISO 604) — for PETG/PLA
       coupons that bracket the strut material;
     * **Cellular / cushioning compression** (ASTM D1621, ASTM D3574,
       ASTM D7726, ASTM F1614, ASTM D575/ISO 7743 for rubber-like cells) —
       these are the closest analogs to a tensegrity unit cell;
     * **Sandwich-core / lattice compression** (ASTM C365, ASTM C297) for
       through-thickness modulus of repeating unit cells;
     * **Polymer tension** (ASTM D638, ISO 527) and **elastomer tension**
       (ASTM D412, ISO 37) for material-card coupons of PETG and TPU 85A
       (FFF-printed, with build-orientation reporting per ASTM F2971 / ISO/ASTM
       52921 / 52900);
     * **Additive-manufacturing-specific** standards: **ISO/ASTM 52900,
       52902, 52921, 52939, 52941**, and any newly-issued ASTM F42 work
       items addressing stiffness / energy-absorption testing of
       AM lattice / cellular parts.
   Please flag which of these are *normative* (must follow) vs.
   *informative* (good practice) for a peer-reviewed AM-tensegrity paper at
   ASME JMD / IDETC level, and give the most-cited published examples that
   followed each standard for a similar geometry/material.

2. **Best practices / pitfalls** for the actual Instron test.  Specifically:
     * Crosshead speed and strain rate (and how to report them — true
       vs. nominal, gauge length, machine-compliance correction).
     * Platen choice (flat, spherically seated, lubricated, anti-friction
       film, parallelism tolerance) and how it affects measured *initial*
       stiffness of soft-cell specimens.
     * **Machine compliance correction** — protocol for measuring the load-
       string compliance and subtracting it from the specimen
       displacement.  This is *critical* at low loads where TPU tendons
       dominate.  Please cite the canonical references.
     * Preload / contact-find protocol; toe-region removal per ASTM E111.
     * Use of a non-contact extensometer (DIC / video) vs. crosshead
       displacement for sub-mm compliance regimes.
     * Conditioning: **Mullins effect** in TPU — number of preconditioning

## 2. Best Practices / Pitfalls for the Actual Instron Test

### 2.1 Crosshead Speed and Strain Rate
A crosshead speed of **1 mm/min** is the most common quasi-static rate for lattice/cellular compression in the published analog set (raghavendra2021uniaxialstaticmechanical pages 5-7, solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11, sabounizawadzka2024experimentalinvestigationson pages 6-11). For a 25–50 mm specimen this yields a nominal strain rate of 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ to 6.7 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Report both the commanded crosshead speed and the nominal engineering strain rate (crosshead speed / initial specimen height). If using DIC-derived local strain, report that separately. Bates et al. (2016) tested TPU honeycombs at higher strain rates (0.03–0.3 s⁻¹), which is relevant for later energy-absorption studies but not first-round stiffness (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 7-10).

### 2.2 Platen Choice
Use **flat, hardened steel platens** per ASTM E9 fixture practice (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11, potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 6-11). Consider PTFE anti-friction film between platen and specimen if barreling or friction-induced stiffening is suspected; keep the choice fixed within a batch. The NIST interlaboratory study found that lubrication vs. no lubrication changed measured modulus by approximately 5.7% and yield strength by 3.1% in metal compression (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 18-21). For tensegrity cells where the top face may not be flat, a **thin compliant shim** (silicone sheet, ~1 mm) can improve contact uniformity, but this must be documented and the shim compliance subtracted. Spherically-seated platens are an option for alignment but introduce a rotational degree of freedom that may activate the tensegrity mechanism prematurely; use with caution and document.

### 2.3 Machine Compliance Correction
This is **critical** for sub-mm deformations of soft cellular specimens. Crosshead displacement includes load-string compliance (load cell, platens, couplings) that cannot be distinguished from specimen deformation without correction (biesiekierski2020mechanicaltestingof pages 13-16). The recommended protocol:
1. Run a platen-to-platen (no specimen) compression to the expected peak load, recording force vs. crosshead displacement.
2. Fit a linear compliance curve C_machine = Δδ/ΔF (mm/N).
3. Subtract C_machine × F(t) from the measured crosshead displacement at each time point.
4. Alternatively, and preferably, use a **non-contact extensometer** (DIC or video gauge) to measure specimen deformation directly, bypassing compliance entirely.

Solyaev et al. (2023) performed compliance correction per ASTM D790 and noted it was important for accurate modulus extraction from lattice tests on an Instron 5969 (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11). The NIST study found that actuator-displacement-based stress was ~1.4% higher than extensometer-based measures even after correction (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 21-24). For your TPU-dominated specimens at low loads, compliance errors can exceed 50% of apparent deformation; DIC or a clip-on displacement transducer on the platens is strongly recommended.

### 2.4 Preload / Contact-Find and Toe Correction
Apply a preload of **0.5–1.0 N** at a slow approach speed (0.5 mm/min) to establish contact (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 6-11). Zero the displacement reference at this preload. For toe-region removal, the NIST ASTM E9 study shifted stress-strain curves so that a linear fit in the range 50–175 MPa (for aluminum) intercepted the origin (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 6-11). For your low-force polymeric cells, apply an analogous procedure: identify the initial linear region of the force-displacement curve, extend the linear fit back to zero force, and shift the displacement origin accordingly, per the intent of ASTM E111 (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 29-34, potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 24-26).

### 2.5 Non-Contact Extensometry
Bates et al. (2016) used a **video gauge with speckle-pattern markers** on the compression platens to verify crosshead-derived positional measurements (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 7-10). Pahari (2024) applied **2D DIC** with simultaneous front and side imaging to detect interfacial strain concentrations in multi-material FFF parts (pahari2024analysisofthe pages 65-70). For your specimens, a camera-based approach is ideal: apply speckle or fiducial markers to the top and bottom platens (or directly on the specimen if it has a flat PETG face) and compute the relative displacement at ≥10 Hz. This eliminates frame compliance from the stiffness calculation and provides strain-field data useful for detecting joint slip.

### 2.6 Conditioning: Mullins Effect in TPU
TPU exhibits a complex cyclic response that differs from classical Mullins softening in crosslinked rubbers. Scetta et al. (2021) demonstrated that soft TPU shows large hysteresis on the first load-unload cycle, pronounced softening after the first loading, marked residual deformation, and — importantly — a **stiffening** effect (not just softening) under step-cyclic loading at strains above ~1.5 Hencky strain, attributed to hard-domain fragmentation and additional physical crosslinking (scetta2021straininducedstrengthening pages 6-12, scetta2021straininducedstrengthening pages 1-6, scetta2021straininducedstrengthening pages 12-17). Holzweber et al. (2018) explicitly applied "pre-cycles to avoid the Mullins- or softening effect" and noted that hysteresis decreases with increasing cycle count (holzweber2018characterizationandmodeling pages 4-6). Zhou et al. (2025) used an energy-ratio metric W₄/W₁ (fourth-cycle loading energy over first-cycle) to quantify Mullins-related softening, with lower ratios indicating stronger preconditioning damage (zhou2025enhancingtheenergy pages 12-15).

**Recommendation:** Run **5 preconditioning cycles** to 5% nominal strain at 1 mm/min with 30 s pause between cycles. Compare the loading stiffness of cycles 1 and 5 to quantify conditioning magnitude. Report W₅/W₁ and note any irreversible residual strain. Do not precondition to more than 5% strain on a stiffness test — larger strains risk activating tensegrity buckling mechanisms that should be reserved for the energy-absorption campaign.

**Humidity:** PETG is hygroscopic — "absorbed water chemically attacks the polyester chains via hydrolysis" (lesniowski2025enhancingtheperformance pages 16-18). TPU is also moisture-sensitive, with absorbed moisture affecting melt viscosity and mechanical properties (lopes2024interfaceboundarymechanical pages 33-37). **Dry all filaments** before printing (60°C for PETG, 50°C for TPU, 4+ h) and condition finished specimens at 23 ± 2°C, 50 ± 5% RH for ≥48 h before testing (zhang20213dprintingof pages 44-52).

### 2.7 Definition of "Stiffness" to Report
Report at minimum:
- **Structural stiffness k** = dF/dδ (N/mm) — the tangent of the force-displacement curve in the initial linear region after toe correction. Specify the displacement or strain window used (e.g., 1–5% nominal strain).
- **Secant structural stiffness** k_sec at a specified strain level (e.g., at 5% strain) — useful for comparing specimens with different toe-region behaviors.
- **Effective modulus** E_eff = k × h₀ / A₀ (MPa), where h₀ is the initial specimen height and A₀ is the projected bounding-box cross-sectional area. This is an apparent material-like property; it is not a true material modulus but is useful for comparison.
- **Non-dimensionalized relative modulus** E*/E_s = E_eff / E_solid and **relative density** ρ*/ρ_s = (mass / bounding volume) / ρ_solid, plotted in Gibson-Ashby fashion.

For the Gibson-Ashby framework, the canonical scaling is E*/E_s = C₁(ρ*/ρ_s)^n, where n ≈ 2 for bending-dominated open-cell structures and n ≈ 1 for stretching-dominated architectures (maskery2015mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-4, roberts2002elasticpropertiesof pages 3-6, maskery2017aninvestigationinto pages 1-3, roberts2001elasticmoduliof pages 1-3). The prefactor C₁ "includes all of the geometric constants of proportionality" and depends on unit-cell topology, cell size, stress type, and global shape (maskery2015mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-4). Tensegrity structures involve a mix of tension (stretching in tendons) and compression (strut buckling), so expect n between 1 and 2; fitting n from your data is itself a scientific contribution.

Bauer et al. (2021) defined E as the maximum slope of the linear regime, σ_y from a 0.2% offset, plateau stress σ_p averaged between 20–40% strain, and absorbed energy U as the integral of stress-strain to densification (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 7-8). This reporting framework is directly applicable to your later energy-absorption tests.

### 2.8 Replicates and Statistics
**Minimum n = 5** replicates per design variant for stiffness. Report mean ± SD and 95% CI. The ASTM E9 interlaboratory study found within-lab repeatability of ~1.1% CV and between-lab reproducibility of ~2.0% CV for yield strength of well-machined metal specimens (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 26-29); for FFF cellular parts expect substantially higher variability (5–15% CV). Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski (2024) tested groups of seven and reported mean curves with standard deviation bands (sabounizawadzka2024experimentalinvestigationson pages 6-11); this is a good minimum. Produce extra samples to discard obviously defective prints (sabounizawadzka2024experimentalinvestigationsona pages 11-13). For later failure-related quantities (strength, SEA), report Weibull parameters if the dataset is large enough (≥15 specimens).

### 2.9 Build-Parameter Documentation per ASTM F2971 / ISO/ASTM 52921
For each specimen, record and report: build orientation (Z-up vs. XY-flat, per ISO/ASTM 52921 coordinate system), layer height (0.2 mm), nozzle diameter (0.4 mm), number of perimeters (≥3 for TPU tendons), infill pattern and density (100% for structural members), raster angle, nozzle temperature (by material), bed temperature, print speed, and any post-processing (none for initial tests) (daglı2025mechanicalcharacterizationand pages 4-7, lesniowski2025enhancingtheperformance pages 16-18). This information is normative for peer review and essential for the BO loop.

## 4. Stiffness-Specific vs. Strength/Energy-Absorption Test Design

The issue title is *stiffness testing*, and the differences from energy-absorption testing are critical:

| Parameter | Stiffness Test (current) | Energy-Absorption Test (later) |
|---|---|---|
| **Load limit** | 15–20% nominal strain (well below densification) | Full densification (60–80% strain) or until failure |
| **Strain window for metric extraction** | 1–5% strain for tangent stiffness; 0–10% for secant | Full curve: plateau stress (20–40% strain), densification onset, area under curve |
| **Preconditioning** | 5 cycles to 5% strain; establishes stable baseline | May include 5 cycles to full target strain; Mullins damage is intentional and itself a metric |
| **Replicate count** | n ≥ 5 per design; focus on precision of mean stiffness | n ≥ 5 for mean SEA; n ≥ 15 for Weibull failure statistics |
| **Reportable metrics** | k_tangent, k_secant, E_effective, E*/E_s, hysteresis ratio | Peak F, plateau σ, SEA (J/g), volumetric EA (J/cm³), compaction efficiency η, transmitted force |
| **Specimen reuse** | Specimen should be reusable (no damage at 15–20% strain) | Specimen may be consumed / damaged |

**Recommendation:** Measure stiffness in a **separate dedicated test campaign** rather than extracting it exclusively from the loading branch of energy-absorption tests. Reasons: (a) stiffness is sensitive to toe-region artifacts that are less critical for EA integral calculations; (b) the low-strain regime is where machine compliance errors are largest; (c) preconditioning for stiffness should be limited to small strains to avoid Mullins-altered response; (d) dedicated stiffness tests preserve specimens for potential re-testing or microscopy. However, also extract the **unloading tangent stiffness** from the first unloading cycle of EA tests (analogous to ISO 13314's cyclic unloading method) as a secondary stiffness metric for cross-validation (raghavendra2021uniaxialstaticmechanical pages 5-7, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 7-8).

## 5. Multi-Material FFF-Specific Considerations for Stiffness Data Quality

### 5.1 Layer-Stack Orientation Effect
FFF parts are inherently anisotropic. For PETG, tensile properties are strongest along the raster direction and weakest across layers (Z-direction), with modulus reductions of 15–40% reported for Z-built vs. XY-built specimens depending on material and parameters (lesniowski2025enhancingtheperformance pages 16-18, daglı2025mechanicalcharacterizationand pages 4-7). **Recommendation:** Test struts printed in at least two orientations — (a) struts parallel to build direction (Z) and (b) struts perpendicular to build direction (XY) — using standalone coupon tests per ASTM D695/D638. For the full tensegrity cell, document the build orientation of the complete assembly and note which strut axis is closest to the build Z-axis.

### 5.2 PETG–TPU Interface Integrity and Joint-Slippage Detection
Multi-material FFF interfaces are weak zones. Arifvianto et al. (2022) found that PLA/TPU interfaces showed poor adhesion with torn/delaminated regions and TPU fibers lying over PLA rather than bonding (arifvianto2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 6-8). Dağlı (2025) reported SEM-observed microcracks, interlayer gaps, and delamination at multi-material boundaries, with fractures often initiating at interfaces (daglı2025mechanicalcharacterizationand pages 11-14). PETG–TPU peer-reviewed interface strength data does not exist in the literature surveyed.

**How to detect joint slippage in load-displacement data:**
- **Sudden force drops** (>10% at constant displacement rate) that are not associated with visible buckling indicate joint failure (daglı2025mechanicalcharacterizationand pages 11-14, arifvianto2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 6-8).
- **Slope changes** in the loading curve that cannot be attributed to known geometric nonlinearity (e.g., tensegrity mechanism engagement) may indicate progressive slip.
- **DIC** at the interface region is the most reliable detection method. Pahari (2024) demonstrated 2D DIC with simultaneous front and side imaging to capture heterogeneous deformation at multi-material boundaries in FFF parts (pahari2024analysisofthe pages 65-70).
- **Post-test inspection** of joint regions under magnification (10×–20× stereo microscope) looking for whitening, necking, gap opening, or fibrillation.

### 5.3 Mass / Dimensional Check Protocol
- Mass: 0.01 g precision balance; average two readings.
- Dimensions: digital calipers, 0.01 mm resolution; measure height and two orthogonal widths at three locations each and report mean ± range.
- If available, CT or structured-light scan to compare as-built vs. CAD geometry and compute actual relative density. Raghavendra et al. (2021) used µCT to quantify morphological deviations and found ~5% lower porosity in built vs. designed specimens, which materially affected stiffness predictions (raghavendra2021uniaxialstaticmechanical pages 13-17).

### 5.4 Aging / Batch Effects and Control Specimens
Print a batch of **control specimens** (a single, simple design variant — e.g., 3-bar prism in PETG+TPU) at the start of the campaign. Retest one control specimen every N = 10 test specimens (or once per test session, whichever is more frequent) to monitor for:
- Machine drift (load-cell calibration shift, platen wear).
- Material aging (PETG hydrolysis, TPU moisture uptake, UV exposure if stored near windows).
- Print-batch variability (filament lot, nozzle wear).

Track control-specimen stiffness on a control chart. If the control shifts by >2σ from the initial baseline, halt testing and investigate. This matches the campaign protocol described in the `idetc-abstract.tex` framework.

- The closest tensegrity architecture analogs (Bauer et al. 2021; Pajunen et al. 2019; Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski 2024) used single-material prints (IP-Dip polymer, PA2200, or PolyJet resins) rather than multi-material FFF (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 3-4, sabounizawadzka2024experimentalinvestigationson pages 6-11).
- The closest material/process analogs (Bates et al. 2016; Arifvianto et al. 2022) tested TPU or PLA/TPU multi-material but not tensegrity architectures (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 4-7, arifvianto2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 6-8).
- Notably, **none of the tensegrity papers cited a named ASTM/ISO compression standard** — they all used custom compression protocols. This is a gap your paper can address by explicitly citing ASTM D1621 or C365 (adapted) and disclosing deviations.

---

## 7. Equipment-Specific Recommendations

### 7.1 Load Cell Selection
Your available 5 kN load cell is appropriate but may be at the upper limit. For tensegrity specimens of 5–30 g at 15–20% strain, expected peak forces will be in the range of approximately 1–200 N (based on Pajunen et al.'s initial stiffness of ~10–48 kPa for ~48 mm specimens giving forces of ~10–50 N, and your stiffer PETG struts potentially reaching higher values) (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 3-4, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 4-5). The Instron 5 kN cell has accuracy ±0.5% down to 1/1000 of capacity (per Solyaev et al. on the 5969 platform), meaning ±0.025 N at 5 N and ±2.5 N at 500 N (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11). At forces below ~5 N, the signal-to-noise ratio will be poor. If you find that peak forces consistently fall below 50 N, consider requesting or borrowing a **500 N or 1 kN load cell** for better resolution in the tendon-dominated low-strain regime. Bates et al. (2016) used a 1 kN load cell on an Instron 3343 for TPU honeycombs, which is a good precedent for soft cellular specimens (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 7-10).

### 7.2 Load-Cell Verification
Verify the load cell per **ASTM E4** (Force Verification for Testing Machines) before beginning the campaign. The standard requires verification at ≥5 points across the range and ±1% accuracy for Class A verification.

### 7.3 Data-Acquisition Rate
Acquire at **≥10 Hz** for quasi-static tests at 1 mm/min (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 7-10). Solyaev et al. (2023) used 2.5 kHz on an Instron 5969 (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11); Raghavendra et al. (2021) used 1 kHz (raghavendra2021uniaxialstaticmechanical pages 5-7). Higher rates are beneficial for capturing any sudden events (joint slip, strut snap) but generate larger files. A practical recommendation is **50–100 Hz** — high enough to resolve transient events without excessive data volume.

### 7.4 Instron Platform Notes
- **Instron 5965** (5 kN maximum): Excellent choice if available; matched to your expected force range.
- **Instron 5969** (50 kN maximum): Workable but the 5 kN cell operates in the lower end of the frame capacity. Solyaev et al. (2023) successfully used this platform with a 50 kN cell for polymer lattices (solyaev2023improvedmechanicalperformance pages 11-11), but your forces will be much lower.
- **ElectroPuls E3000** (3 kN dynamic): Better suited for later cyclic/fatigue work or if you need precise displacement control at low forces. Pahari (2024) used this platform for interface shear tests (pahari2024analysisofthe pages 65-70).
- **MTS Insight**: Comparable to the Instron 59xx series; follow the same protocols.

---

## 8. Open Questions / Things the Lab Should Decide Before the First Test

1. **Platen interface:** Bare steel, PTFE film, or compliant shim? Run a quick pilot (3 specimens, one condition) comparing bare vs. PTFE before committing to a batch protocol.

2. **Preload threshold:** 0.5 N or 1.0 N? For very soft TPU-dominated cells, even 0.5 N may cause measurable deformation. Start with 0.5 N and verify it produces a clean toe-to-linear transition.

3. **Strain limit for stiffness test:** 15% or 20%? Test one sacrificial specimen to full densification to identify where the tensegrity mechanism engages (buckling plateau onset) and set the stiffness-test limit well below that transition.

4. **DIC availability:** Can a camera be set up to view the specimen during loading? Even a smartphone at 30 fps with fiducial markers provides useful backup displacement data. If a proper DIC system (e.g., GOM, VIC-2D, or open-source ncorr) is available, use it from day one.

5. **Load-cell swap:** Will a smaller load cell (500 N or 1 kN) be available or borrowable? If so, it is worth running a comparison test to quantify resolution improvement.

6. **Control-specimen design:** Finalize which single design variant serves as the batch control. Ideally choose the simplest cell (3-bar prism) with the most robust joints, so control-specimen failures are informative rather than routine.

7. **Joint-type priority for first batch:** The repo mentions anchor-bulb, dovetail, and TPU-rebar joint variants. Decide whether the first test batch sweeps all three joint types or fixes one and sweeps architecture.

8. **Temperature and humidity logging:** Is a lab datalogger running continuously? If not, record ambient temperature and humidity at the start and end of each test session. Both PETG and TPU are sensitive to moisture (lesniowski2025enhancingtheperformance pages 16-18, lopes2024interfaceboundarymechanical pages 33-37).

9. **Filament drying protocol and verification:** Confirm that PETG and TPU filaments are dried before printing. PETG dries at 60–65°C for 4+ h; TPU at 50°C for 4+ h. Print a test specimen immediately after drying to establish the baseline.

10. **Post-test specimen disposition:** Will tested stiffness specimens be retained for later energy-absorption tests (possible if undamaged at 15–20% strain), or dedicated only to stiffness? Retaining them allows paired stiffness → EA data on the same specimen, which strengthens the BO surrogate model.

11. **Strain-window definition for k_tangent:** Fix the strain window (e.g., 1–5%, or 2–8%) before batch testing so that all specimens are compared on the same basis. The Scibetta-Schuurmans algorithm used in the NIST E9 study recommends that the fit range cover at least 40% of the elastic-region stress range for reliable modulus estimation (potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 24-26, potts2010repeatabilityandreproducibility pages 26-29).

12. **Compression direction for tensegrity prisms:** Define whether loading is axial (along the prism axis) or transverse. For Snelson-class 3-bar prisms, axial loading activates the tensegrity mechanism; transverse may collapse joints differently. Document and fix the loading direction per design family.

info.query:
We are kicking off the **first round of Instron stiffness tests** for a
multi-material 3D-printed *tensegrity-inspired* unit-cell program (BYU
Mentored Research Grant; PIs Hill & Baird; repo
``vertical-cloud-lab/tensegrity-optimization``; tracking issue #49). The
overall campaign is a closed-loop **design -> print -> test -> Bayesian
optimization** workflow targeting energy-absorption / cushioning
applications (impact-protective gear, packaging, planetary-lander egg-drop
analog). Initial tests are *quasi-static* on an Instron-class screw-driven
load frame; later phases add drop-weight impact and (potentially) wave
propagation.

**Specimens (initial batch):**
* Architecture: Snelson-class 3-bar / 6-bar tensegrity prisms and
  tensegrity-inspired truncated-octa / icosa unit cells, single cell and
  small (2x2x2) tilings. Bounding cube ~25-50 mm, mass ~5-30 g.
